articles.title: Fidelity’s $500,000 crypto settlement leaves IRAs outside wallet-transfer terms
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Fidelity’s $500,000 settlement requires written notice if retail crypto transfers end, while preserving restrictions for security.
- Fidelity Crypto IRAs are excluded from the transfer obligations, and the product remains unavailable in California and Oregon.
- California customers already had ordinary transfers by June 2025; the agreement’s planned IRA launch still has no stated date.
Fidelity Digital Assets’ $500,000 settlement with California adds a written-notice commitment if it stops offering ordinary retail crypto transfers. Tax-advantaged accounts, including individual retirement accounts, remain outside the agreement’s transfer obligations.
Attorney General Rob Bonta announced the deal Oct. 16 over allegations about past withdrawal restrictions at Fidelity Digital Asset Services. The settling entity, Fidelity Digital Assets, National Association, is its successor. Fidelity denies wrongdoing and entered the agreement without admitting a violation of law.
The company agreed to pay the attorney general $500,000 in recognition of investigation-related fees and costs and to settle the released potential claims. The agreement specifies no customer compensation fund.
The agreement describes a period from November 2022 through April 2025 when California retail customers could buy and sell crypto but could not transfer it directly off the platform. Regulatory permission came in April 2025, and the transfer feature reached all California customers by June 2025.
The settlement recognizes that existing ability to transfer crypto to external wallets, subject to applicable law. If Fidelity decides to stop offering transfers as a feature for retail customers, it must give its California customers reasonable written notice.
Fidelity can still restrict or disallow transfers to protect its platform or individual account holders.
Fidelity’s state-availability page, checked Oct. 18, continues to list crypto deposits and withdrawals for ordinary Fidelity Crypto accounts in California.
IRAs retain separate access rules
The agreement says Fidelity plans to launch Fidelity Crypto IRA accounts in California, without specifying a launch date. It also expressly excludes the covered tax-advantaged accounts from its transfer obligation, including IRAs and accounts subject to federal requirements for nontaxable transfers between retirement accounts.
Fidelity’s current IRA FAQ says the product remains unavailable in California and Oregon.
Where Fidelity Crypto IRAs are offered, the FAQ says crypto transfers are unavailable and customers cannot withdraw money or crypto directly from the account. Instead, they can move money from its U.S. dollar position to the linked Fidelity brokerage IRA and use that account’s withdrawal features.
See CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin IRA comparison for other retirement-account providers.

articles.title: Zcash’s planned Sprout freeze would leave private keys unable to move funds
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Zcash's proposed NU7 rules would leave remaining Sprout funds unspendable on the upgraded network, even with intact private keys.
- Mainnet activation remains undecided, with an October 20 decision planned and November 5 still a conditional target.
- Sprout exits expose amounts, while recovery can require days of scanning and no future spending mechanism is guaranteed.
Zcash's proposed NU7 upgrade would close the spending route out of its oldest privacy pool, Sprout, which still held about 22,309 ZEC on Oct. 17. Holders could keep their private keys and still lose the ability to move those funds on the upgraded network.
Mainnet activation remains undecided. The NU7 deployment specification leaves the activation height unassigned, with a final decision planned for Oct. 20 after testnet experience. Nov. 5 remains the target, conditional on that decision.
The zkp.baby dashboard recorded 22,309.44195128 ZEC in Sprout at block 3,521,260, updated at 19:10:09 UTC on Oct. 17.
The change is set out in ZIP 2003, a Zcash improvement proposal whose listed owner is Daira-Emma Hopwood. It proposes rejecting version 4 transactions from NU7 onward. Sprout transfers require that format; neither version 5 nor version 6 supports them.
A private key authorizes a spend, but the network must also accept the transaction carrying it. Under the proposed rules, Sprout holders would have no supported format in which to exercise that authority.
The restriction reaches every version 4 transaction, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions. The consequences differ by pool. Users can recreate non-Sprout transactions in a supported format where possible. Sprout has no equivalent replacement. Merely re-signing a version 4 transaction cannot fix its invalid format, and even newer formats need signatures appropriate to the consensus branch.
ZIP 2003 explicitly leaves Sprout's remaining balance in issued supply. It allows the theoretical possibility of re-enabling version 4 transactions or creating another retrieval facility, while warning that spending may never be restored.
Recovery takes work, and exiting exposes amounts
Moving to current wallet software does not necessarily move the coins. Zallet's migration documentation explicitly excludes Sprout spending keys and funds from its import process and tells users to preserve their original wallet.dat.
The Argos recovery tool documents a route for holders with a legacy wallet file or standalone Sprout spending keys. A wallet containing usable note data and a cached witness can avoid a historical scan. With a key alone, recovery may require reconstructing the additional data needed to build a valid spend.
For that full-block scan, Argos estimates roughly 280 GB of transfer and potentially days of processing, while retaining less than 500 MB on disk.
Argos also documents a specific destination: its Sprout sweeps land in Sapling, a newer shielded pool, including when a Unified Address is supplied. Moving the recovered funds onward is a separate operation.
Exiting carries a privacy trade-off as well as fees and recovery work. ZIP 308's migration design explains that Sprout-to-Sapling value passes through public pool accounting, exposing the amount without requiring a transparent address.
In the Sprout-to-Sapling scheme specified by ZIP 308, transaction timing is coordinated and amounts are randomized to reduce the chance that individual transactions can be linked. ZIP 2003 warns that a short or poorly coordinated exit period can make distinctive amounts and timing easier to associate with holders.
The security benefit is shared, while the migration burden falls on individual holders.
Hopwood's proposal gives a concrete reason to remove Sprout's spending path. Its specialized verification and handling of private notes and spent-note identifiers still add work to live transaction acceptance despite little use. Verification costs also matter for denial-of-service exposure in pending-transaction and block processing.
Some protections are already shared with newer systems. Sprout uses cryptographic components also used by Sapling, and pool accounting checks limit potential balance violations. The proposal argues that these safeguards still leave Sprout-specific complexity to maintain. Retirement would reduce that burden for implementations validating the network.
The direction has a history. ZIP 211 stopped new value entering Sprout while preserving the ability to extract existing funds. ZIP 2003, created on Oct. 31, 2024, would take the further step of closing spending under NU7.
A mainnet decision still lies ahead
Testnet implementation is already running. The Zcash Foundation announced Zebra 7.0.0-rc.0 on Oct. 2, scheduling NU7 at testnet height 4,465,026 around Oct. 6. An Oct. 10 engineering reply confirmed that testnet had passed activation.
The September coordination announcement, posted by the forum account ebfull, reported agreement among ecosystem organizations and engineering teams after polling and discussions. CryptoSlate's earlier poll coverage described the coinholder result as advisory.
Zcash's upgrade mechanism makes activation depend on a specified block height. For NU7, ZIP 259 also waives the usual recommendation of roughly three months after the first supporting release and the requirement tied to deprecation of unsupported software. It warns that unsupported software may remain online and follow pre-NU7 rules. Operators need compatible software to validate the upgraded network.
A community recovery thread published Sept. 20 adds to the public notice history. The decision planned for Oct. 20 is the next concrete signal. Approval and an assigned mainnet height would establish an operational cutoff. Sprout holders would need to confirm a valid migration before that height.

articles.title: Crypto doesn’t need your party to win, just its candidates
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Six House candidates are slated for $1 million each in outside support.
- Bipartisan backing gives crypto relationships across competing congressional coalitions.
- The most important thing is what the next bill permits, requires, and leaves out, rather than how many supported candidates win.
The crypto industry has finally found a way to participate in America's partisan warfare without committing to either of the (only) two available parties: help elect people who agree with it about crypto, then let them argue about everything else.
Fairshake's latest House spending plans cover 32 candidates, with 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats on the list. Six are slated for $1 million each in support, while the amounts for the other races haven't been disclosed, according to the AP.
The Super PAC is essentially giving both parties a reason to keep crypto on its policy agenda no matter what voters decide about who controls Congress.
Nothing wrong with that. Since the dawn of time, companies whose businesses depend on financial law have wanted a say in what that law looks like.
Their owners, investors, and ultimately their customers expect them to defend the business, and the people doing the defending would rather have friends than foes writing the rules.
The crypto industry has grown so much that dozens of crypto companies in the US can and want to defend their business with the same strength and money as their much larger tradfi counterparts. And seeing how crypto is largely politically ambiguous, these companies can attack both fronts with the same amount of strength.
They invest almost equally in Democratic and Republican candidates, from local municipal contests to Congressional elections.
They can defend their donations any way the wind turns: Democrats can make their involvement in crypto regulation sound like tightening the reins on evil capitalist corporations, while Republicans can make it look like they're liberating hard-working Americans from the shackles of government-controlled money.
Crypto companies don't really care what it looks or sounds like; they just want to reap tangible legislative crops from the seeds they've sown.
But Fairshake is a federal independent expenditure-only committee, which means it can only finance political activity outside candidates' campaigns, under rules that specifically prohibit coordination.
So when we hear that it announced $1 million in support for a candidate, it doesn't mean it just gave them a million in cash.
Your party is your business, your crypto vote is ours
Republicans French Hill, Bryan Steil, and Bill Huizenga are among the six candidates receiving the disclosed $1 million commitments. Hill chairs House Financial Services, Steil chairs its digital-assets subcommittee, and Huizenga is the full committee's vice chair.
The three Democrats are Janelle Bynum, Steven Horsford, and Derek Tran, Roll Call reported.
The selection of Republican candidates puts money behind people that already have significant influence over financial legislation. The Democratic donation rewards members of the coalition that voted for the industry's largest and most consequential bill: the CLARITY Act.
In July 2025, the House passed CLARITY 294–134, with 216 Republicans and 78 Democrats voting yes. Every voting Republican supported it, while Democrats split.
That's why backing Democrats who crossed that divide tells other Democrats that there can be electoral help (i.e., money) on the other side of a pro-crypto vote. Backing the Republican committee leadership just protects relationships with the people already doing the legislative work.
While Fairshake's political spending is and has to be transparent, the motivations behind each candidate's support for crypto never are. There are a million reasons why a politician would support the crypto industry, so we can't assume any of the candidates were bought with the donations. Donors usually choose allies who already agree with them or at least somewhat agree.
The money just creates a pretty good incentive for other politicians who might be on the verge of supporting actually to jump ship.
In a hypothetical race, suppose an outside group spends heavily to advertise your campaign while your opponent has to buy the same airtime with their own money. Your campaign can then devote more of its own money elsewhere.
The assistance is valuable even if you never helped write the advertisement, and even if the advertisement discusses local jobs. In this example, the outside group helps pay for the politician's general public image while pursuing a much narrower policy goal.
Buying allies is easier than passing a bill
Crypto companies are right when they complain about doing business under rules that leave basic classifications unsettled. The industry needs to know which regulator it answers to, what registrations and licenses require, when software creates obligations, and which disclosures it must provide, to name a few.
The fact that we need more laws is one of the few things Republicans and Democrats actually agree on. However, they usually don't agree on what those laws should include.
So the wording of a proposed bill matters more than the bill's existence, because every word assigns costs, permissions, and consequences to somebody.
Both parties align themselves with grand, abstract goals like reducing government interference and defending consumers. But when it comes to legislation, both have to deal with the petty and trivial: titles, subtitles, chapters, subchapters, sections, subsections, paragraphs, subparagraphs, and clauses.
Their preferred campaign language still has to translate into an enforceable rule, complete with costs somebody will pay.
The bills also have to address officials profiting from business affected by their public decisions. Roll Call reported that disputes over ethics provisions helped prevent agreement on CLARITY before the Senate blocked its advancement last month.
Senators still had to agree on those provisions, regardless of the size of the House coalition.
The commercial desire for predictable rules is therefore compatible with a political desire to scrutinize the rules. Companies can both be right about the cost of uncertainty and self-interested about the solution.
Lawmakers can oppose a weak provision without declaring war on every American who owns Bitcoin. The public shouldn't have to choose between endorsing the whole industry package and returning to regulation by litigation.
Shared donors, competing obligations
Supporting both parties is sensible insurance when neither can promise permanent control. It also lets an entire industry build relationships within each coalition, including with lawmakers who may disagree on taxation or immigration but share a view on financial regulation.
Voters tend to choose representatives that align with their broad views about how their city/district/state/country should be governed. Industries, on the other hand, are laser-focused. They don't care where a candidate falls on the political compass, just how big and fast an impact they can have on crypto legislation.
Issue-based political spending builds that asymmetry. Someone voting on housing costs may help elect a candidate whose expensive campaign was financed by companies focused on an exchange-registration provision the voter has never heard of.
Crypto companies are entitled to make their argument, including when they identify an actual defect in financial regulation.
Their interests also need to be weighed against those of everyone else using an open blockchain. What a large exchange wants from a law can differ from what an individual developer needs. So can the priorities of a token issuer and a customer who wants to understand what happens to their money in bankruptcy.
Everyone should be at least a little skeptical here. Republicans shouldn't get automatic credit for financial freedom because donors like their bill. Democrats shouldn't get automatic credit for consumer protection because they dislike the donors.
Read the obligations each side proposes, and ask yourself which companies gain permission, which users gain recourse, and who pays to comply.
Fairshake will count its electoral victories in November.
Customers will have to judge what those victories produce when Congress next takes up the rules. Friendly lawmakers give the industry access to that process, but customers will get their rights from the resulting text, long after the applause has stopped.

articles.title: Two Aave stablecoin backstops shrank $12.4 million as reward rates rose
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Aave’s tracked Ethereum V3 Umbrella USDC and USDT stakes fell $12.43 million between the September 17 and October 17 observations.
- Capital multiplied by displayed extra rates implied about $1.994 million annualized at each endpoint, separate from realized spending.
- Umbrella stakes cover deficits in their own asset and network, with a DAO-funded offset before stakers absorb losses.
Aave’s two tracked Ethereum V3 stablecoin backstops shrank by $12.4 million between Sept. 17 and Oct. 17 even as their extra reward rates increased. Together, the USDC and USDT positions held $116.09 million at the later observation, down 9.67% from $128.52 million.
The positions belong to Umbrella, Aave’s system for using staked assets to absorb lending deficits. Participants keep earning underlying lending yield and receive additional rewards for accepting the possibility that their stakes will be used to cover losses.
The figures measure dollar-valued stakes. Their movement includes asset valuation as well as changes in the amount deposited, so a decline in the balance alone cannot identify withdrawals or losses.
Multiplying each position’s tracked dollar value by its displayed extra reward rate implies approximately $1.994 million annualized at both endpoints. A richer percentage rate coincided with less tracked protection capital, while that indicative aggregate reward amount barely moved.
DefiLlama’s USDC history records a decline from $58,739,617 to $53,437,993. Its USDT history shows a fall from $69,783,937 to $62,655,694. Those are reductions of $5.30 million and $7.13 million, respectively, adding to $12,429,867.
Both comparisons use the Sept. 17 observation at 23:01 UTC and the Oct. 17 observation at 15:01 UTC, in 2026. The timestamps are slightly less than 30 days apart. The percentages below are the additional reward component displayed for those observations.
| Ethereum V3 Umbrella stake | Capital, Sept. 17 | Capital, Oct. 17 | Extra reward rate, Sept. 17 | Extra reward rate, Oct. 17 | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| USDC | $58,739,617 | $53,437,993 | 1.66% | 1.82% | 
| USDT | $69,783,937 | $62,655,694 | 1.46% | 1.63% | 
The tracked positions are wrapped-aToken Umbrella stakes on Ethereum V3. DefiLlama identifies them as stkwaEthUSDC.v1 and stkwaEthUSDT.v1; their token identities match the current Aave address book.
The USDC extra rate increased by 0.16 percentage points and the USDT rate by 0.17 points. Lending yield moved separately: USDC’s base rate rose from about 3.60% to 3.77%, while USDT’s increased from about 3.02% to 3.12%. The base component reflects the lending return. The extra component compensates for staking and slashing risk; only that component belongs in this safety-incentive calculation.
How the reward rate can rise
For each observation, the calculation is the tracked dollar value multiplied by the displayed extra reward percentage, divided by 100, then summed across the two stakes.
Using the September values gives $1,993,923.12 annualized. Using the October values gives $1,993,859.28. Both round to $1.994 million.
These amounts are indicative annualized run rates derived from snapshots. Actual accrual and payments depend on the path of rates, stake values, reward configuration and participation over time.
Umbrella’s reward-controller documentation explains a mechanism through which the percentage rate can rise without a larger aggregate distribution. Its emission curve relates the amount of rewards distributed to the amount staked relative to a configured target.
Aggregate emissions reach their maximum at the target. Between the target and 120% of target, emissions decline toward 80% of that maximum. At or above the 120% boundary, aggregate emissions are flat. In that region, fewer stakes can share the same reward stream, increasing the rate per unit of capital.
Below target, the curve boosts rewards per unit to encourage participation, while aggregate emissions remain below their peak. The plateau provides one way for a smaller denominator to receive a higher percentage rate. Establishing whether it applied to these pools at both observations would require matched contract settings and balances; the histories alone leave that specific explanation unresolved.
A Sept. 25 proposal from TokenLogic sought to renew the allowances used to pay Umbrella rewards while leaving emission rates, target liquidity, cooldown parameters, deficit offsets and the Dec. 2, 2026 distribution end unchanged.
The proposed allowances covered rewards already accrued but unclaimed, including amounts owed to former stakers, plus remaining emissions through that distribution end. They replaced the remaining allowances. Reading those amounts as a fresh annual incentive budget would therefore combine past obligations with prospective payments.
What the smaller balances say about protection
Aave’s documentation confines staking risk to the relevant asset and network: USDC stake covers USDC deficits, while USDT stake serves its own reserve. The combined total measures the scale of the two positions. Each reserve’s protection depends on its own allocated stake.
Slashing follows a realized reserve deficit that exceeds the applicable deficit offset. LlamaRisk’s coverage explanation describes that offset as a DAO-funded first-loss layer before Umbrella stake is used.
The exit rules also matter to stakers weighing the extra return. Aave documents a 20-day cooldown followed by a two-day withdrawal window. Rewards keep accruing during cooldown, and the stake remains exposed to slashing while the holder waits.
The DefiLlama adapter values provider-reported total assets using an associated price. Wrapped aTokens have an exchange rate, so valuation is part of the measured balance.
The distinction also applies to Aave’s separate V4 coverage plans. CryptoSlate’s September reporting on the V4 proposal concerned proposed targets for different protection modules. Those targets concern different protection modules from the observed V3 balances.
At the October observation, the extra rates were higher and the two tracked balances were smaller. The incentive offer and the capital accompanying it had moved in opposite directions.

articles.title: Richard Heart Caught ‘Off-Guard,’ QDay Gets Even Closer: Hodler’s Digest
articles.text:
Richard Heart caught ‘off-guard,’ QDay gets even closer: Hodler’s Digest
HEX founder Richard Heart detained in early morning raid in Istanbul, Starknet plunges almost 50% as it votes to become an L1, and Bitwise says all signs point to Crypto Spring.
HEX erases $246 million in market cap after founder detained in Turkey
The HEX market cap fell from $561 million to $315 million this week after founder Richard Schueler — better known to the crypto community as Richard Heart — was detained by authorities in Istanbul on October 14.
Police seized $7.15 million in cash along with firearms and ammunition during an early morning raid in Istanbul’s Beşiktaş district, alongside searches of 15 related addresses according to Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek.
Police impounded nine luxury vehicles registered to Schueler’s wife according to news agency Anadolu. The haul reportedly included 28 watches, 300 bags and 19 graphics cards.
Interpol issued a “Red Notice” for Schueler’s two years ago over allegations of tax fraud and assault, after Finnish authorities sought his arrest.
A spokesperson for Finland’s National Bureau of Investigations declined to comment on the matter.
Turkish media refer to Schueler as “Whale James” and have linked him to a $1 billion unregistered securities offering in the US. However that case was dismissed by a US judge in February 2025.
Images circulating in Turkish media appear to show a surprised Heart with no trousers on, and the bottom half of his body blurred out, provoking much merriment on social media. Vocal Hex critic Eric Wall, who has debated Schueler on video and social media, said he initially thought the image was AI generated but now believes it is real:
“i’m pretty much certain i died in a plane crash in 2015 and ever since that day i am still only alive in a fringe reality where everything is designed to be as funny as possible.”
Hex supporters claim that authorities are yet to confirm if Schueler has been formally arrested or charged.
Images circulating on Turkish media.
Ledger’s answer to wallet tampering costs $849 and ships next year
Ledger unveiled a new device on Thursday with stronger protections against tampering, days after confirming that wallets sold through a reseller in Asia contained malicious implants.
The French hardware wallet maker introduced Atom, an $849 device that combines a crypto wallet with everyday apps through a smartphone-like design. Atom separates Android apps from sensitive wallet operations and includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the recent Asia incident. It claims to detect tampering even when switched off.
Expected to become available in summer 2027, Atom will also support AI agent approvals, encrypted messaging and post-quantum cryptography.
Meanwhile a war of words has broken out between former Mt Gox CEO Mark Karpeles, and Ledger CEO Pascal Gauthier. Kapeles claims that at least two people notified Leger of spyware discovered inside  tampered Ledgers as far back as December 2025 — and notes the company had even written about the issue on its website in March 2026. He says the company failed to act properly to secure its reseller supply chains, which have now been suspended across Asia after more than $90 million was stolen.
Gauthier snarkily replied on X that Karpeles was “no white knight” and referred back to his failures in the lead up to the Mt Gox hack. 
Karpeles replied: 
“I was hoping you guys were better than that. I’ve been holding Ledger at a higher standard than what happened at MtGox, because I trusted you to do better by learning of my failure — to be better than me.”
QDay gets even closer as Starknet votes on becoming post quantum L1
Google has demonstrated a new process called “magic state cultivation” on its Willow quantum processor that reduces errors 40-fold. The technique achieved a record 99.99% accuracy rate for a specialized quantum state required to perform advanced calculations.
Meanwhile Theta Labs has posted three news quantum circuits that could reduce the number of qubits required to break elliptic curve cryptography by 28% from Google’s current estimate of 1,175 logical qubits.
With fears that AI is now getting so good at math that it may be able to break elliptic curve cryptography even before QDay arrives, Starknet has opened a vote to transform itself from an Ethereum L2 into a post quantum L1. StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson says that Ethereum’s post quantum roadmap may be too slow to meet the challenge from AI, meaning that Starknet needed to consider becoming a fully post quantum L1.
“Quantum-proofing crypto is urgent, so we must move at lightning speed,” he told Cointelegraph. More than 99% of votes cast to date are in favor of the move. Starknet’s token has lost almost 50% in value this week, after a big surge last week.
Standard Chartered pushes $2T stablecoin forecast to 2030 as EU embraces USDC
Standard Chartered says stablecoin transaction activity continues to grow even as the market’s overall value has stalled, suggesting existing stablecoins are circulating more frequently rather than new supply driving growth.
The bank said it now expects stablecoin market capitalization to reach $2 trillion by 2030, two years later than initially projected, after the market plateaued at roughly $309 billion this year.
Meanwhile the European Banking Authority has classified Circle’s USDC stablecoin as a significant e-money token under the region’s Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) framework. The classification has only been granted to 45 projects. 
Binance.US seeks $1B valuation in potential $100M funding round
Binance.US reportedly seeks to raise up to $100 million in a funding round that could value the cryptocurrency exchange at $1 billion.
According to a Thursday Bloomberg report, the US-based crypto exchange is pursuing private investment as it looks to expand its business. The potential $1 billion valuation would be well below the $4.5 billion pre-money valuation it secured in 2022, when it raised $200 million in seed funding.
Winners and Losers
At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 3.8% to trade at $81,484, Ethereum (ETH) is down 5.7% to trade at $2,386 and XRP (XRP) is down 8.3% to $1.28. The total market cap is at $2.72 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.
Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Monero (XMR) with a 9.7% gain, Injective (INJ) on 5.6%, and Celestia (TIA) on 5.1%.
The top three altcoin losers of the week are Starknet (STRK) which was down 46.7%, Pump.fun (PUMP) down 27.1% and Raydium (RAY) down 26.5%.
Prediction of the Week
Bitwise’s Hougan says Q3 charts point to ‘crypto spring’
Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan says Q3 may have been “one of the best quarters in crypto’s history,” arguing a sharp rebound in crypto prices and growing onchain markets point to the start of “crypto spring.”
In its quarterly market review published Thursday, Bitwise reported a 46.4% quarterly gain in its large-cap crypto index, along with $6 billion in US spot Bitcoin ETF inflows that brought year-to-date net flows back into positive territory.
“Page after page after page, it’s all the same: The most recent part of the chart is turning sharply upwards,” Hougan wrote. “That’s exactly what you want to see if you’re looking for the start of a crypto spring.”
Top FUD of the Week
MSCI adopts index exclusion rules that could oust Strategy
Index provider MSCI has adopted new rules that could lead to Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi being removed from its global indexes, while leaving several other crypto treasury companies facing potential exclusion.
In August, Strategy opposed the changes but also played down the potential disruption, saying funds tracking MSCI’s Global Investable Market Indexes hold approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding. The company said those holdings amount to less than one day’s trading volume.
Russia to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trades starting July 2027
Russia will ban direct peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency transactions between individuals starting next year, requiring individuals to use authorized intermediaries for such trades.
The regulator said the ban would come into place on July 1, 2027.
The regulator also clarified that individuals are not allowed to transfer crypto assets from their digital accounts to their own non-custodial, or self-custodial, wallets.
Ex-Trump crypto adviser profited after helping pass stablecoin bill: WSJ
Bo Hines, previously a crypto adviser to US President Donald Trump who later joined stablecoin issuer Tether, reportedly kept a stake in a company that profited from the passage of a stablecoin bill when he was still at the White House.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Hines had a one-third stake in the investment company he co-founded, Nxum, while pushing US lawmakers to pass the GENIUS Act. Nxum reportedly received $6.3 million as part of a deal with stablecoin issuer Tether, with the first payment going through while Hines was still serving in government.

articles.title: JUST Completes 5th JST Buyback & Burn: Over 170M Tokens (~$23.53M) Burned Ahead of Major Deflationary Upgrade
articles.text:
On October 17, JUST, the leading DeFi infrastructure in the TRON ecosystem, announced the completion of its fifth buyback and burn of its native token JST as scheduled. Over 170M JST were burned in this round (approx. 1.72% of total supply), backed by nearly $23.53M in capital deployed—all funded directly by JustLend DAO's net operating revenue.
Over the past five rounds, a total of 1.88B JST tokens have been burned, driving the cumulative deflation rate past 19% with over $100M revenue deployed.
JST has reached a key operational milestone following this latest burn: the remaining 70% of JustLend DAO's initial treasury reserves has been fully deployed according to the original plan. This marks the successful completion of the first phase , paving the way for a major mechanism upgrade.
170M+ Tokens (~$23.53M) Burned in JST's Fifth Buyback Round
According to the official announcement released, the fifth JST buyback and burn was successfully completed. As a routine buyback for Q3 2026, a total of 170,723,144 JST tokens (approx. 170M) were burned, representing about 1.72% of the total token supply, with a total value exceeding $23.53M.
Maintaining similar levels of burn scale and capital investment to the previous four rounds, this burn round continues the stable, predictable execution cadence of JST buybacks and burns.
Looking further into the source of funds, the funds invested in this buyback and burn came entirely from JustLend DAO's net operating income, specifically composed of two parts: the remaining $10.34M from JustLend DAO's existing income and the $9.28M QoQ increase in Q3's net income.
In terms of quarterly revenue performance, JustLend DAO's Q3 net income remained steady compared to previous quarters. With quarterly earnings consistently anchored at the eight-figure ($10M+) level, the ecosystem's core revenue streams continue to prove their resilience.
At the same time, deploying the remaining 70% of the initial revenue reserve means that the early-stage treasury reserve plan has officially reached its conclusion—setting the stage for a brand-new phase of the buyback program.
One Year, Five Burns: JST's Price Soars 300% with $100M Deployed from JustLend DAO's Revenue
From its launch in October 2025 to the fifth round on October 16, 2026, the JST buyback and burn mechanism has completed one full year of operation across five consecutive burn rounds. A total of approximately 1.881B JST tokens have been burned, representing a cumulative deflation rate of > 19% with more than $100M deployed from JustLend's revenue.
A breakdown of the five buyback and burn executions is as follows:
- Round 1 (October 19, 2025): Burned ~559M JST (~5.66% of total supply), with ~$17.72M deployed.
- Round 2 (January 14, 2026): Burned ~525M JST (~5.3% of total supply), with ~$21M deployed.
- Round 3 (April 15, 2026): Burned ~271M JST (~2.74% of total supply), with ~$21.3M deployed.
- Round 4 (July 17, 2026): Burned a total of ~355M JST (~3.59% of total supply), with ~$34.59M deployed. In addition to the routine quarterly buyback, this round incorporated dedicated burn funds from USDJ's historical stability fees (~$10.39M) for the first time.
- Round 5 (October 16, 2026): Burned ~170M JST (~1.72% of total supply), with ~$23.53M deployed.
In terms of operational intensity, the execution of five consecutive rounds in a single year—averaging roughly $20M per round, with over $100M committed from real protocol earnings and nearly one-fifth of the total token supply burned—places JST among a select tier of buyback programs rarely seen in the DeFi sector.
This continuous execution has transformed the buyback from a series of short-term news catalysts into a permanent value engine. Rather than acting as an isolated marketing tactic, the program transmits its impact systematically through a five-pillar chain: Capital Foundation—Execution Assurance—Transparency & Trust—Deflationary Scarcity—Market Feedback, cementing a durable foundation for long-term valuation.
On the capital foundation, JST buybacks rely directly on authentic business cash flows. Except for the historical USDJ stability fee allocation in Round 4, every dollar of the $100M+ deployed across all five rounds originated directly from JustLend DAO's organic operating earnings.
In execution assurance, both capital scale and operational cadence have been uncompromisingly delivered. Single-round commitments began at $17.72M in Round 1, stabilized around $20M thereafter, and reached $34.59M in Round 4. Throughout all five quarters, every burn landed strictly on schedule—free from delays, disruptions, or arbitrary cuts.
For transparency and trust, every buyback follows the standard procedure of “pre-disclosed rules, on-schedule execution, and verifiable on-chain proof”, backed by immutable on-chain transaction records and open official disclosures.
In deflationary impact, around 1.881B JST tokens have been burned across five rounds, contracting total supply from 9.9B down to ~8.02B—a nearly 19% reduction that continuously compounds structural scarcity.
Ultimately, market feedback validates the mechanism through synchronized gains in both token price and market cap. CoinGecko data shows JST climbing steadily from its ~$0.03 low in October 2025 to an October 10 peak of $0.142—a 300%+ year-to-date surge marking a new high since 2022—while circulating market cap surged past $1B.
This closed-loop flywheel—fueled by authentic revenue, reliable execution, complete transparency, structural deflation, and market validation—has elevated the buyback program far beyond short-term hype, solidifying it as the central pillar sustaining JST's long-term economic value.
Buyback Mechanism Poised for Comprehensive Upgrade as Capital Sources Diversify
With five consecutive rounds now complete, the JST buyback program arrives at a watershed moment: the first phase officially concludes, setting the stage for a new upgraded phase.
Looking back at the initial phase, the framework was initially structured to draw backing jointly from JustLend DAO and USDD. Under the original terms, USDD's cross-chain ecosystem revenue was to feed into the buyback pool once cumulative earnings hit $10M—a threshold not yet reached. Consequently, this early phase operated primarily on JustLend DAO's accumulated treasury reserves alongside the increment in quarterly net revenue. Specifically, the $59M+ reserve earmarked at inception under the plan of “30% upfront, 70% in phased tranches” has now been fully deployed across five rounds. This signifies that the initial phase has smoothly achieved its objectives, clearing the path for the comprehensive upgrade.
As outlined in the JST Q1 2026 financial report released in April, the upgraded JST buyback mechanism will broaden capital sources beyond the existing framework by incorporating revenues from new business streams such as GasFree, providing deeper and more diversified funding for ongoing buybacks.
With the upgraded phase around the corner, JST's long-term deflationary momentum and value-return capabilities are poised to enter an even more sustainable and predictable cycle. For specific plans regarding capital allocation, execution cadence, and ecosystem integrations under this upgraded mechanism, follow JUST's official X account @JUST_DAO for the latest updates.
JUST Team
Singapore
media@just.network

articles.title: SEC approves Coinbase earnings bets that stay settled when the numbers change
articles.text:
Quick Take
- The SEC approved rules for Cboe contracts on Coinbase trading volume and MARA Bitcoin production.
- A restatement after expiration and settlement leaves the amount paid or unpaid unchanged, preserving the contract's resolved outcome.
- Missing figures can delay processing or trigger alternative settlement, while specific series availability and Robinhood eligibility remain unconfirmed.
The SEC approved rules allowing options exchange Cboe to list binary options on Coinbase trading volume and Bitcoin miner MARA's production. Once those contracts have expired and settled, a later correction to the company's reported figure will not change the payout.
The order is dated Oct. 13, 2026, and was published in the Federal Register on Oct. 16. Trading availability for the specific Coinbase and MARA series, and eligibility for Robinhood customers, remained unconfirmed as of Oct. 17.
The eligible metrics include Coinbase's transaction revenue and subscription and services revenue, alongside total trading volume. MARA's permitted metrics include Bitcoin produced and total Bitcoin holdings.
Ordinary settlement uses the designated metric for the specified reporting period in the company's earnings-related SEC filing. Cboe sets the metric and reporting period when listing the option, giving each contract a particular figure to resolve against.
A call pays when that reported figure equals or exceeds the contract's threshold; a put pays when it falls below it. The standard gross payout is $1, subject to adjustments and alternative settlement rules. The buyer's profit or loss also depends on the purchase price and any applicable trading costs.
The restatement provision applies after both expiration and settlement. A later correction leaves the settlement value and the amount paid or unpaid unchanged. An option that settled without a payout therefore does not gain one because the company subsequently revises its number across the threshold. The same finality applies to an amount already paid.
A delayed disclosure can postpone settlement processing while the clearinghouse waits for the metric. Trading still stops on the scheduled expiration date, and that date does not change.
Other cases can trigger alternative clearing procedures, including when a metric will not become available. Those procedures may use the option's last closing price as the settlement amount, producing a different result from the ordinary all-or-nothing payout.
If the closing price is unavailable or the clearinghouse Cboe Clear U.S. judges it unreliable, the option can expire unexercised and worthless.
Cboe's Sept. 30 announcement planned an October rollout across 23 companies, subject to regulatory approval, with Robinhood named as the first retail broker at launch. An Oct. 8 update reiterated the conditional plan.
The approval record also contains Cboe's commitment to wait until applicable Cboe Clear U.S. filings and documents are approved or effective following SEC review before listing the options.

articles.title: Most Americans polled oppose betting on elections
articles.text:
Most Americans polled oppose betting on elections: Reuters
The prediction market industry enables people to bet on US elections and sporting events.
Most Americans polled by Reuters/Ipsos are opposed to betting on US elections and other government actions.
The prediction market industry, led by Polymarket and Kalshi, enables people to bet on US elections, government policy moves and sporting events, which has resulted in a series of lawsuits involving state and federal agencies over who has the authority to regulate these markets.
Some 69% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans polled said they opposed using prediction markets to bet on election results. The Reuters/Ipsos survey of 4,506 adults nationwide was taken on Sept. 30-Oct. 5.
Related: Blockchain.com pursues CFTC approval for prediction markets: CNBC
Even betting on professional sports was opposed by 43% of respondents, while 29% supported it, the poll said.
President Donald Trump’s administration is pursuing federal regulations for the industry through the CFTC, some of which are begin challenged in court by several states. Many expect the dispute to reach the US Supreme Court.
Cointelegraph reported on Oct. 8 that 39 states and the District of Columbia filed an amicus brief in a New Jersey case contending the conflict between the CFTC and state authorities over prediction markets had resulted in a “national turf war” that could not be resolved without an answer from the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Crypto Today: Tether backs AIsa, Circle eyes 40 markets, stablecoin costs
articles.text:
Here’s what happened in crypto today
Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
Today in crypto, AIsa said it had completed its seed extension round with Tether and HIVEN joining as strategic investors, stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to CEO Jeremy Allaire, and a new report highlighted substantial cost savings from stablecoin remittances, especially in emerging markets.
Tether backs AIsa as strategic investor, completing seed extension round
AIsa said it had completed its seed extension round, with Tether and HIVEN joining as strategic investors.
The round brings AIsa’s total funding to more than $9 million. The two new investors joined Alibaba, Tribe Capital, Sumitomo Corporation, Draper Associates, Saison Capital and other backers.
“Enterprise AI agents need trusted information, useful tools and a governed way to transact,” said Jordan Liu, founder and CEO of San Francisco-based AIsa, in a Friday statement. “Our vision is to build the infrastructure that enables agents to discover, access and pay for resources globally, while giving enterprises full control over permissions, spending and transactions. We are excited to welcome Tether and HIVEN as strategic investors as we accelerate the transition from AI assistants to autonomous, production-ready agents.”
Fragmented providers, integrations and billing systems make it difficult for enterprise AI agents to operate effectively in production and manage at scale, according to the statement.
AIsa addresses this by bringing resource discovery, access and transactions into one governed, usage-based network, the Trusted Resource and Transaction Network for Enterprise AI Agents. Its infrastructure connects enterprise agents to external data, AI search, models, APIs, software tools and industry services, combining governed access with usage metering, billing and settlement, the
statement said.
Circle’s Allaire says stablecoin issuer looking to enter 40 developing markets: Report
Stablecoin issuer Circle is seeking to enter about 40 developing markets, according to the company’s CEO and chairman, Jeremy Allaire.
“We’re kind of going through an inflection point...a transition right now, and that transition is essentially moving from the early adopter phase of blockchain technology into the mainstream scaling phase,” Allaire told Reuters, speaking Friday on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok.
Markets in Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Middle East are experiencing increasing demand for stablecoins as businesses and individuals seek to enter the internet-based economic system, Allaire reportedly said.
Stablecoin remittances cost 84% less than traditional transfers, Borderless finds
Stablecoin-funded remittances cost roughly 84% less than traditional money transfers, according to a new third-quarter report from payments network Borderless.xyz.
Sending $200 through stablecoin payment networks costs a median of $2, or 1%, compared with $12.72, or 6.36%, for conventional remittances. The comparison uses Borderless pricing from the third quarter of 2026 and World Bank data from the same period last year.
Savings were particularly pronounced in emerging markets. In Sub-Saharan Africa, stablecoin remittances cost 2.9%, compared with 8.46% for traditional transfers. In Latin America, the respective costs were 1.25% and 5.64%.
Businesses also stand to benefit. A $10,000 stablecoin-funded transfer to the eurozone costs as little as $26, compared with $135 to $150 for an international bank wire, including foreign-exchange costs.
Stablecoin payouts also settled faster in several markets, with a median of two minutes in Brazil and Colombia and three minutes in Mexico. Traditional SWIFT transfers typically settled the next business day.
However, reliability varied. Payment completion rates reached 98.6% in Mexico but fell to 73% in Costa Rica, highlighting differences in local payment infrastructure.

articles.title: MapQuest Now Shows Drivers Where Flock Cameras Are Watching - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- MapQuest added a “Surveillance Layer” that shows known license plate readers from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions’ Vigilant, Axon, Verkada and others.
- A demo shows camera icons with cones marking which way each faces. MapQuest hasn’t said where its location data comes from.
- The feature arrives amid bipartisan backlash against Flock, including a Texas funding freeze and a push by Sen. Bernie Sanders to ban the technology.
MapQuest, the mapping service many Americans last used to print driving directions, now wants to show drivers who’s watching the road.
The company announced on Bluesky that its app includes a “Surveillance Layer,” a toggle in Map Options that plots known automated license plate readers from Flock Safety.
The layer also covers cameras from Motorola Solutions’ Vigilant, Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo’s ELSAG, Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada and other outdoor surveillance systems. “The Roads Have Eyes!” the company wrote.
A demo video showed a dense cluster of eye-shaped icons around Los Angeles’ Marina del Rey neighborhood, each paired with a red cone marking the direction a camera faces. MapQuest didn’t say in its post where the location data comes from.
License plate readers photograph passing vehicles and convert their plates into searchable data. Flock’s AI-powered cameras go further, logging details like make, model, color and even bumper stickers.
These surveillance cameras can be networked so agencies across the country share access, and critics say that allows warrantless tracking of ordinary drivers. Flock is also developing an AI tool that helps police track drivers without the need for license plate data or even a name.
The new Mapquest feature lands amid a growing bipartisan backlash. Earlier this month lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, introduced the Ban Flock Act, which seeks to prohibit federal agencies from using the technology. The move followed Sanders’ earlier call in late August to “stop Flock and AI mass surveillance.”
Also in late August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras after the Texas Tribune found that a state agency had steered at least $30 million toward the network.
In response to the mounting public backlash, Flock CEO Garrett Langley asked Americans to compromise on privacy in exchange for safety. President Donald Trump, breaking his silence on the topic in mid-September, has praised the company’s cameras.
The cameras have also become a cultural target. A Grand Theft Auto mod lets players destroy Flock cameras in-game.
Drivers who switch on MapQuest’s layer can try to plan routes around known cameras. But the map only reflects devices that have been identified, and many destinations may be impossible to reach without passing one. Still, the feature puts a mainstream navigation brand squarely in the middle of the surveillance debate.

articles.title: Claude unpicks an NSA mystery behind Ethereum passkey security
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Anthropic published research showing how Claude reconstructed P-256’s public seed from a timestamp-based generator.
- Ethereum’s EIP-7951 connects the curve to secure hardware and WebAuthn signing, making the finding relevant to passkey wallet builders.
- Anthropic says no user action is needed, while skipped-candidate criteria and P-256’s base-point origin remain unresolved.
Anthropic said on Oct. 16 that Claude had helped reconstruct the public seed behind P-256, a NIST-standardized cryptographic curve supported for Ethereum passkey signing. The finding gives wallet builders new evidence about a longstanding concern over the curve’s origins.
The seed is a public design input used to derive a coefficient in the curve’s equation. It is separate from the private signing credentials that authorize wallet activity. Anthropic says unexplained seeds supplied by the U.S. National Security Agency had fueled suspicion about deliberately weakened parameters.
The company’s published recipe initializes the old C-library generator lrand48 with the timestamp for Aug. 16, 1997, at 01:52:34 UTC. The generator produces a sequence of candidate seeds. Advancing to candidate 1,842 returns the published P-256 value, providing a repeatable recipe for that public constant.
Anthropic says this makes deliberate backdoors less plausible. It describes no new attack or curve weakness and says users need take no action.
The Ethereum connection runs through EIP-7951, which specifies verification of signatures using P-256, also called secp256r1. It names Apple Secure Enclave, Android Keystore and FIDO2/WebAuthn devices as relevant hardware. This connects wallet authorization with signing capabilities built into devices and authenticators.
EIP-7951’s motivation lists device-native signing, multifactor authentication and simpler key management as uses for account abstraction.
Ethereum’s account documentation distinguishes private keys that sign transactions from public information used to verify them; contract accounts are controlled by code.
EIP-7951’s P256VERIFY operation takes a message hash, a signature and a public key, then checks the signature’s validity. The reconstructed public seed is separate from those private signing credentials.
P-256 also differs from secp256k1, the curve already used in Ethereum. The relevance is to P-256-compatible signing, rather than every Ethereum wallet.
Anthropic reports that candidate 876 also yielded a prime-order curve of the required size, leaving selection criteria unclear. The number of generation runs and the origin of P-256’s base point, a separate fixed mathematical point, remain unknown.

articles.title: Cysic crypto bridge halted after unauthorized minting
articles.text:
Cysic crypto bridge halted after unauthorized mint of 10M CYS
Cysic said the incident was limited to bridge message processing and minting and did not affect the mainnet or other operational systems.
Cysic Foundation is investigating an unauthorized issuance on BNB Smart Chain and said the mint size alone does not establish the incident’s dollar impact.
The foundation said in a Sunday X incident report that its cross-chain bridge was suspended after an attacker exploited a processing flaw to mint 10 million CYS on BNB Smart Chain on Saturday, with preliminary findings pointing to unauthorized access to a database supporting the bridge.
The mint occurred at 12:31:38 UTC on Oct. 17, and Cysic added the recipient address to the token contract’s blacklist at 13:47:52 UTC. About 2.8 million CYS remained at that address, with transfers restricted. There are roughly 160.8 million tokens in circulation, according to CoinMarketCap data.
CYS coordinates incentives for users, compute providers, governance participants and contributors in Cysic’s network, according to the project’s tokenomics documentation.
Cysic said the incident was limited to bridge message processing and minting and did not affect the mainnet or other operational systems. “The incident did not result in the theft or unauthorized transfer of existing CYS or other assets held in user wallets,” it said.
The post said the number minted does not establish the final dollar loss; token transfers, swaps and actual losses remain under review. Cysic has hired an unnamed security firm and plans to publish a follow-up report after the current investigation phase.

articles.title: Bitcoin ETFs Shed Nearly $1 Billion in Two Weeks as Uptober Stays Red - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs posted net outflows of $228.6 million this week, after losing $681.1 million the week before.
- Outflows topped inflows on three of five trading days, with Wednesday’s $261.4 million exit the week’s worst session.
- The funds are down about $615 million for October, though cumulative net inflows since launch still stand at $57.3 billion.
Bitcoin ETF investors spent another week heading for the exits.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $82.4 million on Friday, according to Decrypt’s ETF tracker, capping a week in which outflows outweighed inflows on three of five trading days.
The funds lost a net $228.6 million for the week, according to SoSoValue, following a $681.1 million drain the week before. Over the two weeks, about $910 million has left the funds.
It was a choppy stretch. A $175.7 million inflow on Tuesday was wiped out a day later by $261.4 million in redemptions, the week’s worst session. Thursday brought a modest $5.1 million inflow before selling resumed Friday.
Wednesday’s selling coincided with a hot inflation print. The consumer price index showed prices up 3.7% year over year in September, above the 3.6% forecast. A hotter-than-expected producer price reading followed Thursday, reviving bets on another Federal Reserve interest rate hike.
Bitcoin briefly slipped below $80,000 on Thursday, and nearly $950 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, about 90% of them bullish longs, according to CoinGlass. The drop also pushed Bitcoin below the average ETF holder’s estimated cost basis near $82,300, Nexo analyst Iliya Kalchev told Decrypt.
When inflation runs hot, the Fed tends to keep raising rates, pushing up Treasury yields and making a nearly risk-free return of around 5% a tough competitor for riskier bets like Bitcoin. Higher rates also make borrowing costlier and lift the dollar, squeezing the cheap credit that leveraged crypto traders depend on.
The back-to-back red weeks have dragged October deep into negative territory. After opening the month with roughly $293 million in inflows, the funds are now down about $615 million for October, based on Decrypt’s tracker. The slide began in earnest on Oct. 7, when a $484.9 million exit marked the funds’ worst day since June. Ethereum and Solana ETFs have also been in the red this month.
Spot Bitcoin ETFs are exchange-traded funds that hold actual Bitcoin. They trade on stock exchanges like ordinary shares, giving investors exposure through a regular brokerage account without buying or storing the asset themselves.
Since launching in January 2024, they’ve drawn $57.3 billion in cumulative net inflows, according to Decrypt’s tracker, making them a fixture of Wall Street’s crypto exposure. Because issuers report flows daily, and institutions and financial advisers account for much of the money, the figures have become a closely watched gauge of investor sentiment.
Total net assets stand at $104.29 billion, according to SoSoValue, while Decrypt’s tracker puts the figure at $100.2 billion. Bitcoin closed Friday near $81,590, down from about $82,337 a week earlier.

articles.title: Trump waives new Russia tariffs as October 18 oil deadline arrives
articles.text:
Quick Take
- Trump’s October 16 order waives new Russia-linked duties before the October 18 condition for qualifying energy purchases.
- The waivers have no fixed expiry, while specified earlier Russia-related executive-order sanctions and measures remain unaffected.
- The waiver could ease one source of inflation and financing pressure on Bitcoin.
President Donald Trump waived new Russia-linked duties in an October 16 order, keeping those additional tariffs from applying as October 18 arrives. The date is a condition for targeting certain countries over new Russian-energy purchases; the waiver changes one potential inflation and financing-cost risk for Bitcoin.
The order implements the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. It specifies additional duties of 500% on Russian goods and 100% on goods from two country groups: the five largest Russian oil and gas importers that knowingly make new purchases on or after October 18, and the top five facilitators of Russian oil sanctions evasion. Exceptions apply, and the same order waives the duties.
The waivers have no fixed expiry. They remain effective until the president or secretary of state determines further action is appropriate, consulting the Treasury secretary and US trade representative as appropriate.
Earlier sanctions also survive within the order’s specified scope. It preserves measures under executive orders addressing the Russian harmful-foreign-activities emergency as they stood immediately before the act’s enactment, including measures against persons already sanctioned under those orders.
CryptoSlate’s September 19 report framed October 18 as an implementation test and identified waivers as a possible limit on the shock. The administration has now exercised that authority, leaving future waiver decisions as the next policy trigger.
The order names no countries in the two groups. It directs the US trade representative and other officials to monitor Russian energy purchases and sanctions-evasion facilitation, including circumstances that could warrant action on the waivers.
Bitcoin’s inflation and funding-cost channel
Keeping the new duties waived could limit an additional tariff and energy-inflation shock, easing one potential source of pressure for tighter financing conditions. That could ease one source of funding pressure on Bitcoin.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller’s October 8 speech illustrates that constraint. He cited elevated energy costs and threatened new tariffs among persistent inflation pressures, and anticipated further interest-rate increases if incoming data continued as expected. These were his own views, delivered eight days before the waiver.
The connection to crypto comes through financial conditions. Researchers in BIS Working Paper 1219, published in October 2024, found that US monetary-policy tightening weakened crypto prices and reduced stablecoin market capitalization, while prime money market fund assets rose. Their findings support a general channel from US policy into crypto demand and liquidity.
The signals to watch are changes to the waivers and whether renewed trade pressure reaches energy prices, inflation expectations or financing conditions.

articles.title: Banks Hold a Lever Over Stablecoin Adoption, BIS Economists Say - Decrypt
articles.text:
In brief
- A new BIS working paper using U.S. data from 2019 to 2025 found that higher bank deposit rates predict slower stablecoin market growth.
- The effect was stronger for Circle’s USDC than for Tether’s USDT, which the authors tied to USDC’s closer links to U.S. users.
- The authors said regulators should weigh whether issuers can pay yield. The paper reflects their views, not necessarily the BIS’s.
Banks worried about losing customers to stablecoins may already have a counterweight: the interest rate on a savings account.
That’s the takeaway from a new working paper published by the Bank for International Settlements, the Basel-based bank for central banks. Using weekly U.S. data from January 2019 through June 2025, BIS economist Iñaki Aldasoro and Rashad Ahmed of the Andersen Institute for Finance and Economics found that stablecoin growth slows when banks raise deposit rates.
Stablecoin market capitalization grew by about 15% over a typical 10-week span in the sample used by the researchers. A one-basis-point bump in deposit rates, a sizable weekly move for slow-moving savings rates, cut that to roughly 12% under the authors’ baseline estimate. Under a second method designed to isolate cause and effect, it fell to about 6%. Stablecoins kept growing, just more slowly.
To separate cause from coincidence, the authors relied on a quirk in bank behavior. Lenders barely raise savings rates until the federal funds rate passes about 3%, and then they reprice much faster.
The link was stronger for Circle’s USDC than for Tether’s USDT, which the authors attribute to USDC’s closer ties to U.S. users. The paper concludes that banks “retain some influence over the pace of that adoption through deposit pricing.”
The findings come with caveats. Working papers reflect the authors’ views, not necessarily the BIS’s, and the sample spans a single high-rate cycle in which stablecoins paid holders no interest.
The authors said regulators should weigh whether stablecoin issuers may pay holders yield, along with the trade-offs of requiring issuers to keep part of their reserves in bank deposits.
That debate is live in Washington. Banks have lobbied to keep stablecoin yield off the table, a fight that loomed over the Clarity Act’s failed Senate vote. Meanwhile, the OCC, FDIC, and Treasury are writing rules to implement the GENIUS Act, which takes effect in January. The GENIUS Act, signed into law by President Donald Trump in July of last year, essentially legalized stablecoins in the United States and set rules of the road for their issuance, use, and custody.
The BIS has long scrutinized stablecoins and the cryptocurrency space more broadly. In 2021, it argued the rise of blockchain-based digital dollars made central bank digital currencies more urgent, and a 2023 BIS survey warned they could threaten financial stability if widely adopted.
