articles.title: Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
articles.text:
Scientists find a youth protein that helps aging brain cells act young again
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- The Mount Sinai Hospital / Mount Sinai School of Medicine
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a protein linked to youth helps protect the brain’s immune cells from age-related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
- Share:
A protein associated with youth may help aging brain cells regain some of their lost abilities. Scientists at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai have discovered that TIMP2 plays an important role in keeping the brain's immune cells healthy, offering new clues about how the brain changes with age.
In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers found that removing TIMP2 caused brain immune cells, known as microglia, to develop characteristics linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease. When the scientists restored TIMP2 in the bloodstream of older mice, these cells became better at removing cellular debris and showed fewer molecular signs of inflammation and other potentially harmful changes.
The discovery suggests that proteins associated with youth may help preserve the brain's natural defenses as it ages. It also identifies TIMP2 as a potentially important factor in maintaining healthy immune activity in the brain.
Why the Brain's Immune Cells Become Less Effective With Age
Getting older is the greatest known risk factor for Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative disorders. However, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that make the aging brain increasingly vulnerable to these conditions.
One important piece of the puzzle involves microglia, specialized immune cells that serve as the brain's maintenance and defense system. They remove cellular waste, help maintain the networks through which neurons communicate, and respond when brain tissue is injured.
As the brain ages, these cells can lose some of their ability to perform these essential tasks. They may also shift into states that promote inflammation and interfere with normal brain function.
"TIMP2 facilitates healthy function for the brain's immune cells," said Joseph M. Castellano, PhD, Associate Professor of Neuroscience at the Ronald M. Loeb Center for Alzheimer's Disease and The Friedman Brain Institute at The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "By supporting the ability of microglia to clear debris and limit maladaptive responses, TIMP2 may help restore aspects of microglial function that become compromised with age. Since our previous work identified TIMP2 as a regulator of synaptic plasticity through the extracellular matrix, these findings suggest that this factor sits at the intersection of several processes that are critical for normal brain function."
Synaptic plasticity refers to the brain's ability to strengthen or weaken connections between neurons, a process essential for learning and memory. The extracellular matrix is a network of molecules surrounding cells that helps support and regulate their activity.
What Happens When the Brain Loses TIMP2?
To investigate how TIMP2 affects brain immune cells, the research team studied several groups of mice representing different biological conditions.
The study included Brittany Hemmer, PhD, the first author, who was a graduate student in Castellano's laboratory during the research.
Some of the mice were genetically modified to lack TIMP2 throughout their bodies. In others, the researchers removed the protein specifically from either microglia or neurons. Comparing these models allowed the team to examine how TIMP2 influences immune cell behavior in both healthy and aging brains.
The scientists used several advanced techniques to study the changes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing allowed them to examine patterns of gene activity in individual cell nuclei. They also used detailed imaging, functional tests, and a technique called in vivo microdialysis, which collects and measures substances from the fluid surrounding cells in living brain tissue.
The results revealed striking changes when TIMP2 was absent.
Microglia developed several features typically associated with aging and brain injury. Their cellular activation markers changed, their ability to remove debris declined, and they showed molecular signatures linked to cellular senescence, a biological state associated with aging and cellular stress.
The effects extended beyond the immune cells themselves. Using in vivo microdialysis, the researchers also detected higher levels of proteins associated with inflammation and stress in the extracellular environment surrounding brain cells.
Together, these findings indicated that TIMP2 helps prevent microglia from shifting toward potentially damaging states.
Restoring a Youth-Associated Protein Improves Aging Brain Cells
The researchers next explored whether supplying TIMP2 could counteract some of the changes observed with age.
They administered TIMP2 through injections to older mice, allowing the protein to circulate throughout the body. The treatment produced encouraging results.
Microglia became more effective at clearing cellular debris and showed a reduction in molecular markers associated with inflammatory states. In other words, restoring the youth-associated protein helped the aging immune cells recover some of the functions that normally deteriorate over time.
These improvements suggest that TIMP2 influences how microglia respond to conditions within the brain. By supporting their protective activities and limiting potentially harmful responses, the protein may help maintain a healthier environment for neurons.
The results also point to a possible biological connection between factors circulating in the body that are associated with youth and the activity of the brain's innate immune system. This system provides a first line of defense against injury and other threats.
A Potential New Direction for Brain Aging and Alzheimer's Research
The discovery adds to growing scientific interest in whether biological factors associated with youth can influence the aging process.
Because microglia help maintain brain health and can contribute to harmful inflammation when their behavior changes, finding ways to preserve their normal function could have important implications for understanding age-related neurological disorders.
"While additional studies are needed, this work provides new insight into how youth-associated factors influence pathways involved in brain aging and age-related neurological disorders that may ultimately inform therapeutic strategies," Dr. Castellano added.
However, the researchers caution that these findings come from experiments in mice. It remains unknown whether TIMP2 produces similar effects in humans or whether manipulating the protein could eventually become an effective treatment.
Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether TIMP2 itself, or the biological pathways it controls, can be targeted to reduce harmful changes associated with brain aging.
For now, the findings provide a promising new explanation for how a protein linked to youth helps maintain the brain's immune defenses, and how restoring it may recover some functions that weaken with age.
This work was supported by the National Institute on Aging (R01AG061382 (JMC), RF1AG072300 (JMC), 1F31AG079604-01A1 (BMH), T32AG049688 (BMH, SMP), R01AG061382-02S1 (JMC, SMP), and Cure Alzheimer's Fund (JMC).

articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
articles.text:
NASA’s SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a dazzling, jellyfish-shaped glow across the eastern United States as sunlight illuminated its exhaust during an early morning launch. The mission delivered equipment and scientific experiments to the International Space Station, including research that could advance treatments for blindness, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and other diseases.
- Share:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket transformed the early morning sky into a spectacular display of light on October 13, 2026. As the rocket climbed above Earth carrying a Dragon spacecraft, sunlight illuminated its expanding exhaust plumes, creating an enormous glowing shape that resembled a jellyfish.
This striking phenomenon, known as a "jellyfish," occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight reaches the exhaust high in the atmosphere, making the spreading plume shine brightly against the darker sky below.
See a wider view of the "jellyfish."
SpaceX Launch Creates a Spectacular Sky Display
The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The illuminated exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States, giving observers a remarkable view of the rocket's journey into space.
The launch marked SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
New Space Station Upgrades and Medical Experiments
Among the cargo aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These additional solar panels are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help provide electricity for the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for several scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science.
One experiment will explore manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, where the near absence of gravity creates conditions that cannot easily be reproduced on Earth. The research could help develop technologies to restore vision in people with certain forms of vision loss.
Another investigation will use 3D heart tissue models to support the development of more efficient drug testing methods during future space missions.
Additional experiments will examine how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and investigate brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue grown from cells. These models could help researchers identify new targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.

articles.title: Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
articles.text:
Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
Remarkably preserved 1,200-year-old hairless dogs found in Peru reveal surprising clues about the bond between humans and their canine companions long before the Inca Empire.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Dartmouth College
- Summary:
- Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred, and sometimes discarded their dogs.
- Share:
Archaeologists working at an ancient burial complex in Peru have uncovered remarkable evidence of hairless dogs that lived more than 1,200 years ago, long before the rise of the Inca Empire. The discoveries include naturally mummified remains, unusual skeletal features, and clues about what the animals ate and how they were treated by the people around them.
Peruvian hairless dogs are a distinctive Indigenous breed known for their slender bodies, pointed ears, and lack of fur. They frequently appear in pottery created by ancient societies along the Andean coast. Today, a variation of the breed is recognized by the American Kennel Club as the Peruvian Inca Orchid. The dogs are also an important national symbol, having been officially designated part of Peru's cultural heritage in 2000.
A study published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology reports the first physical evidence of Peruvian hairless dogs at Castillo de Huarmey, the only known Wari Empire site discovered so far on Peru's northern coast.
Ancient Dog Remains Discovered at a Wari Empire Site
Located approximately 190 miles north of Lima, Castillo de Huarmey covers 110 acres and once served as an administrative and burial center for the Wari Empire. The complex was occupied between 600 and 1050 CE, roughly 400 years before the Inca rose to power.
The site has already produced several extraordinary archaeological discoveries. In 2012, researchers uncovered the first undisturbed elite Wari tomb, containing the remains of 58 high-status women, six human sacrifices, and approximately 1,300 artifacts. Another important discovery followed in 2022, when archaeologists identified nearby burials of elite craftspeople accompanied by gold, silver, and bronze tools. Together, these findings have helped researchers understand how the Wari Empire governed its territories.
The newly examined dog remains offer a different perspective on daily life at the site, particularly the complicated relationships between people and animals.
"Our findings indicate that humans and dogs coexisted at this Wari site, but reconstructing their bond is challenging, as past emotions are difficult to capture through archaeological methods," says first author Weronika Tomczyk, a research associate in Dartmouth's Department of Anthropology and a postdoctoral fellow in its Ecology, Evolution, Environment and Society Program.
"The goal of our study was to not only present data on Castillo de Huarmey's dog burials, but also emphasize that people in the past had often contradictory relationships with the animals, just as they do today: a pet for one group of people could at the same time be considered a pest by their closest neighbors."
Remarkably Preserved Dog Mummies Found in the Peruvian Desert
Castillo de Huarmey lies in an extremely dry region of Peru's Pacific coast. The desert's exceptionally arid conditions have helped preserve materials that would normally deteriorate over time, including hair, bones, clothing, leather, pigments, and decorated pottery.
Among the artifacts recovered from the site is an unusual ceramic vessel depicting a seated Peruvian hairless dog with humanlike features. The animal appears to be holding an object resembling a musical instrument.
Between 2010 and 2025, excavations also uncovered numerous remains of South American camelids, probably domesticated llamas and alpacas. Some may have been deposited as offerings during funerary ceremonies, while others appear to have been discarded as waste. Archaeologists also recovered the skeletal remains of dogs.
However, interpreting these discoveries has been complicated by extensive damage and looting. A powerful earthquake in 1970 caused part of Castillo de Huarmey to collapse, exposing burial chambers containing pottery and other valuable objects. Looters subsequently disturbed large sections of the complex.
The deeper archaeological layers remained untouched and retained their original Wari context. In contrast, the upper layers, where most of the animal remains were discovered, contained materials that had become mixed together.
During excavations in the northern section of the main ceremonial area, three sets of dog remains stood out.
One was a naturally mummified skull that still retained visible hairless skin and attached ears. The skull had also been colored with cinnabar, a bright red pigment commonly used in ancient Peruvian funerary traditions.
Researchers discovered a second, larger dog skull, along with the naturally mummified skeleton of a male dog buried in a shallow pit. The male skeleton was almost complete, missing only the lower portions of its front limbs.
At first, the researchers suspected that the mummified dog might have been buried relatively recently, perhaps around 50 years earlier during the period of looting. But Tomczyk noticed two important details: the animal was hairless, and all three dogs lacked their first premolars.
Missing Teeth Reveal the Dogs' Ancient Identity
The missing teeth provided an unexpected clue that helped researchers identify the animals.
"What I noticed is that some of the dog skeletons were missing teeth, and not that they lost them during their lifespan; some teeth, especially first premolars and sometimes last molars, had just never erupted," said Tomczyk. "And then I found in the literature that the same gene which is responsible for hairlessness in dogs is responsible for a reduced number of teeth, indicating that these were Peruvian hairless dogs."
In other words, the animals were not necessarily missing teeth because of injury, disease, or old age. Their reduced number of teeth was linked to the same genetic trait responsible for their hairlessness.
This distinctive biological connection offered evidence that the remains belonged to Peruvian hairless dogs rather than other ancient dog populations.
To investigate further, the researchers applied standard zooarchaeological techniques, which involve studying animal remains recovered from archaeological sites. These methods helped them estimate the ages of the dogs and examine their physical characteristics.
The team also analyzed chemical signatures preserved in the animals' bones and teeth. Known as isotopic analysis, this technique can reveal information about what an animal ate and drank, as well as where it may have lived.
The researchers examined isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and strontium. These are different forms of chemical elements that can preserve clues about diet and environmental conditions. Strontium is particularly useful because its composition varies with local geology and can help scientists trace an animal's geographic origins or movements.
The results were compared with similar measurements from human and camelid remains recovered at Castillo de Huarmey.
"Isotopic analyses of a dog's tooth give a signal of its life as a puppy because dog teeth erupt so fast, and the bone gives a signal of more or less the last year of its life," said Tomczyk. "Such sampling strategy aimed to provide signals from distinct stages of a dog's life."
Ancient Puppies Buried Alongside Elite Members of Society
Altogether, the excavations produced 341 dog bone specimens representing at least 19 individual dogs, in addition to the complete mummified male dog.
Some of the remains were found in particularly intriguing burial contexts.
For example, the bones of a puppy estimated to have been just 6 to 8 weeks old were discovered alongside an elite craftsperson nicknamed the "Master Basketmaker." Other finds included the bones of an adult dog buried within the site's palace and part of a puppy skeleton buried with a male individual identified as XY, who was probably sacrificed to serve as a tomb guardian.
Most of the dogs were adults at the time of burial. However, their remains suggest that the animals did not all receive the same treatment.
Some appear to have been deliberately buried, potentially reflecting a special role in Wari society. Others were found among discarded materials. Only a small number of bones displayed butchery marks, suggesting that dogs were not commonly consumed as food.
Radiocarbon dating provided another important discovery. The complete mummified male dog was determined to be at least 1,200 years old, making it the oldest radiocarbon-dated specimen recovered from Castillo de Huarmey so far.
This result has important implications for understanding the site's chronology because it provides an additional dating reference for the ancient complex.
Ancient Hairless Dogs May Have Eaten Like Humans
The isotopic evidence also revealed surprising similarities between the diets of dogs and people living at Castillo de Huarmey.
Most of the dogs had consumed at least some maize, or corn, which was a major food source throughout the pre-Hispanic Andes. Their diets therefore overlapped with those of the human population.
An especially interesting pattern emerged among the dogs believed to have been hairless.
When these animals were puppies, their diets appeared more similar to those of human children. As they grew older, however, their food sources became more varied.
The findings raise the possibility that some puppies received particular attention or were raised under controlled conditions, potentially as part of an organized breeding practice.
"We do not know if the dogs were intentionally fed maize or if perhaps, they were just eating leftovers or trash," said Tomczyk. "Yet, the distinct dietary patterns of hairless puppies provide insights into what may have been organized breeding."
The researchers emphasize that the archaeological evidence cannot establish whether these dogs were cherished pets, working animals, or animals with other roles in Wari society.
Nevertheless, the differences in burial practices, physical characteristics, and dietary patterns suggest that the hairless dogs held a distinctive place within the community.
"While we will never know if any of the three dogs were pets or how people treated them, it is evident they received different treatment than other dogs," said Tomczyk.
The discoveries provide a rare glimpse into the lives of dogs and humans more than a millennium ago, showing that relationships with animals could be just as varied and complicated in ancient societies as they are today.
The study's co-authors include Miłosz Giersz, Wiesław Więckowski, and Roberto Pimentel Nita of the University of Warsaw, along with Claire Ebert of the University of Pittsburgh.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Dartmouth College. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Weronika Tomczyk, Miłosz Giersz, Wiesław Więckowski, Roberto Pimentel Nita, Claire E. Ebert. The many lives of companion species: a zooarchaeological and isotopic research on Wari dog remains from Castillo de Huarmey, Peru. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology, 2026; 82: 101767 DOI: 10.1016/j.jaa.2026.101767

articles.title: NASA discovers hidden fires burning beneath the Amazon rainforest
articles.text:
NASA discovers hidden fires burning beneath the Amazon rainforest
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- El Niño is fueling a dangerous cascade of wildfires across the tropics, with the Amazon rainforest now experiencing widespread burning and scientists warning that the worst may still be ahead. NASA researchers are uncovering dozens of previously undetected fires, suggesting the destruction could be even more extensive than satellite records show.
- Share:
A dangerous wave of wildfires is spreading across the tropics, and the Amazon rainforest is now facing a growing crisis. Fueled by severe drought linked to El Niño, fires are sweeping through parts of Brazil, filling cities with smoke and threatening forests already damaged by previous fire seasons.
Unlike tornadoes or thunderstorms, which can cause widespread destruction in a matter of minutes, El Niño influences weather patterns over many months. The climate phenomenon can disrupt rainfall across vast regions, creating unusually dry conditions that allow fires to spread rapidly. Scientists warn that the Amazon may be entering the beginning of a prolonged and destructive fire season.
NASA Satellites Detect Surging Amazon Wildfires
Beginning in September 2026, satellite observations revealed a sharp increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon. The growing activity appeared in several monitoring systems, including NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), and NASA Worldview.
The affected area extends from the forests surrounding Manaus and Santarém, two major commercial and transportation hubs in Brazil, eastward toward the mouth of the Amazon River.
On October 12, 2026, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) instrument aboard NASA's Aqua satellite captured an image showing enormous plumes of smoke rising from fires on both sides of the Amazon River.
At the time, thick smoke had engulfed Manaus, the capital of Brazil's Amazonas state. City officials reported dangerously polluted air, with concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. These microscopic particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and pose serious health risks. The measurements placed the city's air quality in the second-worst category of a regional air quality index.
The smoke brought major disruptions to Manaus, which is home to more than 2 million people. Schools shut down, public events were canceled, and children's sports leagues suspended activities as authorities warned residents about hazardous conditions, according to news reports.
El Niño Is Triggering a Wildfire Domino Effect
According to Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, the fires surrounding Manaus and Santarém are part of a much larger pattern.
Morton describes the phenomenon as a "cascade" of tropical fires driven by rainfall disruptions associated with El Niño. The sequence typically begins near the equator, where drought helps ignite peat fires in Indonesia. These fires burn through carbon-rich organic material in the soil. As dry conditions develop elsewhere, fire activity intensifies in the central and eastern Amazon.
This pattern is not new. Following the devastating 2015-2016 El Niño, Morton worked with scientists from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland to examine how tropical fires followed shifting rainfall patterns. Their findings were published in a 2017 study. Researchers observed a similar sequence in 2023.
Now, the 2026 El Niño appears to be producing the same progression.
Indonesia has already experienced months of drought, smoke, and destructive fires beginning in August. During October, wildfires destroyed hundreds of homes, while dense smoke covered entire islands on most days.
"Now, in the Amazon, we're seeing the second domino in the cascade fall," Morton said, referring to the increasing number of fires in the Brazilian states of Pará and Amazonas.
Scientists Warn More Fires Could Spread Into 2027
The current surge may be only one stage of a much longer fire season.
Morton and his colleagues anticipate that fire activity will expand northward during November and December 2026. The regions at risk include the Brazilian states of Roraima and Amapá, northern Pará, and portions of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.
The pattern is then expected to shift southward. By August and September 2027, drought conditions and wildfire danger could reach their highest levels in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay.
One particularly troubling aspect of the current crisis is that many of the threatened forests have burned before.
"It's so striking -- and frustrating -- that this is happening all over again," said Morton, noting that forests affected by the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events are once again catching fire.
Wildfires are especially destructive in tropical rainforests because most of the plants and animals living there have not evolved to withstand frequent burning. Unlike ecosystems where fire is a regular natural process, Amazon forests can suffer severe and lasting damage when flames move through them.
Previous fires have also left parts of the forest more vulnerable. Trees partially burned during earlier events may be weakened or damaged, making the remaining vegetation more susceptible to future fires. Morton warned that some of the current blazes could therefore burn more intensely than before.
He expects fires near Manaus and Santarém to persist until seasonal rains return, likely in December 2026 or January 2027.
However, communities in regions farther north and south still have an opportunity to reduce the danger before conditions deteriorate.
"Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs," Morton said.
Extreme Drought Turns Human-Started Fires Into Wildfires
Although the Amazon is experiencing a severe fire emergency, lightning is rarely responsible for igniting fires in Brazil's rainforest.
The region is normally so wet that lightning causes less than 1 percent of fires, according to Morton. This means that nearly all of the fires currently spreading through the Brazilian Amazon originated from human activity.
What makes 2026 particularly dangerous is the severity of the drought.
Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology reported that rainfall in Manaus was 95 percent below normal in August and 60 percent below normal in September.
These extremely dry conditions have transformed fires that might otherwise have remained confined to managed areas into uncontrolled wildfires.
Morton explained that many of the larger blazes began as deliberately set fires used for land management, such as removing shrubs from grazing land or clearing crop residue from fields. Once the flames escaped, they spread into the rainforest's parched understory, the layer of vegetation growing beneath the taller trees.
Satellite analysis suggests that approximately 50 to 70 uncontrolled fires are currently burning in the Santarém area alone, according to Shane Coffield, an assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland who works at NASA Goddard.
NASA Uncovers Hidden Fires That Satellites Are Missing
The actual number of Amazon wildfires may be substantially higher than standard satellite monitoring systems indicate.
As part of a NASA Earth Action project, Coffield is studying observations collected by VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite), a satellite instrument capable of detecting heat signatures associated with active fires.
His goal is to identify fires that fail to meet the detection requirements used in official FIRMS data products.
These additional detections, known as "candidate fires," could help researchers develop a more complete picture of wildfire activity. Coffield plans to provide their locations to MapBiomas, a collaborative network of universities, nongovernmental organizations, and technology companies that tracks fires and changes in land use throughout the Amazon.
The initial findings suggest that conventional monitoring is overlooking a significant number of blazes.
"For the area around Santarém, we've identified about 40 percent more fires than you'll see in active fire counts from FIRMS," said Coffield.
Detecting fires beneath a rainforest canopy can be surprisingly difficult, even with sophisticated instruments in orbit. Satellite sensors identify wildfires by measuring infrared radiation, which reveals the heat generated by burning vegetation.
However, thick smoke, persistent cloud cover, and dense tree canopies can interfere with those measurements. Fires that burn slowly through the understory are particularly difficult to detect because the vegetation above them can conceal their heat signatures.
As a result, satellite fire counts may sometimes fall even when extensive burning continues on the ground.
"On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn't right."
By identifying fires that existing monitoring systems overlook, NASA researchers hope to provide scientists and land managers with a more accurate understanding of the threats facing the Amazon as the El Niño-driven fire season unfolds.

articles.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
articles.text:
New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
A promising new drug reversed severe fatty liver disease in animals by healing the gut, revealing a surprising new path toward treating liver damage.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Michigan Medicine - University of Michigan
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.
- Share:
An experimental drug developed at Michigan Medicine has reversed a serious form of fatty liver disease in animal studies by targeting an unexpected source of liver damage: the gut.
The compound, known as DT-109, works by reducing harmful gut bacteria, protecting the intestinal lining, and preventing inflammatory substances from reaching the liver. According to findings published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation, this approach successfully reversed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in animal models, offering a promising new strategy for treating a disease that remains difficult to manage.
MASH affects approximately 7% of the world's population. It is a severe form of fatty liver disease in which excess fat accumulates in the liver, causing inflammation and cellular damage. Over time, the condition can progress to cirrhosis, which involves extensive liver scarring, as well as liver cancer and liver failure. Although treatment options have improved in recent years, effective therapies remain limited.
"We see clear evidence that DT-109 protects the gut epithelial barrier, reducing the systemic influx of harmful microbial products that are thought to contribute to MASH development and progression," said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., senior author of the study and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School.
"This compound shows benefits to the gastrointestinal system and has great potential as a treatment for MASH."
How Harmful Gut Bacteria Can Trigger Liver Damage
Chen's research team had previously demonstrated that DT-109, a glycine-based tripeptide, could improve MASH in animal studies. A tripeptide is a small molecule made from three amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. What remained unclear was exactly how the compound produced its protective effects.
The latest research provides an explanation, revealing how changes in gut bacteria can set off a chain reaction that damages the liver and how DT-109 can interrupt that process.
Before examining the drug's effects, the scientists confirmed an important contributor to MASH: excessive growth of Clostridium perfringens, a bacterium that produces ammonia inside the intestines.
When ammonia levels rise, they can damage the gut's protective inner lining. Normally, this intestinal barrier helps prevent potentially harmful substances from escaping the digestive tract and entering the bloodstream.
As the barrier weakens, however, toxins and other products generated by gut microbes can travel to the liver. Once there, they can provoke inflammation and activate immune defenses in ways that worsen liver damage.
One response involves the excessive activation of CD8+ T cells, immune cells that normally help the body destroy infected or abnormal cells. When these cells become overactive, they can contribute to the inflammatory processes associated with MASH.
The findings help explain why a disease centered in the liver can be strongly influenced by events occurring elsewhere in the digestive system.
Experimental Drug Repairs the Gut and Protects the Liver
Through a series of experiments, researchers discovered that DT-109 disrupts this damaging cycle by improving the intestinal environment and reinforcing the gut's protective barrier.
In both mice and nonhuman primates, the compound reduced levels of Clostridium perfringens and lowered ammonia production in the intestines. These changes helped strengthen the intestinal lining, limiting the movement of harmful microbial substances into the body and reducing their potential to damage the liver.
The results were particularly encouraging in nonhuman primates, whose liver biology and gut microbial communities more closely resemble those of humans than those of mice. In these animals, DT-109 reduced liver inflammation and lessened the severity of MASH.
Together, the findings show how targeting harmful processes in the gut can produce beneficial effects in the liver, even though the drug acts primarily within the gastrointestinal system.
"DT-109 connects microbiota modulation with liver protection by restoring gut barrier integrity and limiting the systemic translocation of ammonia and other pro-inflammatory microbial products within the gut-liver axis," said Jifeng Zhang, Ph.D., co-author and research professor of cardiovascular medicine at U-M Medical School.
"We also found that DT-109 primarily acts in the gastrointestinal tract, but its reach stretches much further."
The gut-liver axis refers to the close biological relationship between the digestive tract and the liver. Substances absorbed from the intestines travel to the liver through the bloodstream, making liver health particularly sensitive to changes in gut bacteria and intestinal barrier function.
By targeting this connection, DT-109 may offer a way to address some of the processes driving liver inflammation rather than focusing exclusively on damage that has already occurred.
Potential Benefits Beyond Fatty Liver Disease
Researchers believe the compound's ability to protect the intestinal barrier could make it useful against other conditions involving inflammation and metabolic dysfunction.
Previous research has shown that DT-109 can reduce the formation of atherosclerotic plaques and prevent vascular calcification in nonhuman primates.
Atherosclerotic plaques are deposits of fat and other substances that accumulate inside artery walls, potentially restricting blood flow and increasing the risk of cardiovascular problems. Vascular calcification occurs when calcium builds up in blood vessel walls, making them less flexible and contributing to cardiovascular disease.
These findings suggest that DT-109 could eventually have applications in treating both liver and cardiovascular conditions, an important possibility because metabolic disorders often affect multiple organs.
The researchers are also interested in whether the compound could help people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a group of chronic conditions that includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
Because problems with the intestinal barrier are associated with several gastrointestinal disorders, a treatment that strengthens this barrier might have benefits beyond protecting the liver. However, additional research will be needed to determine whether DT-109 is effective against these conditions.
A Promising Treatment That Still Needs Human Trials
Despite the encouraging results, DT-109 remains an experimental treatment. Its ability to reverse MASH has been demonstrated in animal models, but researchers have not yet established whether it can safely and effectively produce similar benefits in humans.
The next phase of research will involve further evaluation of the compound, with the goal of advancing it toward clinical trials. Those studies will be essential for determining its safety, appropriate use, and potential effectiveness in patients.
"This study presents novel evidence about the pathogenesis of MASH and provides excitement about a therapeutic avenue to explore for a condition that remains difficult to treat," said Elliot Tapper, M.D., Academic Director of Hepatology at Michigan Medicine.
"What patients with MASH need is a safe and effective therapy capable of improving their liver and heart health - of course we are excited about these developments."
The discovery highlights an important shift in how scientists are approaching fatty liver disease. By addressing harmful gut bacteria and restoring the intestinal barrier, researchers may be able to protect the liver through a treatment that acts primarily outside the organ itself.
If future human studies confirm the benefits seen in animals, DT-109 could offer a new therapeutic option for patients with severe fatty liver disease while potentially addressing cardiovascular complications as well.
Funding and Disclosures
Ying Zhao, Oren Rom, Jifeng Zhang, and Y. Eugene Chen are listed as inventors on a patent application (Tripeptides and treatment of metabolic, cardiovascular, and inflammatory disorders).
Chen is also an inventor of DT-109. The University of Michigan holds the patent for the compound and has licensed it to Diapin Therapeutics. Both Chen and the university have an ownership interest in Diapin, which supplied DT-109 for the research and is continuing its development.
The human study protocol, all amendments, and the informed consent form received approval from the Institutional Review Boards at the participating sites. These included the First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University (approval number: XJTU1AF2023LSK330), the Institutional Review Board of Jinan University (approval number: 2016-017), and the University of Hong Kong/Hospital Authority Hong Kong West Cluster (approval number: UW 20-700).
All experimental procedures involving nonhuman primates were approved by the Laboratory Animal Care Committee of Xi'an Jiaotong University (approval number: 20191278) and the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Spring Biological Technology Development Co., Ltd. (approval number: 201901). The study was conducted in accordance with the National Institutes of Health Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.

articles.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
articles.text:
NASA’s Roman Space Telescope exceeds expectations by nearly 30%
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has exceeded expectations after engineers made incredibly tiny adjustments to sharpen its view of the universe. By moving a mirror just one-sixteenth the width of a human hair, the team helped bring its powerful instruments into near-perfect alignment. Roman’s Wide Field Instrument now produces image quality nearly 30% better than predicted, promising exceptionally sharp cosmic surveys.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is performing even better than scientists anticipated after engineers completed an extensive series of tests and precision adjustments. The work has brought the observatory's powerful instruments into exceptionally sharp focus, with its main camera system now delivering image quality nearly 30% better than predicted.
The achievement marks an important step toward the telescope's ambitious mission to investigate dark matter, dark energy, and other mysteries of the universe. Even the smallest improvements in optical precision could help Roman capture clearer images during its sweeping surveys of the cosmos.
"All of Roman's sweeping surveys will rely on the Wide Field Instrument," said Dave Hickey, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "Many of the mission's primary goals, like studying dark matter and dark energy, wouldn't be possible without it, so it's both exciting and a huge relief to see that it's working well!"
NASA Puts Roman's Powerful Camera System to the Test
Following the activation of the Wide Field Instrument in September, engineers began a comprehensive testing campaign to confirm that each component worked properly on its own and as part of the complete system.
Their first priority was examining the instrument's 18 detectors, each roughly the size of a sticky note, along with the electronics that operate them. The team then evaluated the element wheel, a rotating mechanism equipped with filters and other optical components. These allow selected wavelengths of light to reach the detectors and can separate incoming light into its individual colors.
Next came the instrument's internal calibration system. Engineers activated its light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, which function as adjustable light sources that can produce different colors and brightness levels under commands from Earth. By measuring how the detectors respond to these controlled signals, scientists can identify differences in sensitivity and make the corrections needed for accurate observations.
Engineers also tested the instrument's alignment mechanism and moved it from the deliberately unfocused position used during launch to the position expected to provide the sharpest images. They finished by checking the thermal control system, which maintains the temperatures required for the instrument's various components to function correctly.
"Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," said Maxime Rizzo, a Wide Field Instrument systems engineer at NASA Goddard. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."
A Space Telescope Already Close to Perfect Alignment
While one group concentrated on preparing the Wide Field Instrument, another worked to refine the telescope's overall optical alignment.
The results were encouraging from the beginning. Roman's mirrors and other optical components were already positioned with remarkable accuracy, meaning engineers needed to make only minor corrections.
"The telescope's performance was excellent even before we began adjusting the alignment of all the mirrors and other optics, thanks to exceptional preparatory work done on the ground prior to launch," said Matthew Bolcar, Roman's optical systems lead at NASA Goddard. "All of the testing and modeling work done at Goddard and by contractors at L3Harris and BAE Space and Mission Systems left only small corrections for us to make to bring everything into near-perfect alignment."
Achieving that level of precision is especially challenging for a spacecraft. The forces experienced during launch can cause tiny shifts in sensitive equipment, and conditions in orbit differ significantly from those on Earth. Roman launched on August 30, carrying optical systems that had been meticulously tested before leaving the ground.
"Our ground testing couldn't exactly reproduce the environment Roman would experience in space, such as the absence of gravity," Bolcar said. "And there are also slight differences in temperature variations and moisture content. Despite those challenges, the recent assessments showed that our ground testing was excellent, with both instruments either matching or exceeding the performance we had predicted."
A Mirror Adjustment Smaller Than a Human Hair
Roman relies on an intricate arrangement of mirrors and optical components to collect light from distant cosmic objects and direct it toward its two scientific instruments. For the resulting images to remain sharp, the light must follow an extremely precise path.
Even a microscopic misalignment can affect how accurately the telescope brings light into focus.
Fortunately, Roman's optical system was already so well aligned that only incredibly small movements were necessary to improve its performance.
"We moved the secondary mirror by about one-sixteenth of the diameter of a human hair," said Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer working on Roman at NASA Goddard. "This adjustment nudged the height of the secondary mirror above the primary. If we scale that height up to the height of the Empire State Building, the change in height is a little bit less than you would get by stacking a single U.S. penny on top of the tip of the tower."
Although nearly impossible to appreciate at a human scale, such a small adjustment can make an important difference when a telescope is designed to study objects across vast cosmic distances.
The team initially concentrated on Roman's Coronagraph Instrument, which had been producing images that were slightly out of focus. The problem was less severe than engineers had anticipated, making it relatively straightforward to correct.
The coronagraph now meets the team's demanding performance expectations. Engineers will continue refining its camera settings and determining the optimal configurations for its deformable mirrors, which can change shape to make extremely precise corrections to incoming light.
In the coming weeks, the team plans to test the coronagraph's ability to block unwanted light, an essential capability for observing faint objects near much brighter ones.
Once the coronagraph's focus had been optimized, engineers returned to the Wide Field Instrument for another round of adjustments.
Roman's Image Quality Exceeds Expectations by Nearly 30%
The final measurements revealed an especially impressive result. Roman's Wide Field Instrument achieved optical performance nearly 30% better than the team had predicted.
Before launch, engineers established an image quality requirement of approximately 90 nanometers RMS (Root Mean Square). This measurement describes the amount of optical error in the system, or how far the incoming light deviates from an ideal, perfectly focused wavefront.
To put that scale into perspective, 90 nanometers is roughly 1,000 times thinner than a human hair. At these tiny dimensions, even seemingly insignificant imperfections can influence the sharpness of astronomical images.
After the latest corrections, however, engineers measured an optical error of just 63 nanometers RMS, substantially better than the original requirement.
That improvement means Roman should be capable of producing even sharper images than its designers initially expected, strengthening its ability to carry out detailed observations across enormous regions of the sky.
"All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Jurling said. "It's a great outcome from years of careful modeling, precision metrology, and testing."
With both scientific instruments meeting or surpassing their expected performance, Roman has cleared another important milestone in its preparation for routine observations. The results highlight the extraordinary precision of the telescope's design and offer a promising outlook for its upcoming investigations into the hidden structure and evolution of the universe.

articles.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
articles.text:
This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Lund University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.
- Share:
A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects.
The European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns.
Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds.
Why Nightjar Wings Sacrifice Efficiency for Agility
To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings.
The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne.
The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight.
"This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University.
Scientists Discover an Unexpected Wingbeat Trick
The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward.
This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds.
The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying.
"What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson.
What Bird Flight Reveals About Evolution and Flying Robots
The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities.
Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds.
Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings.
Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air.
Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation.
"We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes.

articles.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
articles.text:
Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Edinburgh
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.
- Share:
Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.
The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.
The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.
Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain
The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.
Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.
Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.
Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.
When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.
Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.
The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.
A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness
To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.
Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.
The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.
NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.
To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.
When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.
These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.
Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy
The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.
One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).
Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.
Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.
Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:
"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."
A New Understanding of Cognitive Decline
Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.
Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.
Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:
"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."
The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study was funded by the UKRI Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). The research also involved scientists from the University of Edinburgh's Lothian Birth Cohort studies and Northwestern University.

articles.title: NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
articles.text:
NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Trinity College Dublin
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a powerful new way to decode the weather on distant worlds, revealing surprisingly organized patterns hidden within the turbulent atmosphere of a mysterious object 20 light-years from Earth.
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin used observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf previously associated with phenomena resembling the northern lights. They found that its complex weather is largely governed by just two factors: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.
The discovery offers a new way to understand the atmospheric conditions of distant worlds and could help astronomers investigate planets far beyond our Solar System.
How NASA's Webb Telescope Decoded Alien Weather
To investigate SIMP 0136, the researchers analyzed observations collected by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) using a mathematical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
This technique helps scientists make sense of large, complicated datasets by identifying the strongest patterns within them. In this case, the team examined how the brown dwarf's light changed as it rotated, looking for subtle variations that could reveal what was happening in its atmosphere.
Rather than beginning with detailed assumptions about how the atmosphere should behave, the researchers allowed the observations to reveal the most important processes. The method also helped separate genuine atmospheric changes from minor fluctuations and random noise in the measurements.
Webb's exceptionally sensitive instruments made this possible by detecting extremely small changes in the object's brightness as different parts of its atmosphere rotated into view.
Scientists Discover Hidden Order in Chaotic Alien Weather
The results revealed something unexpected. Although SIMP 0136 appears to have a highly complicated atmosphere, nearly all of its observed atmospheric variability could be explained by just two dominant components, consistent with temperature fluctuations and changes in the vertical arrangement of clouds.
Even more remarkably, the researchers identified three recurring weather states that appear and disappear from view as the brown dwarf rotates.
Together, these states create a shifting atmospheric patchwork. Some regions are hotter and have thinner clouds, while others are cooler and contain thicker cloud layers that extend farther vertically through the atmosphere.
Instead of constantly changing in an unpredictable way, these weather patterns appear to follow an underlying structure.
The findings, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, suggest that the seemingly chaotic atmosphere of SIMP 0136 is actually governed by a remarkably consistent set of processes.
Brown dwarfs occupy an unusual place between planets and stars. SIMP 0136 is larger and hotter than a typical gas giant planet, but it lacks the mass needed to shine like a star. Its atmosphere contains enormous cloud systems that evolve rapidly, making its weather more comparable to an extreme version of Jupiter's than anything experienced on Earth.
These immense weather systems can span planetary scales, continually changing the appearance of the distant world.
"We also discovered that these drivers of the weather patterns on SIMP-0136 persist over time, even as the detailed appearance of the atmosphere evolves over more than a dozen rotations," said first author Merle Schrader, a PhD candidate in Trinity's School of Physics.
"In relative terms, SIMP 0136 is one of the easier brown dwarfs for us to capture high-quality data from. These data have been studied before by established methods, allowing us to compare some of the results from this new technique to what we already know about this object. The technique has also helped us develop a better understanding of what drives the weather on this faraway world and how these weather patterns interact and co-exist, but perhaps even more importantly, it shows how this approach can be further refined and applied to other, less well-known brown dwarfs in different parts of space."
A Remarkable Connection Across 20 Light Years
For Schrader, the research also revealed an extraordinary personal connection to the distant object.
SIMP 0136 is located approximately 20 light years from Earth, meaning its light takes about two decades to reach us. The light captured by Webb in 2023, which provided the observations used in the study, had actually left the brown dwarf during the year Schrader was born.
"Light travels at around 300,000 km/s but, even at that speed, it took two decades to reach us, peering through the JWST lenses," she said.
"When you consider light takes just over a second to reach the Moon after leaving Earth, that gives a sense of how far away SIMP 0136 is, and how incredible astrophysical progress has been. I think it's amazing that we have been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum."
The achievement highlights how much information astronomers can extract from seemingly tiny amounts of light. Even though SIMP 0136 appears as little more than a single point in telescope observations, changes in its brightness at different wavelengths can reveal detailed information about its atmosphere.
What This Discovery Means for Distant Planets
The new technique could have implications far beyond SIMP 0136.
Brown dwarfs are particularly valuable for investigating the atmospheres of giant exoplanets, which are planets orbiting stars outside our Solar System. Because brown dwarfs can often be observed directly, they give scientists an opportunity to study atmospheric processes that are much harder to investigate on most exoplanets.
By examining these objects, researchers can test how clouds form, how heat moves through an atmosphere, and how atmospheric circulation behaves under extreme conditions.
The technique developed by the Trinity team could make those investigations considerably more efficient. By quickly identifying the processes responsible for most of the observed atmospheric changes, astronomers can better determine which features deserve closer examination using more complicated computer models.
Professor Johanna Vos, Associate Professor in Trinity School of Physics, explained the potential significance of the findings.
"Our findings will transform how astronomers analyze future JWST observations. Since our approach rapidly identifies the dominant components of the atmosphere it offers an efficient first step before we begin computationally intensive modeling.
"Applying this technique to a wide range of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets will help us better understand the diverse weather systems that shape worlds far beyond our Solar System."
Ultimately, understanding weather on distant worlds is about more than identifying clouds and temperature changes. Atmospheric behavior can provide important clues about a planet's chemical composition, physical conditions, and overall environment.
Those insights are also relevant to one of astronomy's biggest questions: which planets beyond our Solar System might have conditions capable of supporting life?
By revealing how complex alien atmospheres can be understood from faint changes in light, this new approach could help scientists take another step toward answering that question.

articles.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
articles.text:
A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
Forest soils may be quietly helping fight climate change more effectively than scientists expected.
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Göttingen
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
- Share:
Forest soils are playing a surprisingly powerful role in removing methane from the atmosphere, and new findings suggest that certain effects of climate change could make them even better at it. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, but microorganisms living in the soil can break it down before it builds up in the air.
Scientists from the University of Göttingen and the Baden-Württemberg Forest Research Institute (FVA) analyzed the world's most comprehensive collection of long-term measurements of methane absorption by forest soils. Their findings revealed an unexpected trend: under certain climate conditions that could become more common in the future, forest soils can actually increase the amount of methane they remove from the atmosphere.
The researchers examined measurements collected from 13 forest sites in southwestern Germany over periods of up to 24 years. On average, the amount of methane absorbed by the soils increased by approximately 3% annually. The researchers linked this rise to declining rainfall and warmer temperatures, which create conditions that make it easier for methane to enter the soil and be broken down by microorganisms.
The findings, published in Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, challenge previous research suggesting that climate change is generally reducing the ability of forest soils to absorb methane.
How Scientists Measured Methane Absorption Over 24 Years
To understand how methane absorption changes over time, the researchers examined an extensive collection of soil gas measurements gathered through the FVA's long-running monitoring program.
The measurements included soil gas profiles, which reveal the chemical composition of gases trapped in the soil at different depths. Every two weeks, researchers collected air samples through thin tubes installed beneath the ground and analyzed them in a laboratory. This repeated sampling allowed scientists to track changes in methane concentrations over many years.
To confirm their findings, the team also used an independent measurement technique involving airtight chambers placed directly on the soil surface. By monitoring how gas concentrations changed inside these chambers, the researchers could determine whether the soil was absorbing methane and calculate how much was being removed.
Combining these methods gave the scientists a detailed picture of methane uptake across the forest sites and how it responded to changing environmental conditions.
Why Warmer, Drier Forest Soils Absorb More Methane
Although methane absorption varied considerably between the 13 locations, a clear overall pattern emerged. Forest soils in southwestern Germany were particularly effective at removing methane from the atmosphere during periods of lower rainfall and higher temperatures.
"Our long-term data shows that climate change does not necessarily have a negative impact on how much methane forest soils absorb. While the largest study to date from the US found a decline in methane uptake of up to 80 percent due to increasing rainfall, our significantly more comprehensive field study in south-western Germany found the opposite, " explains Professor Martin Maier at Göttingen University's Department of Crop Sciences, who led the study and was previously involved in the FVA's soil gas monitoring program.
"We observed a significant long-term increase in methane uptake in the forest areas we studied."
The explanation lies partly in how water moves through the ground. When soil becomes saturated with moisture, water fills many of the tiny spaces between soil particles, making it more difficult for gases to move through them. Drier soil contains more pores filled with air, allowing atmospheric methane to travel deeper into the ground.
Once methane enters the soil, microorganisms use it as an energy source, breaking it down in the process. Rising temperatures can slightly accelerate this microbial activity, allowing the organisms to consume methane more quickly.
Together, these two effects help explain why warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall were associated with greater methane absorption in the forests studied.
Findings Challenge Previous Climate Change Research
The results offer a different perspective from several major international research reviews. These analyses, known as meta-analyses, combine findings from numerous individual studies to identify broader patterns. Many have concluded that methane absorption by forest soils is declining.
However, the German study suggests that the relationship between climate change and methane uptake is more complicated than those overall trends indicate. While increasing rainfall can reduce methane absorption by limiting the movement of gas through soil, drier conditions can produce the opposite effect.
The findings do not mean that climate change is beneficial for forests overall. Instead, they demonstrate that its effects on methane absorption can differ considerably depending on local temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions.
The researchers emphasize that these regional differences make long-term monitoring especially important. Shorter studies or analyses that combine measurements from widely different environments may miss gradual changes that only become apparent after years of observation.
"Our results make it clear that taking a series of measurements over many years and running monitoring programs are indispensable for assessing the real effects of climate change," says Maier.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Göttingen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Verena Lang, Valentin Gartiser, Peter Hartmann, Martin Maier. Trend analysis of methane uptake in 13 forest soils based on up to 24 years of field measurements in south-west Germany. Agricultural and Forest Meteorology, 2025; 375: 110823 DOI: 10.1016/j.agrformet.2025.110823
