articles.title: A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
articles.text:
A 47-year study reveals the age when your body starts losing strength
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Karolinska Insitutet
- Summary:
- A 47-year study has uncovered a surprising turning point in physical aging: fitness and strength begin declining around age 35, even among people who exercise regularly. Researchers found that this decline accelerates as people get older, but starting to exercise in adulthood can still improve physical performance.
- Share:
Aging may begin to affect your physical abilities earlier than you expect. A remarkable 47-year Swedish study found that fitness, muscle endurance, and physical performance generally begin declining around age 35, even among people who remain active.
But the findings also offer an encouraging message. Although exercise cannot completely prevent the physical changes associated with aging, becoming more active during adulthood can still produce meaningful improvements in fitness and strength.
Researchers at Karolinska Institutet in Sweden spent nearly five decades tracking how people's physical abilities changed as they grew older. Their findings, published in 2025 in the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, help explain when physical decline begins, how it progresses, and why staying active remains important throughout life.
A 47-Year Study Reveals When Physical Fitness Peaks
The research was part of the Swedish Physical Activity and Fitness study (SPAF), which followed 427 randomly selected men and women born in 1958. Participants underwent physical assessments over 47 years, beginning at age 16 and continuing through age 63.
Unlike most earlier research on physical aging, which compared people of different ages at a single point in time, this project repeatedly examined the same individuals as they grew older.
That distinction matters because physical abilities vary considerably from person to person. Following individuals over decades allowed researchers to observe how fitness changed within the same population rather than relying on comparisons between different generations.
The assessments included aerobic fitness, muscular endurance, and muscle power. Aerobic fitness describes how effectively the body uses oxygen during exercise, while muscular endurance measures how long muscles can continue working. Muscle power reflects the ability to produce force quickly, which is important for activities such as jumping, climbing stairs, and maintaining mobility.
The results revealed a consistent pattern. Aerobic fitness and muscular endurance generally reached their highest levels between ages 26 and 36, with physical performance beginning to decline around the mid-30s. Some abilities, particularly explosive muscle power, peaked even earlier.
The decline was initially modest but became progressively faster with age. By age 63, average performance across the measurements had fallen by roughly 30 to 48 percent from peak levels.
Importantly, the pattern appeared in both men and women. Although individual fitness levels differed, the overall rates of age-related decline were similar between the sexes.
Exercise Can Slow Physical Decline, Even After 35
One of the most striking findings was that regular physical activity did not entirely prevent the decline associated with aging. Even people who remained physically active showed evidence of diminishing performance as they grew older.
However, exercise made an important difference in how well people maintained their abilities.
Participants who became physically active during adulthood experienced improvements in physical capacity of approximately 5 to 10 percent. Those who were already active during adolescence also tended to maintain better fitness, endurance, and muscle power throughout adulthood.
These findings suggest that physical decline is not simply the result of becoming less active with age. Biological changes also appear to contribute, although exercise can help reduce their impact.
"It is never too late to start moving. Our study shows that physical activity can slow the decline in performance, even if it cannot completely stop it. Now we will look for the mechanisms behind why everyone reaches their peak performance at age 35 and why physical activity can slow performance loss but not completely halt it," says Maria Westerståhl, lecturer at the Department of Laboratory Medicine and lead author of the study.
The distinction is important. Reaching an average physical peak in the mid-30s does not mean everyone suddenly becomes weaker at that age. People can continue improving their individual fitness and strength through training, even after the age when population averages begin to decline.
Why Does the Body Start Losing Strength?
Scientists are still investigating exactly why physical performance begins deteriorating relatively early in adulthood.
Several biological processes are thought to contribute. As people age, changes in muscle cells, the nervous system, and the body's ability to produce energy can gradually reduce physical performance.
One possible contributor involves mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells that convert nutrients into usable energy. Changes in mitochondrial function may affect how efficiently muscles produce the energy required for movement.
Over time, muscles can also lose mass and become less responsive to the signals that trigger growth and repair. More advanced muscle deterioration can contribute to sarcopenia, an age-related condition involving the loss of muscle strength and mass that can make everyday activities increasingly difficult.
Although these processes often become more noticeable later in life, the Swedish findings suggest that some underlying changes in physical function begin decades earlier.
The researchers hope to determine which biological mechanisms drive this decline and why physical activity can delay, but not completely prevent, the loss of performance.
Follow-Up Research Links Early Fitness to Heart Health
The importance of maintaining physical fitness throughout adulthood extends beyond muscle strength.
In a 2026 follow-up study published in Scientific Reports, researchers examined additional health outcomes using the same Swedish cohort. They found that people with better aerobic fitness at ages 34 and 52 tended to have less arterial stiffness at age 63.
Arterial stiffness occurs when blood vessels become less flexible, making it harder for them to expand and contract as blood moves through the body. Greater stiffness is associated with increased cardiovascular risk.
Notably, the relationship between earlier fitness and later artery health remained significant even after accounting for several established cardiovascular risk factors, including obesity, smoking, and blood pressure.
The results do not establish that better fitness directly prevented arterial stiffening. However, they suggest that maintaining aerobic capacity during early and middle adulthood may have benefits that extend well into later life.
More Evidence That Staying Active Pays Off
Other research has reinforced the idea that exercise remains valuable even when physical performance inevitably declines with age.
A 2026 study published in GeroScience followed 82 older adults who continued cycling over a nine-year period. Despite maintaining active lifestyles, participants experienced an average 19.7 percent decline in peak aerobic capacity.
Yet their fitness remained remarkably high. Nearly all participants who completed the exercise test performed at or above the 90th percentile for their age when compared with reference populations.
The findings suggest that although regular exercise cannot eliminate biological aging, it can help people maintain unusually high levels of physical function as they get older.
Another 2026 study in The American Journal of Medicine followed 49 men ages 60 to 82 who had not previously participated in structured exercise training.
Over four years, participants who performed weekly resistance exercises improved their upper and lower body strength. Those who combined resistance training with aerobic exercise also improved their aerobic fitness.
Although the study was relatively small and participants chose their training programs, its findings support the idea that meaningful physical improvements remain possible well into older adulthood.
It's Never Too Late to Improve Your Fitness
The original Swedish research is continuing, with investigators planning another round of assessments when participants reach age 68.
The next stage is intended to explore how long-term changes in physical performance relate to lifestyle, overall health, and the biological processes responsible for aging.
Together, the findings point to an important distinction between getting older and becoming physically inactive. Some loss of fitness and strength appears to be a natural part of aging, but the extent of that decline can vary substantially.
While the body may begin losing some of its physical capabilities around age 35, those changes do not eliminate the benefits of exercise. Whether someone begins exercising in their 30s, 50s, or later, becoming more active can still help improve physical performance and preserve the abilities needed for a healthier, more independent life.

Materials provided by Karolinska Insitutet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Nếu Mặt trời đột ngột biến mất, chuyện gì sẽ xảy ra? Khoa học vào cuộc, kết quả bất ngờ!
articles.text:
Nếu không có Mặt trời giữ Trái đất trên quỹ đạo, hành tinh của chúng ta có thể sẽ bắt đầu trôi vào không gian. Trong khi đó nhân loại phải cố gắng sống sót một cách tuyệt vọng.
Khoảng 4,5 tỷ năm trước, Hệ Mặt trời được hình thành sau khi một đám mây bụi và khí khổng lồ sụp đổ. Hệ Mặt trời gồm có Mặt trời và các hành tinh. Trong đó, Mặt trời là ngôi sao lớn tới mức trọng lực của nó có thể kéo và giữ rất nhiều hành tinh, sao chổi và cả thiên thạch quay quanh nó. Điều này có thể thấy rằng Mặt trời có vai trò rất quan trọng.
Nếu Mặt trời đột ngột biến mất, có khả năng Trái đất sẽ đi vào quỹ đạo xung quanh một ngôi sao khác. Đó là ngôi sao có thể cung cấp ánh sáng và nhiệt lượng tương tự như Mặt trời. Tuy nhiên, cho đến khi điều đó xảy ra thì tất cả con người có thể đã biến mất từ lâu.
Trong khi đó, trên thực tế, ánh sáng mất khoảng 8 phút rưỡi để đi từ Mặt trời đến Trái đất. Do đó, nếu Mặt trời biến mất, chúng ta vẫn sẽ có 8 phút rưỡi trước khi Trái đất bị chìm vào trong bóng tối. Ngoài ra, điện cũng sẽ giúp thắp sáng trong một thời gian.
Nếu Mặt trời biến mất thì có thể gây ảnh hưởng rất lớn tới Trái đất. (Ảnh: SciTechDaily).
Một vấn đề đáng lo ngại khác sẽ xảy ra nếu Mặt trời biến mất. Đó là phá vỡ quỹ đạo của những thiên thể trong Hệ Mặt trời. Do lực hấp dẫn của Mặt trời biến mất nên tất cả các hành tinh sẽ lao thẳng về phía trước.
Thế nhưng Trái đất sẽ lạnh đi rất nhanh. Do đó, nếu biết trước ngày Mặt trời sẽ sụp đổ, nhân loại có thể sẽ phải chuẩn bị cho một kịch bản sinh tồn trong 1.000 năm. Điều này có thể xảy ra nếu chúng ta có đủ nguồn lực để duy trì trong khoảng thời gian dài đó.
Trên thực tế, chỉ cách Trái đất vài mét, hành tinh của chúng ta duy trì ở nhiệt độ khoảng 17 độ C. Do đó, nếu con người có đủ thời gian để chuẩn bị, nền văn minh có thể tiếp tục tồn tại bằng cách di chuyển xuống lòng đất. Con người sẽ sống trong một mạng lưới boongke kiên cố khổng lồ.
Trong vòng 1 tuần sau khi Mặt trời biến mất, nhiệt độ ở bề mặt Trái đất sẽ giảm xuống -17,8 độ C. Sau đó, trong vòng 1 năm, nhiệt độ sẽ giảm mạnh xuống khoảng -73,3 độ C. Khi đó, các đại dương trên thế giới sẽ bắt đầu đóng băng từ trên xuống.
Khi không có ánh sáng Mặt trời, quá trình quang hợp sẽ dừng lại. Điều này sẽ khiến hầu hết thực vật sẽ nhanh chóng chết. Những vẫn có một số cây lớn có thể tồn tại thêm vài thập kỷ mà không cần đến quang hợp.
Trong vòng 1.000 năm, bầu khí quyển của Trái đất cũng sẽ sụp đổ. Lúc bấy giờ, những thứ còn sót lại ở trên bề mặt sẽ phải tiếp xúc với bức xạ vũ trụ và tác động của thiên thạch.
Mặt trời chiếm tới 98% khối lượng của toàn bộ Hệ Mặt trời. So với hành tinh dày đặc nhất là Trái đất, Mặt trời lớn gấp 1,3 triệu lần về thể tích.
Theo các nhà khoa học, Trái đất sẽ trở thành nơi rất khác nếu như có cùng kích thước với Mặt trời. Cụ thể, nếu Trái đất lớn bằng Mặt trời về cả kích thước và khối lượng, thì không chỉ gây nguy hiểm cho sự tồn tại của con người mà còn làm phá vỡ toàn bộ Hệ Mặt trời.
Nếu Trái đất lớn như Mặt trời, thậm chí là lớn hơn, thì có thể phá vỡ toàn bộ Hệ Mặt trời. (Ảnh minh họa).
Chúng ta cũng sẽ mất Mặt Trăng theo cách nào đó. Khi Trái đất trở nên nặng hơn, lực hấp dẫn của hành tinh này cũng mạnh hơn. Trong trường hợp này, lực hấp dẫn ở trên Trái đất sẽ mạnh gấp 28 lần hiện tại.
Vì sao Hệ Mặt trời lại chuyển động như bây giờ? Nguyên nhân là do Mặt trời có khối lượng lớn vượt trội. Nhờ vậy, lực hấp dẫn áp đảo đã ép các hành tinh phải vào quỹ đạo của nó.
Thế nhưng nếu Mặt trời và Trái đất đều chiếm tới 49% khối lượng của Hệ Mặt trời, thì điều này có thể dẫn tới sự hình thành của một loại hệ thống nhị phân. Trong đó, Mặt trời và Trái đất quay quanh nhau.
Lúc bấy giờ, quỹ đạo của các hành tinh khác ở trong Hệ Mặt trời chắc chắn cũng sẽ bị ảnh hưởng. Lực hấp dẫn mạnh hơn đáng kể cũng khiến Trái đất tiềm ẩn nguy cơ về việc va chạm với tiểu hành tinh cao hơn.
Ngoài ra, sẽ còn rất nhiều điều phải lo lắng về những tiểu hành tinh. Ngoài ra, các vệ tinh nhân tạo của con người trong không gian cũng có thể rơi xuống Trái đất. Trong khi đó, nhà cửa và cầu đường có thể sẽ bị sụp đổ dưới áp lực trọng trường gia tăng.
Chỉ có những cây thấp và thân dày mới đứng vững. Bởi vì những cây cao khó chịu được trọng lượng tăng thêm.
Con người cũng sẽ nặng hơn đáng kể và gặp khó khăn trong việc đi lại. Hãy tưởng tượng, nếu bạn nặng 50kg trên Trái đất bây giờ, bạn sẽ cảm thấy như nặng 1.400kg khi ở trên Trái đất lớn như Mặt trời.
Đặc biệt, khi lực hấp dẫn tăng lên, thời gian sẽ bị chậm lại. Do đó, con người có thể sống lâu hơn, nhưng đó có lẽ là một cuộc đời dài nằm trên giường với những cơn đau nhức.
May mắn rằng chúng ta không cần lo lắng về cơn ác mộng này, bởi vì Trái đất sẽ không bao giờ lớn bằng Mặt trời. Thay vào đó, thực tế cho thấy Trái đất của chúng ta đang nhỏ đi. Bầu khí quyển của Trái đất đang bị rò rỉ khiến hành tinh xanh mất hàng trăm tấn khối lượng vào không gian mỗi ngày.

articles.title: Tại sao nhiều nhà khoa học cho rằng kiến là sinh vật tiến hóa hoàn hảo nhất trên Trái đất?
articles.text:
Một nghiên cứu gần đây từ các nhà khoa học đã tiết lộ những điều đáng ngạc nhiên về loài kiến. Không chỉ là sinh vật chăm chỉ và có tổ chức, kiến còn có thể là loài sinh vật tiến hóa hoàn hảo nhất trên Trái đất.
Các nhà nghiên cứu cho rằng chúng vượt trội so với con người trong một số lĩnh vực như kỹ thuật xây dựng, nông nghiệp, và "chăn gia súc". Hệ thống xã hội của kiến không chỉ giúp chúng cạnh tranh tốt hơn trong việc sinh tồn mà còn tạo ra một nguồn gene phong phú, giúp chúng trở thành một phần không thể thiếu của hệ sinh thái.
Khi nhìn vào kết quả nghiên cứu này, không ít người đã liên tưởng đến sự tiến hóa và khả năng xã hội hóa của loài người. Việc so sánh hai loài, kiến và con người, mở ra nhiều góc nhìn thú vị về việc chúng ta có thể học hỏi từ thiên nhiên và đặc biệt là từ loài kiến.
Kiến được nhìn nhận như những kỹ sư "hoàn hảo" trong tự nhiên.
Kiến từ lâu đã được biết đến với sự cần cù và trí thông minh, nhưng giờ đây, chúng còn được nhìn nhận như những kỹ sư "hoàn hảo" trong tự nhiên. Đặc biệt, hiệu suất và kỹ năng của chúng trong các lĩnh vực xây dựng, nông nghiệp và chăn nuôi đã khiến nhiều nhà khoa học không khỏi ngưỡng mộ.
Kiến nổi tiếng với khả năng xây dựng tổ một cách hiệu quả và bền vững. Trong quá trình làm tổ, chúng sử dụng các chất do chính cơ thể tiết ra để kết dính các hạt đất lại với nhau. Tổ kiến, mặc dù có kích thước nhỏ bé, nhưng lại là một cấu trúc vô cùng phức tạp. Nó không chỉ là nơi trú ẩn mà còn đáp ứng đầy đủ nhu cầu sống của cả đàn kiến. Khả năng tạo ra những công trình kiên cố với "kỹ thuật tự nhiên" này khiến chúng được xem như những nhà thiết kế tài ba trong giới động vật.
Kiến cũng có khả năng "canh tác nông nghiệp" rất đáng nể.
Không dừng lại ở việc xây dựng, kiến cũng có khả năng "canh tác nông nghiệp" rất đáng nể. Chúng trồng và chăm sóc một số loại nấm hoặc cây trồng xung quanh tổ để tạo nguồn thức ăn cho cả đàn. Những loại cây này được kiến quản lý và chăm sóc kỹ lưỡng, giống như con người trồng rau và chăm sóc mùa màng. Khi những chiếc lá hoặc nấm phát triển đủ lớn, chúng sẽ được sử dụng làm nguồn thức ăn phong phú cho cả đàn kiến. Đây có thể coi là một ví dụ rõ ràng về việc loài kiến biết cách tận dụng môi trường xung quanh để tự duy trì sự sống, mà không cần đến công cụ hay máy móc phức tạp.
Không chỉ biết trồng trọt, kiến còn có "kỹ năng chăn nuôi gia súc" không thua kém gì con người. Một số loài kiến "nuôi" rệp, không phải để ăn thịt mà để khai thác chất ngọt do rệp tiết ra. Để đảm bảo sự an toàn cho những con rệp này, kiến bảo vệ chúng khỏi các loài săn mồi và tạo môi trường thuận lợi cho chúng sinh sản. Điều này tương tự như việc con người nuôi gia súc và lấy sản phẩm từ chúng. Sự phối hợp hoàn hảo giữa loài kiến và những "đàn gia súc rệp" này là một trong những minh chứng rõ ràng về khả năng tổ chức và quản lý tài tình của loài kiến.
Qua nghiên cứu của các nhà khoa học, "gene hoàn hảo" của loài kiến đã mang lại nhiều cảm hứng cho con người, đặc biệt là về cách tổ chức xã hội và tiến hóa. Hệ thống xã hội của loài kiến không chỉ mạnh mẽ mà còn phát triển theo hướng cộng sinh, đồng thịnh vượng. Mỗi cá thể trong đàn đều có vai trò riêng, nhưng đều đặt lợi ích của cả đàn lên trên hết. Điều này giúp loài kiến dễ dàng thích nghi với môi trường và vượt qua các thử thách sinh tồn.
Ở một mức độ nào đó, loài người cũng là những "động vật xã hội". Chúng ta sống và làm việc theo hệ thống xã hội, và sự hợp tác giữa các cá nhân trong xã hội là yếu tố then chốt giúp con người tiến bộ. Tuy nhiên, khác với loài kiến, con người lại có sự khác biệt về di truyền và tính cách, điều này đôi khi khiến chúng ta khó đạt được mức độ tổ chức và đoàn kết cao như kiến. Tuy vậy, chính những khác biệt này lại là yếu tố giúp xã hội loài người phát triển đa dạng và phong phú hơn.
Các nhà khoa học và kỹ sư có thể học hỏi từ loài kiến để thiết kế những tòa nhà tiết kiệm năng lượng.
Bên cạnh các khía cạnh xã hội, loài kiến còn mang lại cho con người những bài học quý báu trong các lĩnh vực như xây dựng, nông nghiệp và chăn nuôi.
Cấu trúc tổ kiến với khả năng chống đỡ và tối ưu hóa không gian là nguồn cảm hứng lớn cho kiến trúc hiện đại. Các nhà khoa học và kỹ sư có thể học hỏi từ loài kiến để thiết kế những tòa nhà tiết kiệm năng lượng, thân thiện với môi trường và có khả năng chống chọi với các hiện tượng tự nhiên như gió bão, động đất.
Cách loài kiến trồng nấm hoặc "chăm sóc cây trồng" xung quanh tổ cũng gợi ý cho con người về mô hình nông nghiệp bền vững. Thay vì canh tác quy mô lớn và gây ảnh hưởng đến môi trường, chúng ta có thể học tập mô hình sản xuất nông nghiệp của kiến, nơi cây trồng được chăm sóc tự nhiên và không cần sự can thiệp quá mức của con người.
Kỹ năng chăn gia súc của kiến, thông qua việc nuôi rệp và bảo vệ chúng khỏi kẻ thù, cũng có thể truyền cảm hứng cho việc phát triển các mô hình chăn nuôi thân thiện với thiên nhiên. Thay vì nuôi gia súc trong môi trường công nghiệp, chúng ta có thể để chúng phát triển trong môi trường tự nhiên, từ đó tạo ra những sản phẩm lành mạnh hơn cho con người.
Từ khả năng xây dựng, nông nghiệp cho đến chăn nuôi, kiến cho thấy sự khéo léo và hiệu quả vượt trội.
Sự tiến hóa và tổ chức xã hội của loài kiến đã mang lại rất nhiều bài học quý giá cho con người. Từ khả năng xây dựng, nông nghiệp cho đến chăn nuôi, kiến cho thấy sự khéo léo và hiệu quả vượt trội trong việc tận dụng nguồn lực thiên nhiên. Chúng không chỉ là những sinh vật nhỏ bé, mà còn là một phần quan trọng của hệ sinh thái toàn cầu. Con người, với trí tuệ và khả năng sáng tạo, có thể học hỏi từ loài kiến để phát triển các lĩnh vực khác nhau, đồng thời hiểu rõ hơn về quá trình tiến hóa sinh học và mối quan hệ hài hòa giữa con người và tự nhiên.
Cuối cùng, loài kiến không chỉ là một biểu tượng của sự chăm chỉ, mà còn là một minh chứng cho sự tiến hóa hoàn hảo của tự nhiên. Sự hiểu biết sâu sắc về chúng có thể giúp con người xây dựng một xã hội bền vững, hài hòa hơn với thiên nhiên.

articles.title: Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
articles.text:
Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Flinders University
- Summary:
- A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history.
- Share:
New research suggests that Australia's Indigenous population before European colonization was far larger than historical estimates have indicated. Scientists now estimate that approximately 2.22 million Indigenous people lived across the continent before the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, potentially up to seven times the number suggested by some earlier calculations.
The findings also reveal the devastating scale of the population decline that followed colonization. According to the researchers, an estimated 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost within less than 80 years of European arrival, a much greater decline than previously recognized.
Professor Corey Bradshaw, a Global Ecology Professor at Flinders University and Chief Investigator at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), contributed to the national research effort. Working alongside Indigenous partners, the team is investigating how Indigenous population numbers have changed throughout Australia's history.
By combining advanced computer models with several sources of historical and scientific evidence, the researchers developed new estimates that substantially challenge previous assumptions.
"Understanding the size of Indigenous populations in Australia before European invasion in 1788 is essential to truth-telling and reconciliation," says Professor Bradshaw.
New Evidence Reveals Millions of Indigenous Australians Before Colonization
To reconstruct Australia's Indigenous population before European settlement, the researchers brought together ethnographic observations, archaeological findings, genetic reconstructions, and computer models. They also examined how many people different environments across the continent could have supported.
Earlier population estimates often relied heavily on calculations made during the 1930s by anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown. His influential assessment placed Australia's Indigenous population before colonization at approximately 250,000 people.
However, Radcliffe-Brown recognized that his estimate did not fully account for the devastating effects of deadly diseases, violence along colonial frontiers, and broader structural violence. Subsequent research has shown that these forces had a much greater impact than was historically acknowledged, suggesting that many early population figures were already substantial underestimates.
Using modeled and genetics-based estimates (supported by, but not relying on, historical or ethnographic accounts), the team calculated a median Indigenous population of 2.22 million before colonization. This corresponds to approximately 0.29 people per square kilometer across Australia.
The figure is substantially higher than earlier historical estimates, which generally ranged from 250,000 to 1 million people.
Researchers believe those lower estimates were influenced by the widespread population losses caused by disease, frontier violence, and systemic oppression before the earliest Australian censuses were conducted.
A Devastating 93% Population Collapse After 1788
The revised population estimate also allowed scientists to calculate the scale of the demographic catastrophe that followed European colonization.
Using their model alongside early census records, the researchers estimated that approximately 2.06 million excess deaths occurred between 1788 and 1861. That represents an average of roughly 28,200 excess deaths annually over the 73-year period.
By 1861, the Indigenous population had declined to an estimated 7% of its size before colonization, representing a staggering 93% reduction.
"These devastating findings highlight the major impacts of invasion experienced by Indigenous Australians, and demonstrate their remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century," says lead author Associate Professor Alan Williams, a Partner Investigator in CIEHF representing EMM Consulting and who is also an Adjunct Research Fellow at James Cook University.
Although Australia's Indigenous population has increased since the 1950s, it has not yet returned to its estimated size before European arrival.
According to the 2021 Australian census, the Indigenous population was approximately 37% of the study's estimated median population in 1788.
If population growth continues along current trends, the researchers project that Indigenous population numbers may not return to their estimated pre-colonial level until around 2047.
What the Findings Mean for Australia's History
Beyond revising historical population figures, the study highlights the long-lasting consequences of colonization for Indigenous Australians.
The researchers say the scale of the demographic collapse has important implications for understanding intergenerational trauma, persistent disadvantage, and the development of policies that better support Indigenous communities.
"The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonization, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people. In addition to recognizing this intergenerational trauma and disadvantage, it is also time to recognize intergenerational privilege," says co-author Distinguished Professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.
The findings also demonstrate why scientists must draw on several independent methods when reconstructing population histories, particularly when written records are incomplete, unreliable, or shaped by historical biases.
By combining genetic research, archaeological evidence, environmental modeling, and historical information, the team was able to develop a more comprehensive picture of Australia's Indigenous population before and after European colonization.
Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO, Chair of the CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee, says the findings demand a fundamental reassessment of the country's history while also recognizing the extraordinary endurance of Indigenous Australians.
"These research findings challenge us to rethink the scale of what happened after 1788. We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonization but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story. But the research also tells us something extraordinary. Our survival is one of Australian history's most remarkable stories," said Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO Chair, CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee.
The study, "Large size of the Australian Indigenous population prior to its massive decline following colonial invasion," was published in Nature Human Behaviour. Its authors are Alan Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew Nitschke, Michael Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, and Corey Bradshaw.
The research received joint funding from the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CE230100009) and the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Australian Biodiversity and Heritage (CE17010001).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Flinders University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alan N. Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew C. Nitschke, Michael I. Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian J. McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, Corey J. A. Bradshaw. articles.title: 'A uniquely direct route that might cause damage': Scientists uncover link between air pollution and eye diseases like glaucoma
articles.text:
'A uniquely direct route that might cause damage': Scientists uncover link between air pollution and eye diseases like glaucoma
A review of 41 studies found that higher exposure to air pollution was linked to greater odds of glaucoma and cataracts, with PM2.5 pollution showing the clearest association.
Aging is one of the biggest risk factors for developing glaucoma or cataracts — but as scientists look more closely at what happens to the eyes over a lifetime, they are finding that people's exposure to air pollution also plays a role in whether they develop these eye conditions.
Glaucoma, which affects about 80 million people worldwide, is a group of diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It can lead to permanent vision loss, usually affecting peripheral vision at first and later central vision. Cataracts are even more common, affecting more than 94 million people globally; the condition occurs when the eye's lens becomes cloudy, causing blurred vision and, eventually, blindness.
Aging raises the risk of both diseases, as do certain medical conditions, such as diabetes. But now, a review of 41 studies suggests that people who are exposed to higher levels of air pollution may also face a greater risk of these diseases. The research, presented in September at the 44th Congress of the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons in London, brought together evidence from dozens of studies collectively involving millions of people across East Asia and the U.K.
The studies were observational, meaning they can only draw a link between air pollution and the eye conditions, rather than prove that air pollution causes the diseases. But still, "this reframes glaucoma and cataract as conditions shaped by where you live and breathe, not just how long you've lived," said study co-author Dr. Ahmed Alnabihi, an ophthalmologist at King Khaled Eye Specialist Hospital and Research Center in Saudi Arabia, who presented the findings. These environmental exposures may compound age-related decline in the eye as they do in cardiovascular disease, he said.
PM2.5 shows the clearest links
The researchers examined exposure to several pollutants, including different sizes of particulate matter (PM), such as fine PM2.5 and larger PM10. They also looked at nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide.
Most studies included in the review estimated people's long-term exposure based on the pollution levels around their homes and in their communities. They used a range of methods, including government monitoring systems, satellite data and computer models designed to estimate pollution levels. A few studies examined short-term exposure and its relation to more sudden eye issues, such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency that can quickly cause vision loss.
Using this wealth of data, the team compared pollution exposure with rates of glaucoma, cataracts and age-related macular degeneration (AMD), another common eye condition that impairs vision. PM2.5 — tiny particles that measure 2.5 micrometers or smaller — showed the clearest associations with glaucoma and cataract risk.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
People with the highest exposure to PM2.5 had 70% higher odds of glaucoma, compared to those with the least exposure. Plus, an increase in PM2.5 exposure equivalent to the difference between the 25th and 75th percentiles of exposure within each study was associated with 8% higher odds of glaucoma and a 4% higher hazard of cataracts.
The evidence was less consistent for air pollution and age-related macular degeneration, which damages the central part of the retina that's responsible for sharp, detailed vision. And unlike the clear connection seen with PM2.5, other pollutants showed less consistent links to eye disease. For instance, nitrogen dioxide was not significantly tied to AMD, ozone was not tied to cataracts, and neither pollutant was linked to glaucoma. Sulfur dioxide and PM10 showed no significant associations with any of the three conditions.
The association between PM2.5 and glaucoma was relatively consistent across the reviewed studies, said Nidhi Singh, an environmental epidemiologist at the IUF-Leibniz Research Institute for Environmental Medicine in Germany, who was not involved in the study. The findings for PM2.5 and cataracts were moderately consistent, albeit more variable than the glaucoma data; still, she said that the analysis seems to support a link.
Singh did caution that the underlying evidence is observational. "Therefore, the results demonstrate an association, not by themselves a causal effect of PM2.5 on glaucoma or cataract," she told Live Science.
What explains the increased risk?
The exact biological mechanisms behind these links remain unclear, but Alnabihi noted that fine particulate matter is small enough to be absorbed into the body. This can trigger oxidative stress, in which harmful molecules overwhelm natural defenses and cause damage. It also drives chronic, low-grade inflammation, in which the immune system stays mildly activated for long periods, he explained.
In the eye's lens, these processes can "damage the crystallin proteins that keep it transparent, causing them to misfold and cloud, which is what a cataract is," Alnabihi said.
In the optic nerve, the same processes are thought to damage retinal ganglion cells, a special type of neuron that relays information from the retina to the brain. This can contribute to glaucoma independent of internal eye pressure, he said, which is another big risk factor.
"Unlike the lungs or gut, its [the eye's] surface is in direct, continuous contact with outdoor air, giving pollutants a uniquely direct route that might cause damage," he added.
Related stories
- 'Wildfire smoke is the fastest-growing environmental threat in the US': How a warming world will poison the air we breathe
- China's huge push to reduce air pollution had an unexpected consequence in the Arctic
- Pollution may fuel depression, anxiety and other mental health problems, emerging research suggests
Other studies have found clues that support the link between PM2.5 and eye damage. Mice that were exposed to ambient PM2.5 for nine months developed elevated pressure inside their eyes, a glaucoma risk factor. The researchers observed both oxidative stress and nitrative stress — a similar phenomenon — in the tissues that drain fluid from the eye, which may help to explain the rise in pressure.
Studies of humans and human cells have uncovered similar patterns. In data from more than 480,000 people in the UK Biobank, a large repository of health information, those exposed to higher PM2.5 were more likely to develop glaucoma over time. In another study, scientists exposed lab-grown human retinal tissue made from stem cells to PM2.5. The particles disrupted retinal cell development, including that of retinal ganglion cells, while increasing cell death.
These studies offer pieces of a possible mechanism, but for now, how those pieces fit together in people remains unclear.
This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
Sanket Jain is an independent journalist and documentary photographer based in Western India’s Maharashtra state. Sanket’s work has been featured in over 35 publications, including MIT Technology Review, Devex, Wired, Telegraph, Thomson Reuters Foundation, The Nation, British Medical Journal, Verge, USA Today, Progressive Magazine and others. He was the winner of the 2025 Eric and Wendy Schmidt Award for Excellence in Science Communications. He was awarded an honorable mention for the 2026 Evert Clark/Seth Payne Award, which recognized a Live Science article and three others that addressed the impacts of air pollution and extreme heat on physical and mental health.

articles.title: A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
articles.text:
A forgotten fossil reveals a fearsome dinosaur with giant claws
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- University College London
- Summary:
- A 120-million-year-old fossil forgotten in a museum for nearly a century has revealed a terrifying new dinosaur that may have been more dangerous to humans than a T. rex. The tiger-sized predator also provides the first evidence of megaraptorans in Europe, helping explain how these mysterious dinosaurs eventually became gigantic hunters.
- Share:
A dinosaur fossil that spent nearly a century overlooked in a museum collection has turned out to belong to an entirely new species of prehistoric predator. About the size of a large tiger and armed with enormous curved claws, the animal roamed what is now Britain approximately 120 million years ago.
The discovery was made by researchers led by University College London (UCL), who examined a fossil skull fragment originally found on the Isle of Wight. Their findings, published in the journal Royal Society Open Science, identify the dinosaur as Invictibellatrix amberina, the first known European member of a mysterious group of carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans.
These agile predators walked on two legs and were closely related to tyrannosaurs, including the famous Tyrannosaurus rex. However, their hunting equipment was strikingly different. Rather than relying primarily on massive jaws, megaraptorans had relatively narrow skulls, powerful arms, and huge curved claws that helped them seize their prey.
Some members of this group eventually became enormous predators, rivaling tyrannosaurs in size. Invictibellatrix, however, was among the earliest and smallest megaraptorans discovered so far.
Its name translates to "unconquered female warrior," a reference to the powerful predators that later emerged from this evolutionary lineage.
A Forgotten Dinosaur That Could Have Hunted Humans
The fossil consists of part of the rear of the dinosaur's skull. Although the Natural History Museum acquired it in 1924, its scientific importance went unrecognized for generations.
By comparing the fragment with fossils from related dinosaurs, researchers were able to estimate what this long-extinct animal might have looked like and how it lived.
Lead author Dr. Cassius Morrison (UCL Earth Sciences) said: "Based on what we know about its closest relatives, Invictibellatrix would have been three to four meters long and just over a meter and a half in height -- about as tall as a human. It would likely have had feathers and its claws might have been about 10cm to 20cm long. It would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals -- occupying a similar role in the food chain to the hyena today.
"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.
"It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years. Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight -- who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."
Although humans never encountered these dinosaurs, Morrison's comparison highlights an intriguing difference between predators of different sizes. A relatively small carnivore might have regarded a human as worthwhile prey, whereas an enormous hunter such as T. rex may have preferred much larger animals.
Discovery Solves a Mystery About Dinosaur Evolution
Beyond identifying a previously unknown species, the fossil provides an important missing piece in the evolutionary history of megaraptorans.
These dinosaurs remain among the least understood groups of large meat eaters because their fossils are exceptionally rare. Scientists have long suspected that they first evolved in Asia before spreading through Europe and eventually reaching the southern supercontinent of Gondwana (including present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica).
There was one major problem with that explanation: Until now, no megaraptoran fossils had been identified in Europe.
The discovery of Invictibellatrix provides the evidence researchers needed to support that proposed migration route.
Co-author Charlie Scherer, a PhD student at UCL Earth Sciences, said: "This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south."
The finding suggests that Europe was an important part of the journey that eventually brought these predators to the southern continents, where some of their descendants became dominant hunters.
CT Scans Reveal the Dinosaur's Hidden Anatomy
To determine exactly what kind of dinosaur they were examining, the scientists used CT scanning technology to investigate the fossil in detail.
The scans allowed them to build a three-dimensional reconstruction of the skull fragment, along with a model of its internal cavity. This provided clues about the shape of the space that once housed the dinosaur's brain.
The team then compared its anatomy with fossils from several other groups of meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs, raptors, and other predators that walked on two legs.
Several unusual features helped distinguish the specimen from known species. These included an oval opening where the spinal cord connected to the brain and a distinctive crest shaped like an hourglass.
Together, these anatomical characteristics indicated that the fossil represented a previously unidentified dinosaur.
The researchers also used computer algorithms to compare its skeletal features with those of other dinosaurs. These analyses consistently placed Invictibellatrix within the megaraptoran group, providing further support for the identification.
How Giant Megaraptors Conquered the Southern Continents
The team went beyond examining the fossil itself, using mathematical models to reconstruct how megaraptorans spread and evolved over millions of years.
Their analysis combined the available fossil record with evolutionary relationships among dinosaurs, ancient geography, and climate conditions.
The results suggest that megaraptorans were distributed widely around the world during the Early Cretaceous (i.e., at the time of Invictibellatrix).
However, their fortunes appear to have changed dramatically as the Cretaceous continued.
By the Late Cretaceous, tens of millions of years later, megaraptorans had probably disappeared from the northern supercontinent of Laurasia (including modern-day Europe).
In the south, the story was very different. Megaraptorans continued evolving across Gondwana, eventually becoming some of the largest and most formidable predators in their ecosystems.
Some developed claws measuring up to 35cm (14") long. One particularly impressive example, Maip macrothorax, lived in what is now Argentina and is estimated to have reached nine to 10 meters in length, with a body weight comparable to that of an elephant.
Exactly why megaraptorans apparently vanished from northern regions remains uncertain. The researchers suggest several possibilities, including changes in climate, shifts in environmental conditions, and competition from other large carnivorous dinosaurs such as tyrannosaurs.
A Century-Old Museum Fossil Finally Reveals Its Secret
The fossil that made this discovery possible was originally collected by amateur paleontologist Reginald Walter Tooley near the base of a cliff on the southwestern coast of the Isle of Wight.
Tooley discovered more than 1,000 fossil specimens during his lifetime. Following his death, the Natural History Museum acquired his collection, including the skull fragment that would eventually be identified as Invictibellatrix.
The discovery highlights how important fossils can remain unrecognized even after spending decades in museum collections.
Professor Paul Barrett, the study's senior author from the Natural History Museum, said: "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive.
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made."
The researchers also gave the dinosaur's name a deeper meaning.
In their paper, they explained that Invictibellatrix was chosen to "give hope and strength to all those who are bullied, discriminated, victimized, and oppressed that tomorrow will be theirs and not to give up in face of such odds."
The second part of its name, amberina, honors both the amber found in the rock layers where the fossil originated and the female name Amberina.
The study received funding from the Palaeontographical Society, the Royal Society, and UKRI.
With a single forgotten skull fragment revealing an entirely new dinosaur and helping reconstruct the ancient movements of giant predators, the findings demonstrate that some of paleontology's most intriguing discoveries may already be sitting in museum drawers, waiting for someone to take a closer look.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University College London. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: Tại sao khi luộc trứng thì protein của trứng lại bị đông đặc lại?
articles.text:
Để hiểu rõ hơn về thành phần trotein trong trứng cũng như vì sao khi luộc trứng thì protein trong trứng bị đông đặc lại, mời bạn đọc theo dõi bài viết dưới đây!
Trong một quả trứng gà cỡ lớn có chứa khoảng 7 gram protein, cụ thể: Lượng protein trong lòng trắng trứng là 4 gram và lượng protein trong lòng đỏ trứng là 3 gram
Một lòng đỏ sống từ một quả trứng gà lớn tiêu chuẩn cung cấp những điều sau: 55 calo - 2,70g protein - 4,51g chất béo - 184 miligam (mg) cholesterol - 0,61 g carbohydrate - 0,10 g đường - 0 g chất xơ.
Protein trong lòng trắng trứng có chứa đầy đủ tất cả chín axit amin thiết yếu.
Lượng protein chiếm đa phần là trong lòng trắng trứng nhưng lại ít calo. Trên thực tế, lòng trắng trứng chiếm khoảng 67% tổng số protein có trong trứng. Protein trong lòng trắng trứng có chứa đầy đủ tất cả chín axit amin thiết yếu với số lượng mà cơ thể cần để hoạt động tốt nhất.
Protein có thể giúp kiềm chế sự thèm ăn của bạn. Vì vậy, ăn lòng trắng trứng có thể khiến bạn cảm thấy no lâu hơn. Tuy vậy, bạn vẫn nhận đủ được hàm lượng protein cần thiết, nhất là những bạn đang trong quá trình giảm cân.
Tuy nhiên, so với quả trứng thì lòng trắng trứng có ít chất dinh dưỡng khác hơn. Trứng nguyên chất chứa nhiều loại vitamin và khoáng chất, protein bổ sung và một số chất béo lành mạnh. Hơn nữa, mặc dù hàm lượng cholesterol cao, nhưng nó không có mối liên hệ nào giữa lượng trứng và nguy cơ mắc bệnh tim.
Khi luộc trứng thì protein của trứng lại bị đông đặc lại là do lòng trắng trứng hầu hết được cấu tạo bởi Protein. Hiện tượng trứng sau khi luộc bị biến đổi cấu trúc này gọi là hiện tượng đông tụ của protein. Protein có đặc điểm khi gặp nhiệt độ cao sẽ bị biến tính, xảy ra hiện tượng đông tụ, làm thay đổi cấu trúc ban đầu, trở thành dạng rắn hơn. Đó là ví do tại sao khi luộc trứng thì protein của trứng lại bị đông đặc lại.
Bình thường, protein có cấu hình không gian 3 chiều đặc trưng. Khi chịu tác động của nhiệt độ, protein mất đi cấu trúc 3 chiều và trở nên duỗi thẳng. Khi ở trạng thái này, các đầu kị nước của chúng bị lộ ra ngoài, tiếp xúc với nước ngoài môi trường. Vì vậy, lập tức theo tương tác kị nước, các đầu kị nước quay lại vào nhau, các đầu ưa nước quay ra ngoài, vì thế khiến protein bị đông tụ lại.
Lượng protein trong trứng gà có chứa tất cả 9 loại axit amin thiết yếu với tỷ lệ thích hợp. Tuy nhiên, lượng protein mà cơ thể thực sự nhận được dường như phụ thuộc vào cách chế biến trứng.
Ăn trứng gà sống chỉ cung cấp cho bạn một lượng nhỏ protein. Một số nghiên cứu đã đánh giá lượng protein được hấp thụ từ trứng nấu chín so với trứng sống và cho thấy những người tham gia có thể hấp thụ được tới 90% lượng protein trong trứng nấu chín và chỉ hấp thụ được 50% protein từ trứng sống.
Một nghiên cứu khác cũng đã phát hiện ra rằng, những người khoẻ mạnh khi ăn trứng nấu chín có thể hấp thụ được 94% lượng protein, trong khi đó chỉ có khoảng 74% protein từ trứng sống.
Điều này cho thấy trứng nấu chín sẽ giúp protein dễ tiêu hoá hơn và dễ tiếp cận hơn với cơ thể bạn. Ngoài ra, việc ăn trứng sống cũng tiềm ẩn những nguy cơ sức khoẻ như nhiễm vi khuẩn hoặc ngộ độc thực phẩm.

articles.title: Cá kiếm sống sót với cơ thể đầy lỗ khoét kinh dị
articles.text:
Các ngư dân kinh ngạc khi bắt được một con cá kiếm mình đầy lỗ khoét, thủ phạm nhiều khả năng là một loài cá mập đặc biệt.
Các ngư dân kéo con cá kiếm kỳ lạ lên tàu. (Video: TK Offshore Fishing).
Khi đang đánh cá ở biển San Hô, Australia, thuyền trưởng T. K. Walker cùng thủy thủ đoàn bắt gặp một con vật khác thường, Newsweek hôm 21/7 đưa tin. Sau khi kéo một con cá kiếm lớn lên khỏi mặt nước, họ phát hiện cơ thể nó có hàng chục lỗ hình bầu dục, giống như tác phẩm của dụng cụ cắt bánh quy. "Tôi chưa từng chứng kiến vụ tấn công nào như vậy trong suốt 40 năm làm việc", Walker chia sẻ.
Thủ phạm gần như chắc chắn là cá mập cắt bánh quy (Isistius brasiliensis), còn gọi là cá mập xì gà, hay đúng hơn là cả một đàn cùng tấn công. "Chắc hẳn là một cuộc tấn công tập thể. Chúng đã kiếm được nhiều hơn là một bữa ăn nhẹ", Walker nói.
Cá mập cắt bánh quy là loài vật nhỏ, hình dạng giống điếu xì gà, hiếm khi dài quá 0,5 m, theo Viện Nghiên cứu Cá mập (SRI). Chúng phân bố ở các vùng biển nhiệt đới thuộc Đại Tây Dương, Ấn Độ Dương và Thái Bình Dương.
Con cá kiếm với nhiều vết khoét trên cơ thể.
Điểm đặc trưng nhất của loài vật này có lẽ là chiến lược kiếm ăn khác thường. Mặt dưới của cá mập cắt bánh quy có các cơ quan nhỏ phát sáng gọi là photophore. Chúng tạo ra ánh sáng xanh lục ở mặt dưới của cá mập, dùng để dụ những con cá khác.
Răng của cá mập cắt bánh quy cũng rất khác thường. Chúng có 37 chiếc răng nhỏ ở hàm trên, trong khi hàm dưới có những chiếc răng tam giác lớn hơn và nối liền với nhau ở gốc, giống như dụng cụ cắt bánh quy. Sau khi dụ được con mồi, cá mập dùng miệng mút và những chiếc răng nhọn bám vào cơ thể đối tượng, sau đó vặn mình 360 độ để lấy đi một miếng thịt. Bằng cách này, chúng có thể tấn công những loài lớn hơn nhiều như cá ngừ, cá kiếm, cá heo và cả những loài cá mập khác.
"Chúng lao vào trong khi con cá đang bơi, cắn một miếng thịt rồi lại cắn tiếp trước khi con cá lớn hơn kịp phản ứng. Tôi có thể hình dung chuyện này giống như muỗi vo ve xung quanh những con cá kiếm và cá ngừ lớn", Walker cho biết.
Theo Walker, loài cá mập này tương đối phổ biến ở biển San Hô. "Chúng tôi thấy những vết cắn này hàng ngày và thường thì cá sẽ có 3 hoặc 4 vết cắn mới, thêm nhiều vết đã hoặc đang lành", ông nói.
Tuy nhiên, rất hiếm cá có nhiều vết cắn mới như con cá kiếm Walker bắt được. "Nó vẫn còn sống khi được chúng tôi kéo lên tàu. Các vết cắn vẫn đang chảy máu nên chuyện này chỉ vừa mới xảy ra", Walker nói.

articles.title: Black Death had dramatic effect on species diversity as humans abandoned farmland, study finds
articles.text:
Black Death had dramatic effect on species diversity as humans abandoned farmland, study finds
Researchers have found that during the Black Death, when a third of the population of Europe was wiped out, biodiversity fell. Understanding their farming practices could help us increase diversity in modern agriculture.
When millions of people died in Europe during the Black Death, biodiversity suffered too, new research suggests. The findings suggest that human activities once promoted biodiversity in the landscape — and experts say we could use these findings to boost biodiversity in our modern agricultural landscapes.
The 14th century was a tumultuous time for the people of Europe. Persistent cold, wet weather at the beginning of the century led to widespread agricultural failures and unprecedented levels of starvation in what became known as the Great Famine from 1315 to 1317.
This was followed by the Black Death, an epidemic of bubonic plague caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis that killed more than a third of Europe's population. As a result of the widespread deaths and resultant social upheaval, large swaths of agricultural land were abandoned. Population levels didn't begin to recover until the 16th century.
The Black Death era is the perfect opportunity to look at the effects of humans on biodiversity over a longer period, Jonathan Gordon, a paleoecologist at the Leverhulme Centre for Anthropocene Biodiversity at the University of York and first author of the paper, told Live Science.
In the study, which was published March 4 in the journal Ecology Letters, the researchers compared more than 100 European pollen records that included about 4,600 samples. The records came from sites ranging from the lowlands of France and uplands of the southwest United Kingdom to the Swiss Alps.
The pollen records "give us information on the past diversity of the plant records," Gordon said.
For example, cereal grains — such as wheat, barley and rye — were a fundamental part of medieval agriculture. The representation of pollen from these types of crops in the pollen record points to historic land use.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The researchers divided the pollen data into three categories based on the presence of cereal pollen: places where agricultural production went up, places where it went down, and places where there was no evidence of cereal cultivation.
"We found a decline in biodiversity overall, but the decline overall was driven by those landscapes that declined in agricultural production," Gordon said.
"In those landscapes where agricultural production went down, there was a reduction in biodiversity of around 40%. Then, after about 150 years, as populations started recovering and landscape disturbances started increasing again, biodiversity went up to slightly above the level it was before."
Mosaic landscapes
Many people think there was a "stable and pristine world in which the entry of people has only one result: net loss of species and homogenization," Erle Ellis, an agroecologist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "The paleoecologists have always known the story is far more complicated."
There is a growing body of evidence showing that people's long-term cultural shaping of their landscapes often creates more diverse habitats, known as "mosaics," that can sustain more species than simple homogenous landscapes can, he said.
Whereas modern agriculture focuses on single crops on plots of land, in previous centuries, "you had all these different types of agriculture operating within the same landscape," Gordon said.
"In that landscape, you had lots of natural features that remained from the Middle or Early Holocene (which began after the last Ice Age about 12,000 years ago)," he added. "You had old bits of woodland, you had heaths, you had ponds, and bits of secondary forest. It was all interlaced with these agricultural mosaics, and that led to raised biodiversity because there were more habitats for different plant species to exploit."
The findings highlight the differences between medieval and modern land use practices — and their consequences for biodiversity. Research suggests that during the 20th century, global biodiversity declined by up to as much as 11% and human activities, such as land-use changes, pollution, and climate change, are the major culprits. In agriculture, the practice of monoculture — where a single crop species is grown over a large area — reduces biodiversity.
"What this work contributes to showing is that, until relatively recently, even in Europe, very different forms of land management and interaction were practiced than exist today," Patrick Roberts, director of Department of Coevolution of Land Use and Urbanisation at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, told Live Science in an email.
Related stories
- Aspen trees provide a natural buffer against wildfires, even as fire season intensifies, study shows
- Extreme heat waves are making our cities buckle. Investing in urban nature is no longer optional.
- 66 billion trees have been planted in China's Great Green Wall — and they appear to be growing faster than natural forests
"Rather than the monoculture, plantations, or uniform changes to landscapes we see in the 20th and 21st centuries, emphasis was placed on maintaining 'mosaics,'" said Roberts, who was not involved in the new research.
In the study, "we can see how relationships between people and biodiversity have changed through time and how people can actively use landscapes while maintaining biodiversity and mixed ecosystem functions," he said.
There is still more to understand about how humans' disappearance from landscapes in the Black Death era affected the natural world, Gordon said. "There are a lot of other types of diversity — not just the number of types, but what the different types present actually do." There may be a hundred types of plants in a landscape, but if they do the same thing, "you have low functional diversity," he said.
Functional diversity "is super important for how ecosystems adapt to changes in climate and how resilient they are, which is something we need for future-proofing our agricultural system," Gordon said.
Gordon, J. D., Fagan, B., Finch, J., Gillson, L., Milner, N., & Thomas, C. D. (2026). Black death land abandonment drove European diversity losses. Ecology Letters, 29(3), e70325. https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.70325
Sarah Wild is a British-South African freelance science journalist. She has written about particle physics, cosmology and everything in between. She studied physics, electronics and English literature at Rhodes University, South Africa, and later read for an MSc Medicine in bioethics.
Since she started perpetrating journalism for a living, she's written books, won awards, and run national science desks. Her work has appeared in Nature, Science, Scientific American, and The Observer, among others. In 2017 she won a gold AAAS Kavli for her reporting on forensics in South Africa.

articles.title: Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
articles.text:
Cancer is rising in younger adults, and scientists can't fully explain why
Cancer rates are rising among younger adults despite improvements in several lifestyle risk factors, and scientists say obesity alone can't explain why.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- BMJ Group
- Summary:
- A major study found that several cancers are rising faster among younger adults in England, even as smoking, diet, and other established risk factors have generally improved. Excess weight explains only part of the increase, leaving scientists searching for other possible causes, including changes in the gut microbiome and early-life exposures.
- Share:
Cancer rates are increasing among adults of different ages in England, but a new study has uncovered a particularly concerning pattern among younger people. Rates of bowel and ovarian cancer have risen among younger adults (under 50), while the same increases have not been observed in older age groups.
The findings, published in the open-access journal BMJ Oncology, also show that several other cancers are becoming more common at a faster pace among younger adults than among those aged 50 and older.
Although excess body weight appears to play an important role, researchers say obesity alone cannot account for the increases. The findings suggest that additional factors may be contributing to the growing burden of cancer in younger generations.
Similar increases in cancer among people under 50 have been reported outside England. However, scientists still do not fully understand whether changing lifestyle habits and other established risk factors can explain these trends.
Cancer Rates Rise Across Multiple Age Groups
To investigate, researchers examined cancer incidence records collected by England's National Disease Registry Service between 2001 and 2019. They compared trends in more than 20 cancer types among men and women aged 20 to 49 and adults aged 50 or older.
The team also analyzed national health survey data to track changes in established cancer risk factors. These included smoking, alcohol consumption, diet (high red/processed meat, low fiber intake), excess body weight (BMI), and insufficient physical activity. The researchers assessed how these factors changed across age groups and sexes and estimated how much they contributed to cancer cases.
The results revealed widespread increases in cancer incidence. Among younger women, 16 of the 22 cancer types examined showed statistically significant increases. Among younger men, rates rose significantly for 11 of 21 cancers.
Of particular concern were 11 cancers associated with known behavioral risk factors that became significantly more common among adults under 50. These included cancers of the thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, bowel, pancreas, mouth, breast, and ovary, along with multiple myeloma and cancer of the uterine lining (endometrial).
Most of these cancers also increased significantly among adults over 50. However, bowel and ovarian cancers stood out because their incidence rose significantly among younger adults but not among older people.
The researchers also identified several cancers whose incidence increased more rapidly in younger women. These included endometrial, kidney, pancreatic, multiple myeloma, and thyroid cancers. Among men, multiple myeloma was the only cancer found to be increasing significantly faster in the younger age group.
Obesity Is a Major Factor, but It Doesn't Explain Everything
The researchers examined how established lifestyle risks might help explain the increases. Of the 11 cancers of particular interest, 10 were associated with obesity, with mouth cancer being the exception.
Six cancers (liver, bowel, mouth, pancreas, kidney, and ovary) were linked to smoking, while four (liver, bowel, mouth, and breast) were associated with alcohol consumption. Three (bowel, breast, and endometrial) were connected to physical inactivity, and one (bowel) was linked to dietary factors.
Yet the findings revealed an important contradiction. Apart from excess weight, most of these established risk factors either remained relatively stable or improved among younger adults over the previous one to two decades.
Red meat consumption, for example, showed some of the largest reported improvements, with reductions of around 7% in the survey trends examined. Among younger men, average daily consumption fell from 38 grams in 2008 to 17 grams in 2018. Among younger women, it dropped from 22 grams to 10 grams over the same period.
Younger women also consumed substantially less processed meat than younger men, averaging about 10 grams per day compared with approximately 20 grams.
Fiber intake remained a concern, with more than 90% of younger adults failing to consume enough fiber in 2018. Nevertheless, average intake was generally stable or improved slightly among both sexes between 2009 and 2019. Older adults showed broadly similar dietary trends.
These findings raise questions about why cancer incidence continued to increase even as several recognized lifestyle risks were moving in a more favorable direction.
How Much Cancer Is Linked to Known Risk Factors?
Despite these improvements, established behavioral risk factors were still associated with a substantial proportion of cancer cases.
For men in 2019, the researchers estimated that these factors accounted for 68% of mouth cancer cases among younger adults and 65% among older adults. The corresponding figures were 42% and 48% for liver cancer, 49% and 53% for bowel cancer, 29% and 33% for kidney cancer, and 36% and 34% for pancreatic cancer.
Among women, the estimated proportions attributable to these risks were 52% for younger adults and 45% for older adults for mouth cancer. For endometrial cancer, the figures were 35% and 42%, while liver cancer accounted for 44% and 46%.
The corresponding estimates were 38% and 42% for bowel cancer, 33% and 37% for kidney cancer, 31% and 28% for pancreatic cancer, and 19% and 24% for gallbladder cancer.
Excess body weight was associated with more of the cancer types examined than any other individual risk factor. In 2019, the estimated proportion of cases attributable to excess weight varied considerably, from 5% for ovarian cancer to 37% for endometrial cancer.
Even so, the researchers found that increases in obesity could not fully account for the broader cancer trends.
"These patterns suggest that while similar risk factors across ages are likely, some cancers may have age-specific exposures, susceptibilities, or differences in screening and detection practices," write the researchers.
Scientists Search for Other Explanations
The study was observational, meaning it could identify associations and trends but could not determine whether particular risk factors directly caused the increases in cancer incidence.
The researchers also acknowledged several limitations. Reliable national data covering long periods were unavailable for some risk factors, and the analysis focused exclusively on England rather than the entire United Kingdom.
In addition, their calculations assumed a 10-year delay between exposure to a risk factor and the development of cancer.
"The observed increasing cancer incidence despite declining trends in several behavioral risk factors may reflect the net effect of multiple influences operating in different directions. Other contributing factors not evaluated here, for example, reproductive history, early-life or prenatal risk factors, and changes in cancer diagnosis and detection practices, may also play a role," they explain.
The researchers emphasized that obesity remains important, but increases in cancer cases cannot be attributed to weight alone.
"Although overweight and obesity are linked to 10 of the 11 cancers evaluated and account for a substantial proportion of cancer cases, both BMI-attributable and BMI-non-attributable incidence rates have increased -- though the latter more slowly -- suggesting other contributors," they add.
Other potential explanations have been proposed for the increase in cancers among younger adults. These include greater consumption of ultra-processed foods and sugary drinks, childhood obesity, physical inactivity/sedentary behavior, antibiotic exposure, and air pollution.
However, many of these possible contributors have not shown the increases that might be expected if they were solely responsible for rising cancer rates.
"While these factors are common in England, most have shown stable or declining trends in the last decade," the researchers note.
One possibility that deserves closer examination is disruption of the gut microbiome, the community of microorganisms living in the digestive system. Changes in these microbial populations have been suggested as a potential influence on cancer risk, although further research is needed to establish their role.
Cancer Remains More Common in Older Adults
While the rise in cancer among younger people is concerning, the researchers cautioned against overlooking the much greater number of cases that still occur among older adults.
The findings highlight the need to investigate cancer risk throughout life, including the possibility that exposures during childhood or even before birth may influence disease decades later.
"Although increases in cancer in younger adults are concerning, the absolute burden remains far higher in older adults, underscoring the public health and clinical importance of studying risk factors across all ages," they conclude.
Story Source:
Materials provided by BMJ Group. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Montserrat Garcia-Closas, Zoey Richards, Reuben Frost, Marc J Gunter, Amy Berrington de Gonzalez. Temporal trends in behavioural risk factors for cancers with rising incidence in younger adults: an analysis of population-based data in England. BMJ Oncology, 2026; 5 (1): e000966 DOI: 10.1136/bmjonc-2025-000966

articles.title: Famous supernova that lit up skies in 1181 is now full of mysterious knots — Space photo of the week
articles.text:
Famous supernova that lit up skies in 1181 is now full of mysterious knots — Space photo of the week
Pa 30, linked to a supernova seen in 1181, reveals chains of tiny gas knots in a new image from the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii.
Quick facts
What it is: Pa 30, a supernova remnant
Where it is: 7,500 light-years away, in the constellation Cassiopeia
When it was shared: Oct. 6, 2026
A mysterious "guest star" recorded by medieval astronomers nearly 850 years ago has revealed new secrets after scientists obtained the clearest images yet of its explosive aftermath.
New observations of Pa 30, thought to be the leftovers of a historic supernova called SN 1181, show that its spectacular firework-like filaments are not smooth streams of material. Instead, they consist of chains of tiny gas knots.
SN 1181 is so called because astronomers in China and Japan recorded its brief appearance in the year 1181, when they saw it as a naked-eye object in the constellation Cassiopeia. Eight surviving texts date its appearance to between Aug. 4 and 6 of that year. The mysterious object remained visible for 185 days.
"It's rare to get this level of detail on a supernova we can date to a specific week in history," Timothy Cunningham, an assistant professor of astronomy and astrophysics at the University of Warwick who led an international team of researchers to study the object, said in a statement.
SN 1181 is one of only five supernovas in the Milky Way galaxy known to have been witnessed from Earth before the invention of the telescope. (Those optical instruments first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608.) Now, advanced ground-based telescopes can produce wonderfully detailed images of those historic remnants. This latest image is from the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii and reveals about 10 times more filamentary structures in Pa 30 than have been seen before. This extraordinary detail gives astronomers fresh clues about the unusual explosion and the environment surrounding the star.
"These images give us the clearest picture yet of Pa 30's structure, and it's not what we expected," said Cunningham, whose team published their findings in The Astrophysical Journal. "The filaments are made of chains of tiny knots rather than smooth streaks, providing new constraints on the nature of the space around the star before it exploded and the physical processes that have shaped the expanding ejecta."
The knot-like structures may have resulted from variations in temperature or density in material surrounding the star as debris from the explosion expanded.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
Related stories
- A star 20 times the size of the sun died in a supernova — and telescopes around the world joined forces to watch it
- Scientists mapped the shape of a supernova for the first time ever – and it's not what we expected: Space photo of the week
- Scientists find evidence of 'supernova graveyard' at the bottom of the sea — and possibly on the surface of the moon
Pa 30 contains another unusual feature: a surviving star that sits almost exactly at the center of the remnant. That's highly unusual, because a supernova explosion typically sends stars away from their original positions. It suggests that the original explosion was highly symmetrical, the researchers said.
Furthermore, Pa 30 is thought to be a Type Iax supernova. Unlike standard Type Ia supernovas, which destroy their stars, a Type Iax event is a lower-energy, incomplete explosion of a white dwarf star that can leave behind a remnant known as a "zombie star." It's the only Type Iax supernova ever found.
Jamie Carter is a Cardiff, U.K.-based freelance science journalist and a regular contributor to Live Science. He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.
