articles.title: Why you might not want to join two Ethernet cables (and what you should do instead) - Engadget
articles.text:
Why you might not want to join two Ethernet cables (and what you should do instead)
Longer cables or a network switch could save you a lot of hassle.
Move your desk a few feet and you may find that the perfectly good Ethernet cable that once easily connected your computer is now too short. If you happen to have a second Ethernet cable close by, a small RJ45 coupler will allow you to connect them together with little effort. There's no need to find an outlet for power, read through a setup guide or even become certified as a network professional. A quality coupler shouldn't noticeably slow your internet connection either.
But that small adapter does add another connection you'd need to check if the network starts acting up. For a permanent setup, a single longer cable is usually simpler, but if you've already routed the cable and want more wired ports at the other end, a network switch makes a lot more sense.
Why joining Ethernet cables can cause problems
An Ethernet coupler is as simple as network hardware can be: two RJ45 sockets connected together. It does not increase signal strength or establish a separate Ethernet link. With good connectors, one coupler works perfectly well. The additional connection is a potential failure point, though, especially if the adapter is poorly made or prone to bumps.
A bad join could result in occasional dropouts, transmission errors or a link falling back to 100 Mbps instead of 1 Gbps. If so, use a good-quality cable without the coupler before spending an afternoon rebooting your router and calling your internet provider.
The other limit is Ethernet cable length. The standard copper Ethernet channel limit is 328 feet (100 meters), including patch cords, so joining two 200-foot cables would exceed that limit. A coupler isn't going to reset it.
trueCABLE tested various combinations of Cat6 and Cat6A cables and couplers with a Fluke DSX-8000 cable tester. Configurations with three couplers generally passed, although one earned a marginal pass (technically a failure). Configurations with four couplers failed. This is not a universal breaking point, as the tests were conducted on specific cables and couplers. It does show why adding more joins than necessary is a bad idea.
What to use instead of an Ethernet coupler
If you're using a single PC or console, perhaps begin with a single Ethernet cable that is long enough to reach. You eliminate the additional connection and you won't need an outlet for more hardware. Also, ensure you leave some slack when routing it around furniture rather than pulling it tight behind a desk. Typically, a Gigabit connection can be achieved with good Cat5e or Cat6 cable. Even an expensive Cat8 cable won't magically fix poor cord routing.
Replacing an existing cable is a different proposition. After spending half an afternoon routing an Ethernet cable to your entertainment center, you might now have a TV, console and streaming box waiting for ports. Here, a small unmanaged network switch makes sense. Connect the incoming cable to one port and the devices to the others. A five-port model leaves four ports available for additional devices as one is used to connect to the router.
The switch creates separate Ethernet links, each with its own distance limit, unlike a coupler. Basic unmanaged five-port Gigabit switches can be purchased for around $15 and require no configuration. The switch still needs power, though, and a 1 Gbps model will downgrade transfers via faster cable standards.
If you're installing a security camera or wireless access point, one more thing to note: a standard non-PoE switch will not supply Power over Ethernet to connected devices. You'll need a PoE-capable switch or injector for devices that require such support.

articles.title: Lenovo’s fast, comfy SteamOS handheld is hundreds off
articles.text:
The Legion Go S with SteamOS is a pretty solid alternative to the $789 Steam Deck OLED. It runs identical software, but ships in a design with two-stage triggers, a bigger eight-inch IPS screen (1080p and up to 120Hz versus 800p and 90Hz in the Deck OLED), and it’s got double the RAM and storage (32GB and 1TB, respectively), not to mention a slightly faster processor in the Ryzen Z1 Extreme.
Lenovo’s fast, comfy SteamOS handheld is hundreds off
With double the RAM and storage of the base Steam Deck OLED, plus a slightly faster processor, this is a great deal.
At $999.99, its current discounted price at Best Buy, it’s worth considering if you’re deciding on a handheld. The Legion Go S is not as powerful as the $1,299.99 Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 that just launched, which has the Z2 Extreme and a OLED screen, but it’s no slouch, either.
This model launched with Windows 11 and the Ryzen Z2 Go. Despite being a newer chip, it’s less powerful than the Z1 Extreme in the discounted model. SteamOS and the faster internals within this configuration will provide a better experience. Check out my colleague Sean Hollister’s review of multiple configs of the Go S, and see how it stacks up in his benchmarks.

articles.title: Supreme Court weighs video privacy law in Paramount case
articles.text:
The US Supreme Court appeared ready to side with a man who says a Paramount website shared his video history with Facebook. The case could expose many websites to privacy lawsuits.The justices heard arguments in Salazar v. Paramount Global on Wednesday, CNET reported. Paramount’s case did not seem to persuade them, Bloomberg Law reported.
The case
In 2022, Michael Salazar signed up for a newsletter from 247Sports, a Paramount-owned college sports site. He then watched videos on the site while logged into Facebook.
A Meta tracking tool on the site, known as the Pixel, sent details of those videos to Facebook without his consent, he says. He wants to bring a class action seeking up to $2,500 per person.
His claim rests on the Video Privacy Protection Act. Congress passed it in 1988 after a journalist published the video rental history of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork.
Who counts as a consumer?
The law protects ‘consumers’ of video providers. Lower courts threw out Salazar’s case, ruling that a newsletter is not video content, so he did not count.
Paramount’s lawyer, Paul Clement, said Salazar’s reading would turn a law about video rentals into a sweeping internet privacy regime. He warned sites might put videos behind consent walls.
Justice Elena Kagan said websites had two simple choices: get consent or stop selling private data. Justice Sonia Sotomayor said gating videos behind consent would leave the choice to users.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked whether it was right to repurpose a video law for web ad tracking.
“It’s going to be over-broad consent, no doubt,” he said.
What’s at stake
A win for Salazar could open the door to more lawsuits against sites that use tracking tools on video pages. A ruling is expected by next summer.
Paramount, which recently won approval for its Warner Bros deal, is not the only media firm facing viewer lawsuits. Twitch and Amazon face their own class action over AI training on livestreams.

articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 18/10: Thế giới có tuần tăng mạnh, dầu diesel dưới 30.000 đồng/lít
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Giá dầu quốc tế trong tuần này trải qua tuần biến động mạnh, với 3 phiên tăng và 2 phiên tăng, giảm trái chiều.
Cụ thể, trong phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (12/10), giá dầu thế giới tăng gần 2%, trong bối cảnh các vụ tấn công của lực lượng Houthi ở Yemen vào Saudi Arabia, làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguồn cung dầu từ Trung Đông.
Tới phiên giao dịch 13/10, giá dầu thế giới tăng, giảm trái chiều trong biên độ hẹp, khi triển vọng thỏa thuận xuất khẩu dầu diesel của Nga làm dấy lên hi vọng nguồn cung năng lượng được cải thiện, trong khi các cuộc tấn công tại Yemen và Saudi Arabia làm gia tăng lo ngại về nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung tại Trung Đông.
Giá dầu thế giới tăng nhẹ trong phiên giao dịch 14/10 sau khi lực lượng Houthi ở Yemen (được Iran hậu thuẫn) tấn công vào một tòa nhà hành chính của Saudi Aramco, tập đoàn dầu khí quốc gia của Saudi Arabia.
Đến phiên giao dịch 15/10, giá dầu thế giới lại biến động trái chiều khi giới đầu tư đánh giá khả năng Mỹ nới lỏng một số hạn chế đối với tàu chở dầu Nga trong bối cảnh căng thẳng tại Trung Đông tiếp tục leo thang.
Chốt phiên giao dịch 15/10, giá dầu Brent giảm 0,13%, xuống còn 105,9 USD/thùng. Trong khi đó, giá dầu WTI của Mỹ tăng 3,03%, lên mức 97,97 USD/thùng.
Ở phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần này (16/10), giá dầu thế giới tăng tới gần 4%, chạm mốc 110 USD/thùng, mức cao nhất kể từ tháng 5, trong bối cảnh lo ngại nguồn cung từ Trung Đông gia tăng và thị trường đánh giá khả năng Nga cung cấp thêm dầu diesel cho thị trường toàn cầu.
Tính chung trong cả tuần này, giá dầu Brent tăng gần 5%, trong khi dầu WTI tăng hơn 10%.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần này ở mức 109,9 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần ở mức 101,4 USD/thùng.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Ở thị trường trong nước, giá bán các mặt hàng xăng dầu tuần này được điều chỉnh theo hướng xăng và dầu diesel giảm, dầu mazut tăng.
Cụ thể, ở kỳ điều hành 15/10, giá xăng E5RON92 hạ 732 đồng/lít, giá bán lẻ không cao hơn 26.971 đồng/lít.
Giá xăng E10RON95-III được điều chỉnh giảm tới 1.225 đồng/lít, xuống mức 27.029 đồng/lít.
Trong khi giá dầu diesel 0.05S giảm nhẹ 22 đồng/lít, xuống mức giá không cao hơn 29.106 đồng/lít.
Ở chiều ngược lại, giá dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 1.043 đồng/kg, lên tối đa 22.135 đồng/kg.
Trong chiều 15/10, Tập đoàn Xăng dầu Việt Nam (Petrolimex) tiến hành giảm thêm 300 đồng/lít hoặc kg đối với các mặt hàng xăng dầu so với mức giá bán tối đa được công bố trong kỳ điều hành 15/10.
Tổng công ty Dầu Việt Nam (PVOIL) cũng giảm 350 đồng/lít đối với hai loại xăng và dầu diesel từ 0h ngày 16/10.
Dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương cho thấy, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip
articles.text:
Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.
The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”
"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.
The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.
Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.
“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.
In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.
Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”
The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.
7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.
Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.
Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.
Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”
Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)
Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.
Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.
“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”
It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.
A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.
Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.
Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.
Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.
“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”
What We’re Writing
Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.
Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!
What We’re Reading
- Maine’s senate race was not on our data center midterms to watch, but apparently it should’ve been! Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise.
- CoreWeave has been on a wild ride this week as the bonds it sells to finance its data centers have seen wild selloff and corresponding stock drop. Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public.
- Westfield, Massachusetts, killed a $3 billion data center project, boston.com reports. The small western Massachusetts town’s planning board pilloried developer Servistar for missing deadlines and being slow to develop the project.
Comments
Back to top

articles.title: You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should) - Engadget
articles.text:
You don't have to turn off your phone to switch SIM cards (but you probably should)
A quick step removes the small chance of anything going wrong and requiring more of your time.
If your phone has a SIM tray, it's not something you likely open often, but there are still reasons to. You may be switching to an MVNO to save money, or maybe you're temporarily swapping out your normal SIM for a cheaper local carrier when travelling. In some cases, your carrier will send you a replacement card if yours is damaged.
Most of today's smartphones let you switch SIMs with the phone on, so you don't need to switch your device off for the process. But there are modest benefits if you do, and for something so quick, it's better to be safe if you have a few minutes.
How to replace the SIM
We're talking about physical SIM cards, which you have to remove from your phone by hand. eSIM replacement should be as simple as using a QR code, carrier app or direct transfer between different smartphones. Most eSIM-compatible phones can store many eSIMS, though only a few can be active at once.
Physical SIM card replacement involves these steps:
- Optionally, power down your phone or enable airplane mode.
- Pop the tray out, usually by gently pushing a paperclip or SIM ejector tool into the ejection pinhole on the phone.
- Change the card, ensuring you use the correct card size.
- Pop the tray back into place.
- Enter your PIN or restart if the phone requests it.
If you have a dual-SIM phone that supports two physical cards, check which SIM you intend to swap before you begin.
While many argue eSIM is a superior technology because it requires no moving parts, others still appreciate the convenience and relative privacy true SIM cards provide. They make it easy to install and use over-the-counter pay-as-you-go SIM-based accounts, for example.
The small potential risks of SIM replacement
Most potential dangers of SIM replacement are physical. You might accidentally insert dirt, grime or moisture into the SIM tray, or force a larger card into a smaller slot incorrectly. You could also break the SIM tray so it no longer aligns correctly, or otherwise harm the card. A damaged SIM card or one incorrectly inserted may cause the phone to continue trying (and failing) to create a network connection, draining its battery and causing it to overheat.
Most people never encounter these problems, since slowing down and being careful does the trick. In most cases, your phone will take a moment to read the new SIM and find the network. Then it will be available for service, subject to account setup requirements.
The benefit of turning your phone off before swapping the SIM is minor. It forces your phone to look at the fresh information provided on the new card when it powers on again, helping register your device on its new network more quickly by reading the new carrier settings. This reduces the chance you'll encounter a software-based "network error" message when you swap.
More to think about when swapping SIMs
Before the 2010s, SIM slots were usually located underneath a phone's removable battery, which obviously required powering off the device to access. Over time, as removable batteries became less common, SIM trays were moved to the outside of phones. Early models using this setup would often show a network error if you swapped SIMs while the phone was on, but they quickly became hot-swappable and this was no longer a problem.
You don't even need to switch your device off completely to make the phone refresh its carrier settings from the card. You'll get a similar result if you turn on airplane mode, wait 30 seconds before swapping the SIM and turn airplane mode off again once the new SIM is inserted. This should prevent any carrier hiccups during the process.
A warning on SD cards
Unlike the iPhone, some Android devices still include a microSD card slot. In some cases, this is in the same tray as the SIM, though placement varies. If this is the case for you, as when ejecting an external drive, it's important to unmount the microSD card before removing the SIM to prevent losing data. On Samsung devices: open the My Files app, find the SD Card, tap the three-dot menu next to it and choose Unmount. Search the Settings app or check online documentation if you're not sure how this works for your device.
So while the benefits are slight, switching off your phone when replacing the SIM can prevent software-related glitches. If you don't want to power down, use airplane mode instead. And in case you encounter a network error after swapping, always try restarting your device first.

articles.title: J Mascis has nothing better to do
articles.text:
Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. He stands stoically onstage, barely moving, as he seemingly effortlessly works through deft guitar solos and lopsided riffs. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.
J Mascis has nothing better to do
Dinosaur Jr.’s frontman finally addresses the AI video for ‘Old Friends.’
That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.
While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”
What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.
For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”
The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.
When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”
But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”
Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”
About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. We have amps and you know, just, I think some people are responding to the reality of it. Like they really need something that’s not, you know, computer-generated or something.”
He bemoaned the lack of amps onstage (Mascis plays in front of three full stacks, even in a 280-person-capacity club) and the reliance on high-tech front-of-house setups. “It’s very weird. Now, soundmen create the sound instead of capture the sound,” he said. Of course, his recognition of the visceral power of live music and directly connecting with an audience makes his indifference to AI all the more baffling.
Dinosaur Jr. are currently touring the US behind There Near, which is out now.

articles.title: Lương 20 triệu vẫn ‘cháy túi’ vì ly cà phê, cốc trà sữa
articles.text:
Mất gần 4 triệu đồng mỗi tháng vì những khoản chi nhỏ
Là nhân viên văn phòng thu nhập 20 triệu đồng/tháng, chị Nguyễn Mai Hoa đặt mục tiêu tiết kiệm hàng tháng.
Chị xây dựng quy tắc chi tiêu khá chặt chẽ, trong đó tiền ăn sáng giới hạn ở mức 30.000 đồng/ngày. Tuy nhiên, sau đó chị thường gọi thêm một ly cà phê hoặc trà trái cây giá 65.000 đồng để lấy tinh thần làm việc. Những khoản chi lẻ tưởng chừng vô hại này bắt đầu âm thầm rút cạn ví.
Tuần đầu tiên, ngoài ly cà phê buổi sáng, chị gọi thêm trà sữa 55.000 đồng hoặc phần bánh ngọt 45.000 đồng. Tổng chi phí trong tuần đầu lên tới 820.000 đồng.
Tuần kế tiếp, công việc áp lực khiến tần suất gọi đồ uống tăng lên. Bên cạnh ly cà phê sáng, chị tiện tay mua thêm chai nước ép đóng chai 40.000 đồng và vài gói hạt khô nhâm nhi lúc làm việc. Tổng số tiền thanh toán qua ứng dụng trong tuần là 950.000 đồng.
Các tuần sau đó, thói quen này trở thành phản xạ tự nhiên. Cứ đến 3h chiều, chị lại mở ứng dụng đặt đồ ăn. Chưa kể những lần thanh toán bằng mã QR cho các món đồ lặt vặt như kẹo cao su, gói khăn giấy cao cấp hay tiền gửi xe phát sinh, tổng chi tiêu cho các khoản “lặt vặt” trong hai tuần cuối chạm mốc 2,1 triệu đồng.
Khi xem dữ liệu tài khoản ngân hàng cuối tháng, chị Hoa mới giật mình nhận ra tổng số tiền chi cho cà phê, trà sữa và đồ ăn vặt trong 30 ngày đã chạm con số 3,87 triệu đồng.
So với khoản ăn sáng 900.000 đồng/tháng, chi phí cho cà phê, trà sữa và đồ ăn vặt cao gấp hơn 4 lần. Nếu tính trên mức thu nhập 20 triệu đồng/tháng, tiền ăn sáng chiếm 4,5% thu nhập, trong khi các khoản chi vặt lên tới 19,35%, tương đương gần 20% lương tháng.
Mỗi giao dịch chỉ từ 40.000 đến 65.000 đồng, một số tiền quá nhỏ để khiến chị phải suy nghĩ hay đắn đo khi thanh toán. Chính số tiền nhỏ trong từng giao dịch đơn lẻ đã khiến chị không đạt được mục tiêu tiết kiệm 4 triệu đồng/tháng.
Khi những khoản chi nhỏ cộng dồn
Bà Phạm Thu Trang, chuyên viên tư vấn tài chính, cho rằng giá trị giao dịch nhỏ và hình thức thanh toán không dùng tiền mặt khiến người tiêu dùng không có cảm giác mất mát khi tiêu tiền.
Một ly cà phê 65.000 đồng không đòi hỏi người mua phải cân nhắc như một đôi giày 1,5 triệu đồng. Tuy nhiên, nếu nhân con số 65.000 đồng đó với 365 ngày, khoản chi này lên tới gần 24 triệu đồng/năm, tương đương một khoản tiền có thể dành cho tiết kiệm hoặc đầu tư.
Để kiểm soát chi tiêu, người tiêu dùng có thể áp dụng một số biện pháp thực tế.
Đầu tiên, thực hiện nhật ký chi tiêu trong 14 ngày. Mỗi cá nhân cần ghi lại chính xác từng khoản chi, dù chỉ là 5.000 đồng gửi xe hay 10.000 đồng mua chai nước. Việc nhìn thấy tổng số tiền sau 2 tuần sẽ giúp mỗi người điều chỉnh hành vi chi tiêu.
Thứ hai, áp dụng quy tắc thay thế 50/50. Người tiêu dùng không nhất thiết phải cắt giảm hoàn toàn sở thích cá nhân vì điều này dễ gây cảm giác ức chế. Thay vì mua cà phê thương hiệu giá 65.000 đồng mỗi ngày, đủ 5 ngày/tuần, có thể giảm xuống còn 2 ngày/tuần như một phần thưởng. Những ngày còn lại, người tiêu dùng có thể tự pha cà phê tại nhà hoặc sử dụng cà phê văn phòng.
Thứ ba, cài đặt hạn mức ví điện tử hoặc tài khoản chi tiêu vặt. Mỗi cá nhân nên tách riêng một tài khoản hoặc ví điện tử chỉ dành cho chi tiêu vặt, với hạn mức cố định như 500.000 đồng/tháng. Khi số dư về 0, người dùng nên ngừng các khoản mua sắm ngẫu hứng cho đến tháng tiếp theo.
Việc theo dõi các khoản chi nhỏ không đồng nghĩa với việc phải cắt bỏ mọi niềm vui thường ngày. Quan trọng hơn là xác định mức chi phù hợp với thu nhập, duy trì kỷ luật tài chính và dành tiền tiết kiệm ngay khi nhận lương, thay vì chỉ tích lũy phần còn lại vào cuối tháng.

articles.title: Trump says Google kisses his ass
articles.text:
During a rally on Saturday, October 17th, in Highland Heights, Kentucky, Donald Trump bragged about how much more powerful and influential he was during his second term. While listing off his accomplishments, he mentioned his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.
Trump says Google kisses his ass
Trump bragged at a rally that ‘Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.‘
“This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that’s unbelievable … I called Google, Google Maps. See, Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.”
Trump seems to be implying that he convinced Google to reflect the name change personally. That would seem to contradict Google’s statement on the matter, in which it said that it simply reflects “official government sources, which is GNIS for the US … These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”
Throughout his second term, however, Silicon Valley — including Google and its CEO Sundar Pichai — has gone out of its way to try and ingratiate itself with President Trump, lavishing him with gifts, compliments, and donations to his pet projects. Google did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: This Serious Home Projector Lets Cinephiles Make All the Adjustments They Could Want
articles.text:
Classy premium design. Sensational image quality, brightness, and black levels. Google TV makes for a simple setup. Great remote. Superb connectivity and compatibility.
TIRED
Given the competition, it’s too expensive for an all-in-one projector. Audio performance does not match the picture quality. Too much projector for casual use.
Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.
At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.
Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?
Setting Up Shop
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that's true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There's also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.
It’s clever tech, though not fully unique, with the XGIMI Horizon range and Nebula X1 offering similar optical-image manipulation. Even so, the VisionMaster Max offers considerably more control than most point-and-play designs. Praise is also due for the remote, which looks and feels great. Many brands scrimp on details like accessories, but Valerion maintains its premium feel throughout.
Looks Great, Sounds OK
Photograph: Chris Haslam
The VisionMaster Max produces a seriously bright image. Its 3,500 ISO lumen RGB triple-laser light source easily projected a 75-inch picture I could happily watch during the day in a bright room. Valerion says it’s good for images between 40 and 300 inches. I maxed out at 130 inches but was impressed by how even the detail remained right to the edges at that size.
While I watched during the day, the colors appeared a bit washed out in this environment, but much less so than I expected. Once I watched in the dark, however, I enjoyed punchy high-dynamic-range (HDR) highlights, excellent detail, and smooth motion.
In terms of color, the Max has 110 percent Rec.2020 coverage, meaning the lasers can reproduce an exceptionally wide range of colors, far exceeding the needs for ultra-high-definition (UHD) and HDR video. In my living room, colors looked rich without becoming cartoonish, while the combination of brightness, detail, and contrast gave movies cinematic quality.
Black levels with most home projectors are good, but not brilliant. Here, however, the proprietary six-stage iris self-adjusts the aperture from scene to scene, closing for darker images to deepen blacks, and opening up when a scene calls for more brightness. Enhanced Black Level (EBL) works alongside the iris, electronically reducing laser output in darker scenes, adjusting the image curve to maintain details. Together, these features dramatically reduce the charcoal-gray blacks common with this type of projector. I was astonished by the depth and shadow detail it produced without losing brighter details. Even the film The Dark Knight, with its muted color grading, looked good.
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Though I didn't put the VisionMaster Max through its paces for video-game testing (I’m not much of a gamer, unless you count Mario Kart battles on the Nintendo Switch), the projector's specifications are nonetheless impressive. It supports refresh rates up to 240 Hz at 1080p, with claimed input lag as low as 4 milliseconds (ms); for 4K, 60-Hz gaming, that input lag is rated at 15 ms. Two HDMI 2.1 inputs and auto low-latency mode further strengthen its gaming credentials, although it lacks a variable refresh rate (VRR) to dynamically smooth out delays.
Less impressive than its picture is its sound: The VisionMaster Max has two 12-watt speakers, and audio is clean, detailed, with effects neatly separated from dialog. But it still suffers from its box form factor. To be fair, with the exception of Anker’s removable satellite speaker designs like the Nebula X1, audio fails to keep up with image quality in many lifestyle projectors. I'd contend that at this price, an all-in-one projector should provide audio that matches the pixel-perfect picture. The Max’s speakers are fine, but push it beyond level 25 of 100, and it just sounds loud.
Thankfully, since the projector supports both DTS and Dolby Atmos, you can connect it to a decent 5.1/7.1 home theater audio system. You can also wirelessly link to a Bluetooth speaker, which makes for a clean living-room setup, although latency can be an issue. For reliable synchronization and true surround sound, HDMI eARC remains the better audio option.
Competition and Verdict
Photograph: Chris Haslam
Valerion is not without stiff competition, and that includes against itself. The Nebula X1 offers a similarly simple Google TV setup and 3,500-lumen brightness, with optional wireless surround sound making it better suited to casual living-room or outdoor use. The Leica Cine Play 1 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) combines superb optics with a more lifestyle-friendly design. Valerion’s cheaper VisionMaster Pro 2 ($2,999) retains key features, including Google TV, RGB triple-laser projection, optical zoom, and EBL, but it loses the Max’s iris and vertical lens shift. For casual movie nights, I’d be happy with this compromise that keeps extra money in my pocket.
While not necessarily casual, the Max is great and likely best suited for the viewer who wants to enjoy its capabilities. Its weight, extensive picture controls, and exceptional brightness encourage a proper screen, external sound, and careful setup, where its superb black levels and cinematic image can be fully exploited.
The brand seems to agree, as it's strongly encouraging customers to go all-in with its baffling array of deals. At the time of publication, you can opt to bundle the $3,999 Max with a choice of screens and four stands—including a tripod and ceiling mount—without paying any additional fee.
It may be overkill for occasional big-screen streaming, but as a compact projector at the heart of a home theater, I highly recommend it.
Chris Haslam is an award-winning consumer technology journalist with over 20 years’ experience. As contributing editor for WIRED he specializes in audio, smart home, sustainability, and all things outdoors. articles.title: The best gadget I bought this year is a milk frother
articles.text:
Back in February, I went to Los Angeles to take in some art and stayed in Koreatown. Down the street from my hotel, there was this little coffee shop — Stagger — that is, I think, best known for its matcha, which is good. But the drink I unexpectedly found myself obsessed with was their cream top, an iced Americano with, yep, vanilla cream on top. When I got back to Oakland, I kept thinking about how badly I wanted one.
The best gadget I bought this year is a milk frother
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
Let me convince you to change up your coffee game.
For more than 20 years, I’ve been drinking my coffee — iced or otherwise — black. Originally this was because I knew I could put black coffee that had cooled off in the microwave to reheat it without worrying that the milk in it would curdle. (Gross, I know.) Then, as I started drinking better coffee, it felt like the best way to appreciate the expensive beans I was buying.
So my attachment to the cream top surprised me. And then, when Oakland had a gnarly heat wave in March, I decided there was one way I’d tolerate it: fancy coffee drinks. I splashed out $14 for the Zulay Kitchen frother and I was off.
A handheld foamer looks and works kinda like an immersion blender. I pour milk into a glass, stick the frother in there, and then hold the power button until it reaches my preferred consistency. When the disposable batteries it uses are fresh, this takes about 30 seconds to a minute. As the batteries degrade, it takes longer; if I’m getting impatient about how long it’s taking me to make my frothy treats, it’s time to change the batteries. The frother also works to beat eggs, mix protein powder or creatine into a drink, and make hot chocolate. But by far it’s gotten the most use making my coffee drinks as I set out to make a cream top of my own.
The cream top descended from the Einspänner, an espresso drink that’s named for a one-horse carriage. The original Viennese version used hot espresso, and the whipped cream on top served as a kind of insulation, which kept the drivers’ drinks hot for them when they were out in the cold. (Obviously, its popularity expanded beyond carriage drivers.) It isn’t clear to me how the Einspänner made it to South Korea, but it exploded in popularity there, with all kinds of variations, mostly iced. And then from South Korea, it made its way to the US, where the ground had already been cleared by Starbucks’ “cold foam” drinks.
The notable thing about the cream top, besides the addition of delicious fat and sugar to coffee, was that the cream wasn’t as light as latte foam, but wasn’t as heavy as ordinary whipped cream. It was melty and dripped slowly into the coffee.
My first experiments with my at-home cream top were pretty simple. I don’t have an espresso machine, but I do make concentrated cold brew in hot weather, which has a strong enough flavor to stand up against the foam. (Some recipes suggest powdered espresso if you don’t want to use concentrated cold brew.)
After I mastered the simple cream top, I began making forays into weirder breakfast treats, my favorite of which I… recreated from a Starbucks ad. It’s a cold brew with coconut ube cold foam, the top of which I dust with toasted coconut flakes. It is dank. (This is a recipe for a more sophisticated version than I make.) So when it was 90 degrees in Oakland for about two weeks running recently, this drink was how I consoled myself.
To be honest, I’m just recommending getting a frother. You can spend a lot on a milk frother and some people do. I relied on America’s Test Kitchen to steer me in the right direction — but outlets like Wirecutter and Bon Appétit have their own preferred options. This one is cheap and simple, and it’s been treating me right. I’m sure the Apple HomeView is nice, too, but in pleasure per dollar can it match a $14 cold foamer that takes AA batteries? I have my doubts.

articles.title: Magnesium May Not Reach Your Brain, Despite Supplement Label Promises
articles.text:
Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throughout the body, taking part in hundreds of essential chemical reactions, including building DNA and proteins and sending signals within our nervous systems and between our brains and the rest of our bodies.
But just because our cells—and especially our neurons—need magnesium doesn't mean that extra magnesium will make them function any better. Not only that, but ingesting more of the element doesn’t mean it’s reaching your brain or really any specific part of your body.
In supplement pills, magnesium isn’t just on its own but part of a compound usually called a “magnesium salt.” This must dissolve to release Mg²⁺, the ionic version that our bodies use. How much of this actually gets into your system—versus gets excreted—depends on a variety of factors including the dose, your stomach contents, and how much magnesium is already in your body. In other words, the higher the dose, the less magnesium gets absorbed.
That’s all if the supplement dissolves in the first place. Magnesium oxide, which is usually the basis of the cheapest pills offered, doesn’t break down all that easily. In reality, magnesium oxide supplements mostly act as laxatives, drawing water into the intestines to flush out the excess salt.
This is where the marketing comes in. There are other types of magnesium compounds that do dissolve better. Magnesium citrate, for example, has been shown to have the highest bioavailability in laboratory tests. Despite the fact that all these salts still break down in the intestine, some supplement labels also claim that their specific chemical blend targets the magnesium directly to certain parts of your body, like your muscles or your brain.
These claims are often based on experiments using rodents, and the animals are typically supplied with magnesium long-term at higher doses than found in a pill. One study in rats found that a salt called magnesium L-threonate increased the amount of magnesium in the brain and improved some manifestations of learning and memory. This is the basis of some of the more overzealous marketing in the supplement world, which proclaims that this special salt will take the magnesium right to your brain.
There are some human studies, but that’s not really what they say. A few small randomized trials reporting improvements in some cognitive tests or sleep have been conducted—but there are several important caveats. Some studies tested a mixture of substances, lasted for only a few weeks, or analyzed a very limited number of outcomes. Many of these studies can also not be considered independent, because they were funded by supplement manufacturers or led by their staff.
Moreover, the studies—for extremely understandable reasons—didn't measure magnesium content in the brain. So maybe a little more sneaks into your gray matter, but based on the scientific understanding of how these salts are processed, in all likelihood, a brain-focused magnesium supplement is still just an expensive laxative.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

articles.title: Hoa hồng Ecuador in hình biểu tượng phụ nữ Việt Nam giá 150.000 đồng/cành
articles.text:
Cận ngày Phụ nữ Việt Nam 20/10, thị trường hoa tươi tại TPHCM trở nên nhộn nhịp. Bên cạnh các loại hoa truyền thống, những dòng hoa độc lạ, có thiết kế riêng tiếp tục thu hút người mua.
Anh Thanh Hoàng, một người dân tại TPHCM, cho biết vừa đặt một bó gồm 100 bông hồng, được kết thành hình trái tim để tặng vợ sắp cưới. Trong đó, ba bông ở vị trí trung tâm được tạo điểm nhấn bằng hình in trên cánh hoa, mang biểu tượng phụ nữ Việt Nam.
Theo anh Hoàng, dù chi phí khá cao nhưng bó hoa mang ý nghĩa đặc biệt với anh trong dịp lễ này.
Là một trong những đơn vị phân phối hoa tươi, bà Lê Thu Hiền, đại diện thương hiệu Flower box, cho biết đơn vị đã nhập 10.000 bông hồng Ecuador bằng đường hàng không để phục vụ dịp Ngày Phụ nữ Việt Nam 20/10.
Trong số này, 500 bông có cánh in logo biểu tượng người phụ nữ Việt Nam 20/10 hoặc dòng chữ Happy Vietnamese Women's Day, được bán với giá 150.000 đồng/cành, cao gấp khoảng 10 lần hoa cùng giống trồng trong nước.
"Năm nào dòng hoa in logo này cũng cháy hàng nhờ sự độc đáo. Bên cạnh đó, cửa hàng còn cung ứng lan hồ điệp in biểu tượng với giá 350.000 đồng/cành, hiện đã có hơn 50 chậu được khách đặt trước", bà Hiền chia sẻ.
Song song với các dòng hoa nhập khẩu được in hình, in chữ, hồng đỏ thông thường vẫn là lựa chọn phổ biến. Theo các tiểu thương tại chợ truyền thống, giá bán lẻ dịp 20/10 dự kiến tăng khoảng 5.000-6.000 đồng/bông so với ngày thường. Tuy nhiên, giá hoa nhìn chung được dự báo tương đương hoặc thấp hơn nhẹ so với cùng kỳ năm trước.
Đại diện chuỗi Hoa Yêu Thương dự báo sức mua năm nay duy trì ổn định do ngày 20/10 rơi vào ngày trong tuần, qua đó thúc đẩy nhu cầu mua hoa biếu tặng từ cơ quan, doanh nghiệp và người dân. Nguồn cung dồi dào cũng góp phần giúp giá bán sỉ nhiều loại hoa tương đương hoặc thấp hơn năm ngoái.
Tại kho sỉ Đà Lạt do đơn vị này cung ứng, các giống hồng ngoại trồng trong nước như hồng vàng Hà Lan, hồng vàng Helen và hồng đỏ Hỏa diệm có giá 158.000 đồng/bó 30 cành, tương đương khoảng 5.300 đồng/cành. Hồng đỏ ớt có giá 115.000 đồng/bó 30 cành, tương đương khoảng 3.800 đồng/cành.
Ở phân khúc cao cấp hơn, hồng đỏ Ecuador có giá sỉ 267.000 đồng/bó 30 cành, tương đương 8.900 đồng/cành. Hồng Red Elegance được bán với giá 197.000 đồng/bó.
Các loại hoa nhập khẩu từ Trung Quốc cũng ghi nhận sức mua tốt nhờ mức giá tương đối phải chăng. Hiện hồng chùm Sophia có giá sỉ 119.000 đồng/bó 10 cành, trong khi hồng chùm chiết xạ có giá 117.000 đồng/bó 10 cành.
Theo đại diện Hoa Yêu Thương, giá nhiều loại hoa tại các kho sỉ ở TPHCM tương đương với Đà Lạt. Riêng một số dòng hoa từ Trung Quốc có giá thấp hơn vài nghìn đồng mỗi bó.

articles.title: How overhead projectors took over your classroom
articles.text:
It used to be so easy to get away with things in school. The teacher, after all, was always turned around writing at the chalkboard! But then came a bit of technology, previously mostly used for military purposes, called the overhead projector. It would change far more than just the disciplinary record of students everywhere.
How overhead projectors took over your classroom
On Version History: How a bit of military tech changed the way we learn forever.
In this episode of Version History, we tell the story of the overhead projector. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Jake Kastrenakes and Stanford professor Antero Garcia to discuss how overhead projectors were developed, how they made their way into classrooms, and how they changed so much about the way kids learn. They also try to figure out why overhead projectors have mostly gone away, and whether the things that replaced them — from PowerPoint presentations to computer screens to those new-fangled smart boards — actually improved on the OHP.
This is the final episode of the fifth season of Version History, all about the most iconic school tech. Thanks so much for watching, listening, sending feedback, and everything else! Other than the OHP, we also spent this season looking at Oregon Trail, the original Chromebook, the One Laptop Per Child program, the LeapFrog LeapPad, and those ubiquitous Texas Instruments calculators. articles.title: Yes, Your AirPods Need a Better Case. These Are the Best for Stylish Protection
articles.text:
The best AirPods cases are subjective, but luckily, you have thousands of options to match your style and mood. You can find a ton of novelty cases online, most of which are just fine. For this guide, we focused on cases with a WIRED angle. Rather than another case that looks like food or a licensed character, the recommendations below add some functionality or protection beyond the basics.
For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best AirPods, Best Wireless Headphones, and Best iPad Accessories.
Featured in this article
Best AirPods Case Overall
Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).
The Dbrand Grip Case looks fantastic, and it doesn't add an irksome amount of bulk or weight to my headphones. The case is made of black rubber and can then be personalized with your choice of skins, plus an optional lanyard. There are more than 40 options, and you can swap them out whenever, though the sticker-like skins aren't reusable. Dbrand provides installation instructions, but I winged it and found it easy to get everything lined up. The skin options are slick, too. I'm partial to the UV-reactive Holo White, but there are some with an x-ray or pixelated aesthetic, circuit patterns, plain colors, and more. This case offers solid protection while still being eye-catching, which is why it's my favorite.
Best Rugged Case
Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation).
UAG is in the business of making tough accessories, and this sturdy option adds a thick layer of rubber around the original AirPods case to protect it from drops. It has a nice grippy texture and snug fit, with squared edges that help me get a better grip when walking around. It also comes with a sweet-looking carabiner that is optional but I quite liked. The action is smooth, and it's not too big. Every feature works as intended, and there are 10 different color options to choose from.
Best MagSafe Case
Compatible with AirPods Pro (3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)
Most cases in this guide have support for wireless charging, but if you're all in on MagSafe accessories, you'll love ESR’s Orbit case. It comes with magnets that attach securely to a MagSafe charger. The top and bottom pieces also snap shut with magnets, which helps keep the lid from accidentally sliding off (a common issue I've experienced with other AirPods cases). It's protective, with a shock-absorbing hard shell that helps protect against drops. This also means it's bulkier than other cases I've tested, but that's not a deal-breaker for me. As someone who constantly drops her AirPods case, I'll take all the extra protection I can get. —Brenda Stolyar
Best Leather Case
Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation)
This leather case is made from Horween leather, which is minimally treated and develops a rich patina over time. It feels slippery, which I didn't love, but it's still protective without adding meaningful bulk to your headphones. It fits snugly and has cutouts for the light and speaker holes. There's a lanyard attachment point, but no lanyard is included. I haven't tried a better leather case.
Best Flip-Open Case
Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (4th generation)
This case actually improved my AirPods experience. Sliding the front switch pops the lid up, so I can easily place my headphones in with one hand. The colors also come in coordinating schemes with the iPhone 17 lineup. The case stays on when I accidentally drop it, and it has a spot for a wrist lanyard, too. I also like that I can still see the charging light through the case, and the bright colors help me spot my AirPods from a distance.
A Case With a Clip
Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).
Most AirPods cases come with a clip you can attach to your bag or keys, but this case from Bandolier elevates the look. I keep it clipped to the outside of my tote bag, but you can attach it to the inside if there's a pocket.
Since it's a pouch, it doesn't attach to the top and bottom of the AirPods case like the other cases in this guide. But it's still protective, covering the entire case (except the charging port). It's made of genuine pebbled leather, giving it a bumpy texture that adds a nice high-end touch. It's also available in several colors, including black, pink, lavender, metallic blue, and more. —Brenda Stolyar
Best AirPods Max Case
Compatible with AirPods Max.
Soft-touch silicone cases are great because they're usually thin, lightweight, and come in tons of colors. But they're also dust magnets. Casetify's Ripple Case is dust-proof thanks to an antistatic coating. This is important considering the AirPods Max don't have a dust-resistance rating. That way, you can worry a little less about dust seeping in.
The Ripple case includes cutouts for the buttons, making them super easy to access. They also fit perfectly over the earcups. And, as the name suggests, they feature a ripple pattern that adds definition to the earcups. I like the color options, though I wish Casetify's logo wasn't stamped smack dab in the middle. —Brenda Stolyar
Other AirPods Cases We Tested
Burga AirPods Max Case ($25): This snap-on case for AirPods Max keeps your ports accessible and is pretty easy to snap on and remove. It's available in dozens of prints, and you can coordinate it with various iPhone accessories like cases and ring holders, too.
Compatible with AirPods Max.
Alpaka x Twelve South Micro Tote ($30): What is it about cute tiny tote bags that drives people cuckoo bananas? Because I really want this limited-edition collaboration between two makers of high-quality accessories, Alpaka and Twelve South. Originally intended for Twelve South's PowerClip portable battery, it's also the perfect size for an AirPods case. Made from Alpaka's durable X-Pac material, it includes a D-ring to hook onto the outside of your bag, belt loop, or keychain. You can also use it for coins and other small items. Although I haven't tested this long enough for a full recommendation, I have had positive experiences using Alpaka and Twelve South products long-term. —Les Shu
Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation).
Bellroy Pod Jacket ($39): Sadly, it's time to replace my trusty Incase Woolenex AirPods Case because it's reached the end of its useful life; I am upgrading to the AirPods Pro 3; and Incase no longer makes this product. Bellroy has stepped in to become my accessories maker of choice, and I love the luxe leather feel of the Pod Jacket, and it's a great alternative to our leather pick above. It includes a corded lanyard, which I don't use since I prefer to keep it in my pocket, and the lanyard just gets in the way. I like that I can still charge it wirelessly. If leather is not your thing, the Pod Jacket is available in other materials. —Les Shu
Compatible with AirPods Pro (2nd and 3rd generation).
AirPods Cases We Don't Recommend
Spigen Classic LS Case: This case makes your AirPods Pro look like the classic Macintosh mouse, but the aesthetics don't outweigh its mediocre functionality. The lid constantly pops off, and while I appreciate that Spigen includes extra adhesive, I don't want to have to deal with it. It was also annoying to open and too bulky to fit conveniently in my purse or pocket.
How Can I Tell Which AirPods I Have?
How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) To find what you have, go to Settings > Bluetooth on the Apple device you paired them with. Tap the “i” icon next to your AirPods' name to see the model number. If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.
Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.
You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.
How We Test AirPods Cases
I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. I tested most of these cases with my AirPods Pro 3, but am hoping to check out more options for the AirPods 4 and the AirPods Max soon.

articles.title: Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing
articles.text:
This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.
The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.
The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.
The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.
Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.
Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”
The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”
Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.
A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.
Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”
He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”
