articles.title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
articles.text:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Frustrated by federal gridlock, cities and states across the political spectrum are taking matters into their own hands to rein in autonomous vehicles.
How it started
The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.
Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.
While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.
The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.
How it’s going
Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.
Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.
It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.
Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.
Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.
What happens next
As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.
Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.
Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.
By the way
- Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.
- Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.
Read this
- Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.
- Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports.
- Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan.

articles.title: India’s Finance Minister blames easy exits and excess liquidity for equity market's underperformance
articles.text:
Excess liquidity in India's equity market has contributed to underperformance and may continue to do so, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.
"Because of the ease of liquidity, ease of availability, people are even exiting easily" from equities, Sitharaman told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday. However, the fundamentals of the Indian economy are "fine," she said.
Since January, India's key benchmark indexes have slipped nearly 12%, as per LSEG data, even though the country's economic growth has been resilient amid trade uncertainty and geopolitical shocks. India has been hit with record outflows by foreign investors from its equity markets, and Sitharaman said that continued capital outflows are one of the biggest risks for India in 2027.
Still, domestic capital continues to flood the market. Indian equity mutual funds have recorded net inflows every month since March 2021, according to data released by industry body Association of Mutual Funds in India earlier this month.
Multinational companies, private equity funds and foreign investors have been able to make partial or full exits from their investments at a premium. Between 2021 and 2025, Indian initial public offerings collectively raised $60.4 billion, of which "a staggering" $37.7 billion, or 63% of total proceeds, went to existing holders who sold their shares to the public, an EY report in August said.
Anti-AI Play
Foreign portfolio investors have sold direct Indian equities of over $33 billion so far this year, as per Indian depository firm NSDL. India has gained a reputation as an anti-artificial intelligence trade, while markets like Taiwan and Korea, with AI champions, have attracted strong investment flows.
The flight of capital toward AI and the U.S., which otherwise moves toward different countries for different sectoral investments, is "a concern," she added.
Taiwan now has the largest market weighting in the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index at 29%, while Korea has moved into second place at 22%, as per a report by Goldman Sachs on Oct. 8. India's share has compressed from 19% a few years ago to 10%, it added.
But with the global AI rally showing cracks, Sitharaman said India wouldn't be "hurt" from any spillover if the bubble burst. India has not received the "AI kind of investments coming into different jurisdictions," she said.
Sitharaman, who is India's longest-serving finance minister to hold the office continuously, added that the South Asian country was "no longer a laggard" in the frontier tech space and investment was being made to set up semiconductor manufacturing.

articles.title: Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption
articles.text:
Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."
The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.
The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported.
The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.
Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.
"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.
Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.
In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

articles.title: Why I am taking the other side of the trade that crushed the market Friday
articles.text: Boy, that was awful; a nightmare. Last week wasn't just a rout; it was an obliteration. We had a lot of streaks and milestones noted — semiconductors, down nine straight days. Egads. CoreWeave back to where it was when it plummeted last time. Oh no. Memory implosion. It can't be. But the simple truth is that this market acted, especially Friday, as if the data center story, the $1.2 trillion or $12 trillion "super-cycle" — in itself a kiss-of-death term, like the coal super-cycle or the fracking super-cycle — is over. That the greatest stock story ever told is over; and you better take every penny and buy Colgate-Palmolive , Coca-Cola , Procter & Gamble and, hopefully, Club name Kimberly-Clark . And all of those AI factories we need? "Desolation Row." Bob Dylan, say it isn't so. How did this happen so quickly? Where were the buyers? I have some answers. Wrong reaction? Let's start by figuring out the reaction ahead of the cause because it might be the wrong reaction. When I look at the breakdown, the concentration of what was being sold last week, culminating in Friday's devastation, it lined up rather perfectly with all of the components of the data center/AI thesis that represents about 25% of the market's market cap, albeit not its absolute percentage, which is far smaller than that. Why the reaction and not the cause? Cart before the horse? No, I don't think so. I believe that what happened last week we will find is an unwind of certain firms' positions coupled with the collapse of some hedge fund we have never heard of that borrowed billions that we don't know about from a firm that hasn't disclosed its own losses yet for lending the manager the money. I could argue that, as my great friend and original TheStreet.com hire, Herb Greenberg, is fond of: This is the end of the line for the debt-fueled hyperscale-hoax. The trillion-dollar con, spawned by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's induced moxie to give everyone money so they could buy the latest and greatest graphic processing units (GPUs) from Nvidia, led to CoreWeave's spike in corporate bond yields. That the marginal buyer is now being margined out by the cruel bond market. Reserve judgment Don't be so quick to judge Jensen. Which brings me to the two narratives that we live with every day of our investing life. They are worth parsing. They deserve critical analysis. Let's use last week's action as a paradigm. When Jensen first stumbled on the concept of accelerated computing, he realized that it could be the accelerant needed for something that really didn't exist: gigantic, instant recognition of patterns that unlocked the ability for machines to adopt thinking. Instant pattern recognition of everything. His pal, Sam Altman of OpenAI, saw ways to profit from those who need intelligence artificially. You would think that everyone would have recognized that people would pay for that, but only a few did — and do. Most big tech companies just thought of the back end, the cloud, the pipes, the service to those who wanted to charge for outcomes. As it stands now, only OpenAI, Anthropic and, to a lesser extent, portfolio holding Alphabet via Google's Gemini have capitalized on the movement at scale. But boy, oh boy, have they capitalized on it. Right now, though, given that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic has gone public, there is a universe of activity mostly funded by Nvidia, a longtime Club name, that has allowed the artificial and generative artificial, and now agentic artificial intelligence, to flourish. If Nvidia hadn't provided the seed money, maybe it would have happened eventually. Jensen wants to win. He wants Nvidia shareholders to win. He wants the United States to win. So, he opened his vault and helped fund companies the way venture capital funds help start new enterprises. The skeptics, the critics, the people who depend on things falling apart and the center not holding, just view Jensen's activities as one big legacy of Lucent, the telco equipment company from the turn of the century that did the most to mask how weak things really were by financing their one world of clients until it was obvious that there was very little business to be had without it. Or, to put it in a way Greenberg and his acolytes believe, passionately, Jensen is playing a game of Lazy Susan. He puts the money on the table, he spins it, you take it, and then you buy product from him, and everyone's happy. Having been on the other side of the Lazy Susan table, both when my mother served the turkey and the gravy and when I ran TheStreet.com, my first instinct was to blow the whistle on the activity, and so I did. It was so obviously dirty. I didn't need the goods. I didn't want them. I didn't want the bogus investment, either. Now is not like then The difference between back then and now? Back then, circa 2000, it was obvious that what was known as "vendor finance" was simply benefitting the vendor, as we didn't need the end product of what the vendor was providing. That's the actual crux of the indictment, again. Nvidia is no more than the second-coming of Lucent, and Jensen is simply Rich McGinn, the charlatan who always made the quarter with increasingly preposterous new clients that you never dreamed had the money for the purchases. Brazilian Telco. But of course, they didn't, and it was just Lucent with a chimerical bankroll. In the end, you wondered, was anything even purchased, or did the money never even come off the Lazy Susan at all; it was just spun right back. You have to believe the Lucent paradigm if you think that all of this current-day edifice is worthless or worth a lot less. It fits so perfectly, so elegantly that it comes under the short-selling rubric: too good to check out. The beauty of it all: the whole build-out really got going with Michael Intrator, a former bitcoin miner turned CEO of CoreWeave, taking billions of dollars from Nvidia in return for buying a ton of Nvidia chips to put up data centers, first largely for Microsoft, but now for most of the hyperscalers. This whole circular song, according to the bears — to let up on Greenberg, who is simply the most vocal of the negative narrators — only worked if CoreWeave, run by a darned bitcoin miner, was able to con enough public debt customers into giving it money to hold up its side of the Lazy Susan. It's almost poetry in motion. The poetry stopped this week when CoreWeave's debt yields blew up to over 15%, where the rate of return on CoreWeave's spend is too low to justify the build. If there is no new build, then there are no new Nvidia orders. If there are no new Nvidia orders, then it is game over. That was the storyline. It held up throughout the week even as there was a nice bounce from Thursday's bottom. The collapse on Friday that wiped out the Thursday reversal foretold, some would say, what happens Monday morning. Friday's session devolved into a case of "get out now" for all but the owners of Phillip Morris, Merck , and Club name Johnson & Johnson . But, at the risk of being right, let me offer you the alternative narrative. The bounce Thursday came about from something Jensen said when asked what to do about CoreWeave. The answer was simple: Don't need to do anything; in fact, things were better than we thought. The answer was brilliant: any other wording that said Jensen was ready to backstop — like he was the "Federal Reserve of Nvidia" — and we would know the Lazy Susan table was still in play and Jensen was blissfully ignorant of the now all-powerful critics. I covered the Jonestown mass murder when I was a homicide reporter in Los Angeles. I talked to the relatives of the deceased who drank the original Kool-Aid. So call me someone who knows the Kool-Aid, what it looks like, what it does to you. Nvidia does not market Kool-Aid. Jensen has something that neither Jim Jones nor the bears now had and have: credibility. The fact is, while the public debt market, the one CoreWeave needs to get bigger and bigger, may be halted for now, Jensen knows something to be true that is denied repeatedly by the haters: Nvidia's chips hold up. They may hold their value for 10 years. That's a godsend for Intrator because Jensen is lending against them for about five years. When that period is up, he takes them back. If their prices hold up and they have — he can sell them; he can lease them again. There is no doubt that they hold up. There are benchmarks of truth. There will be a two-way market in these things soon, like mortgage-backed and auto loan-backed bonds. The loan market knows that now. Intrator has borrowed against them already at much lower rates than the public markets offer. It is rare to say the public markets are wrong or manipulated or both. But I think that's the case with CoreWeave, as it is the linchpin to the thesis that the buildout isn't at its end. You either believe it, or you don't. If you believe it, you are tempted to buy Monday morning as the group is ridiculously oversold. If you think it is all one big sham, then short away or sell. Bottom line I don't think it's a sham. Let me repeat that: I don't think it's a sham. CoreWeave is not Lucent. Nvidia is not Nortel, the almighty vendor of that era. We can step back and say this is just some skirmish in the giant war for or against the data center. The big battle will come with the midterm election if it turns out that data centers really fall behind in the election to the point that even Texas and Pennsylvania don't want them. Last week made it look like a one-two punch of the market's tapped out and the election is going against the data center. I think that neither is the case. I think the market is taking a well-deserved breather, and there will always be localities that welcome data centers. I think that the ultimate build-out will come to $10 trillion to $12 trillion, like Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick threw out in CNBC Leslie Picker's excellent interview . Moreover, I think that both Anthropic and OpenAI will come public, and anyone who needs to get paid will get paid. And, I think that the states that ban the data centers will rue the day they turned down all the money that is now going to flow to the remaining states that haven't voted or voted in favor. The deals the hyperscalers will offer are insane. Full circle: My view has many believers. Too many. Because obviously many of them borrowed money to make, not that investment, but that bet. They may not even understand the sophisticated chain that gets us to where we are now. They are, alas, the problem. Broken hedge funds, not broken paradigms. If I am right, then the morass clears up pretty quickly; the bigger hedge funds that had their positions sold out underneath them will be revealed. The price of CoreWeave's debt goes down, as it was always juiced by credit default swap buying ; and even Oracle's stock goes up. Don't get complacent. The bears need to make their year, too. But be aware of how long Nvidia's chips last. Understand that there will soon be a public market trading compute because BlackRock , the largest repository of assets, has willed it to be. Recognize that generative artificial intelligence, no matter what the threat to mankind, will triumph. And accept that history will be littered with people who thought about the fourth industrial revolution too aggressively or were thinly capitalized or not competitive — like the overused rail analogy from the 1870s — and didn't make it to the promised land. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. articles.title: Brent crude hovers near $109 a barrel as Ukraine resumes energy strikes, tankers attacked in Middle East
articles.text:
Crude oil prices hovered near recent highs on Sunday as traders weighed a Ukraine bombing of oil facilities in Russia and more tankers coming under attack in the Persian Gulf.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, shed $1.04 to $108.82 per barrel. U.S. West Texas intermediate lost 26 cents to $101.15 per barrel.
Fires broke out at an oil terminal and depot in St. Petersburg after Ukraine launched a massive wave of drone strikes on Sunday, St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said in a post on Telegram.
The terminal in St. Petersburg exports about 120,000 barrels per day of refined products, mostly fuel oil, according to data from Kpler. It is unclear how bad the damage is at the facility.
Ukraine briefly paused strikes on Russian energy facilities after President Donald Trump declared on Oct. 11 that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to a truce.
But Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump's announcement. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that Kyiv would resume strikes on Russian facilities in retaliation.
In the Middle East, meanwhile, two tankers were attacked off the coast of Saudi Arabia in the Persian Gulf on Friday, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
A small boat fired a rocket-propelled grenade at an unidentified tanker 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl, according to UKMTO. Another tanker, the ST3, was hit by an unknown projectile, UKMTO reported.
Iran has escalated attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman in an effort to choke off crude oil exports from the region.

articles.title: Nasdaq futures gain as investors buy the dip in the AI trade: Live updates
articles.text:
Stock futures rebounded on Sunday night as traders cautiously dipped a toe back in following last week's rout in shares linked to the artificial intelligence trend.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.4%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked 0.2% higher, or 110 points. S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%.
Stable oil prices early Sunday also lent the equity market some support.
The S&P 500 lost nearly 2% last week, its biggest weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq tumbled 4.5%, snapping a four-week winning streak.
Concerns around the health of the AI trade took center stage after CNBC reported, citing sources, that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue totaled $16.8 billion. And while that's up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, it raised flags among investors about the pace of growth with the AI build-out.
Neocloud stock CoreWeave, which uses large amounts of debt to build data centers that it rents out to tech companies, was at the center of those fears. The AI-linked name plummeted 25% last week — its largest one-week drop since November 2025. Investors in the corporate bond market have started to shun CoreWeave, with the company's credit default swaps reaching distress levels.
It's not just CoreWeave whose moves in the credit market are concerning. Goldman Sachs traders noted Friday: "AI Credit Spreads and hyperscalers specifically are at the widest levels of the year. The last time spreads were nearly this high, the underlying equities were 15% lower."
"The widening across the complex has forced investors to confront what happens as AI spending growth slows. AI Capex has likely peaked and financing, sustainability, and returns on capital have become the debate rather than the next near term earnings revision," they said. "Pessimism is increasing, market breadth is low, and [Friday] we saw the second highest amount of puts traded (right behind June of this year)."
Traders were also keeping a wary eye on oil with ship attacks in the Persian Gulf picking up and Ukraine and Russia trading attacks on energy infrastructure. Ukraine hit an oil terminal in St. Petersburg, Russia on Sunday. Longer-dated oil futures have begun to ratchet higher on expectations energy infrastructure disruptions may last well into 2027.
On Sunday however, Brent and WTI crude futures were both trading a tad lower.
A slew of earnings from major companies such as Meta Platforms and Tesla hit the Street this week with optimism those results will stabilize the market.

articles.title: Here are the 3 big things we're watching in the stock market this week
articles.text: The market has been hard to please so far this earnings season. The week ahead will bring plenty of chances to flip the script. Netflix , Tesla and Club names Meta Platforms and Capital One are among the companies set to report quarterly results in the coming days, as third-quarter earnings season kicks into high gear. There aren't any huge economic reports on the docket either, brightening the spotlight on the stream of earnings updates. There may be little margin for error, if the frosty reception to last week's bank earnings are any indication. Top and bottom-line beats from the likes of Goldman Sachs were met with selling . Those with more apparent blemishes, such as State Street and Bank of America , got hit even harder . We can't say we're surprised. Jim Cramer said in early October that rising bond yields and a Federal Reserve determined to bring down inflation created "a much more difficult backdrop" for this earnings season. What's happened since Jim's warning? Tensions in the Middle East worsened , two September inflation reports came in hotter than expected , and the durability of the AI spending boom has been called further into question. The midterms are also now about two weeks away, injecting more uncertainty into the market. In other words, the backdrop hasn't gotten any easier. Now let's take a closer look at what we're expecting from Capital One, Meta and a few non-portfolio stocks with implications for our names. 1. Capital One earnings: The credit-card issuer starts us off Tuesday night. In the wake of last week's hot inflation readings, CEO Richard Fairbank's commentary on spending dynamics across income cohorts will be especially notable. As for the numbers, net interest income came up short last quarter due to thinner-than-expected net interest margin, so we'll be looking for sequential expansion this time around. Net charge-offs — the amount Capital One assumes it won't be able to recover from borrowers — were also a bit high in July, so we want to see better performance there. Better charge-offs, along with a release on loan reserves — the amount the bank sets aside in anticipation of bad loans — would help instill greater confidence in the quality of the credit the firm has extended. Given what we heard last week from the banks, we do expect credit commentary to be neutral to positive. Capital One's non-interest expenses will be under the microscope. The company has been investing heavily into the business, which has held back earnings in recent quarters and, in turn, the stock. But, at less than 9 times forward earnings, Capital One shares look too cheap to give up on. We also hope to see more tangible benefits from the Discover acquisition, though we recognize full expense synergies are not expected to be achieved until the middle of next year. As of Friday, Capital One is expected to report earnings of $5.50 per share on revenue of $16.26 billion, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. 2. Meta earnings: The Facebook and Instagram parent reports after Wednesday's close, and it is sure to be an exciting earnings call. CEO Mark Zuckerberg is riding high from the viral launch of its agentic AI platform assistant, Muse. While directional commentary on adoption trends figures to be positive, we're interested to see if management shares actual numbers, both in terms of overall engagement (like daily active users) and the breakdown of user types (such as paid versus free). Against the engagement commentary, we must acknowledge that this positive reception will embolden Zuckerberg to press the bet and keep investing aggressively in compute infrastructure. As a result, commentary on AI spending intentions — and how it will be funded — are going to counterbalance the Muse optimism as analysts put pen to paper. How well Zuckerberg and CFO Susan Li are able to explain and justify the spending is sure to impact the stock market reaction. Will they point to current monetization trends, or detail the future revenue potential? Outside of Muse, the focus will be on the company's core Family of Apps business, and whether it's benefiting from the more advanced AI models coming out of Meta Superintelligence Labs. Meta is expected to report earnings per share of $5.94 on revenue of $63.32 billion, according to LSEG, as of Friday. 3. Non-Club reports to watch: Capital One and Meta aren't the only earnings releases on our radar. While it is impossible to cover every name (though we still have to try), there are several companies reporting that every investor should monitor. We'll group them into thematic buckets: AI buildout: Alongside Meta on Wednesday night, we'll hear from Lam Research and Texas Instruments . Lam Research is a capital equipment manufacturer, meaning it makes equipment that chipmakers need to manufacture semiconductors (both logic and memory chips), so it offers a window into efforts to close the supply-demand imbalance. Though Texas Instruments makes semiconductors used across a bunch of industries, its fast-growing business selling power management chips into data centers is what we care about most. On Thursday night, Western Digital reports. The hard-drive maker sits within the broader storage and memory complex alongside Club name Micron (though they make different things).
