articles.title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
articles.text:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine.
U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.
In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.
Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.
"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."
"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.
Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.
Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.
Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA. Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

articles.title: The bloated workweek is coming for Sundays—as some embrace flexibility, others worry about job security
articles.text:
Alessia Montanaro is just about to close her second busy season of the year. Since September she's been logging up to 60 hours of work per week, sometimes going as late as 11 p.m., and making a habit of working Sundays from her home office.
The 30-year-old works in public accounting in Austin, Texas, and has gotten used to these sprints around tax season. She's not the only weekend work warrior.
For many office workers, Sundays have become the unofficial new start to their workweek: Nearly half of workers often clock in on Sundays, according to a recent report from Owl Labs, the video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July with a margin of error of 2%. Some 21% of people surveyed say they work the whole or nearly the whole day, and another 24% say they often do a few hours of work.
Of the remaining set of workers, 11% say they quickly check messages but don't really work, 18% say they rarely do any work on Sundays, and 26% say they never do.
It's been six years since work for many moved home during the Covid-19 pandemic, opening the possibilities of logging hours anytime and anywhere there's Wi-Fi. While some people deprioritized work and put up strict boundaries to protect their personal time, tech use data shows that many years later, working time has bled into every hour of every day. Chat messages sent outside of the standard Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. workweek rose 15% year-over-year, now up to an average 58 messages per user, according to Microsoft's 2025 research on what it calls the rise of the "infinite workday."
Among those working on the weekends, nearly 20% check their email before noon on a Saturday and Sunday, and over 5% are in their inboxes on Sunday nights, per Microsoft.
As far as these online habits show, the sanctity of Sundays off may be vanishing as an always-on work culture takes over.
Daytime distractions push work to the weekend
Some Sunday workers say working weekends or after hours is the only way to get focused work done. During the workweek, "I get pulled in five different directions" with messages or requests from associates and higher-ups, Montanaro of Austin says.
Working a distraction-free Sunday can help workers get more done, says Frank Weishaupt, CEO of Owl Labs. But it can also be a signal that the typical Monday-through-Friday is overloaded with busywork.
The work of getting work done can be disruptive: Employees are interrupted roughly every two minutes during core work hours with meetings, emails or chat messages, according to Microsoft data. Some 38% of workers say they have meeting fatigue, with the most common gripes being that meetings are too long and there are too many of them, according to Owl Labs.
Workers carve out flexibility where they can
Weishaupt says Sunday work periods could be seen as a good thing "as it relates to the employee's desire for flexibility" and a growing interest in "microshifting," a term Owl Labs coined to mean working outside of a traditional Monday through Friday 9-to-5 time block.
Microshifting can be especially helpful to moms, caregivers and anyone who might need to duck out for a few hours on workdays. Kylie Gonzalez, 29, says she'll clock into her account manager job from home on a Sunday if she took some time during the week for doctor's appointments, school pickup for her kids or other events.
But she's wary of spending more than an hour or so working on the weekend, or making a habit of it. "Some companies may take advantage of that fact and add more to your plate because they see so much is being done," she says.
Job anxiety fuels the Sunday scaries
In 2019, the norm was going into the office on a Monday and getting settled for the week ahead, Weishaupt says. That prep work is now shifting to Sundays.
"My Sunday evening feels awful because I'm just thinking about Monday and all the work that I didn't finish on Friday," says Tobi Collins, 28, a strategy consultant in Dallas. Her weekend work helps her curb the Sunday scaries, she says: "If I just get ahead of it, I'm not as nervous about the week."
Dina Otero, 42, of Philadelphia, says she used to regularly log weekend hours, even spending her Sundays back from vacation catching up on emails before her actual return to work. Working a little extra at the start of the week would help her get ahead, she told herself. Really, it was just anxiety and "my own way of thinking that I had control over things that I really did not," she says.
In the current tough job market, when companies are signaling layoffs before they happen, hiring less and raising expectations around artificial intelligence, Weishaupt says Sunday work could also be a sign of overworking when people are worried about job security. Workers are "doing anything they can to hug that job, and that may mean that they're just working a lot more, Sunday included," he says.
That can become a big problem if unchecked. "If 40 hours become 60 hours, you know you're going to have burnout, you're going to have frustration, and then when that pendulum swings the other way, you're going to have a lot of churn," Weishaupt says.
LaToya Allen, 45, in Washington, D.C., isn't sure the extra work hours are always worth it. She found herself in a burn-and-churn cycle in 2020, when she became disillusioned by her corporate tech job and what she saw as a false promise of success and security.
She now runs her own boutique tech consultancy and says working "pretty much seven days a week" comes with the territory of entrepreneurship. For 9-to-5 workers, though, "I don't see how working on a Sunday is going to save your job," she says. "Just because your manager sees you working on Slack on a Sunday, what does that matter?"

articles.title: Iran says it has a 'new operational plan' if the U.S. resumes attacks, as shipping vessels report strikes
articles.text:
A senior Iranian security official warned Sunday that Tehran has prepared a new response plan for any renewed U.S.-Israeli attack, as maritime authorities reported several separate attacks on commercial vessels around the Arabian Peninsula.
"Iran's armed forces have prepared a response to any new act of adventurism that would be far more devastating than the 12-day and 40-day wars," Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said in a post on X, referring to attacks by Israel in June 2025, and the conflict triggered by the U.S. and Israel in February.
"Iran's new operational plan will not follow the rules with which they are familiar," Rezaei said in comments translated by Google.
President Donald Trump said last week that he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country.
Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world."
The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs."
Iranian state media agency IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as saying that while Iran would not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure, it remains ready for dialogue.
Vessels under fire
Meanwhile, shipping vessels operating in waters around the Arabian Peninsula reported coming under fire in recent days.
The British Navy-affiliated UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said a tug traveling south northeast of the United Arab Emirates was hit by two unknown projectiles on Sunday.
On Saturday, a master of a liquefied natural gas tanker southwest of Yemen reported "being approached by a small skiff with seven persons onboard," UKMTO said. The skiff fired twice, and the tanker's security team responded with two warning shots, it said.
Another tanker northeast of Saudi Arabia reported being hit by a rocket-propelled grenade fired from a small boat on Friday.
Crude oil prices rose sharply Friday amid rising tensions in the Middle East, while Ukraine vowed to keep striking Russian refineries.
Brent futures hit a session high of $110 per barrel for the first time since May before easing slightly to settle at $109.86, a 3.7% gain.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.5% to settle at $101.41 per barrel. WTI added more than 10% last week while Brent advanced nearly 5%.
Saudi Arabia intercepted several missiles fired over the Red Sea on Friday, including one that was heading toward the oil export terminal Yanbu, a military spokesman said. Three drones were also destroyed in the kingdom's Riyadh and southern regions, the military said.
Iran-allied Houthi militants in Yemen repeatedly fired at Saudi Arabia last week. The kingdom's energy ministry said oil giant Aramco came under attack when militants hit one of its administrative buildings in Dhahran on Tuesday.

articles.title: I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on
articles.text:
When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do.
Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practices and winning games? Did they clean their rooms and set the table? Are they motivated? Responsible? Social? Can they solve problems, make good choices and eventually become independent adults?
But after years spent working with more than 200 families, I've seen that some of the most important lessons children need to live successful, happy and fulfilling lives — and to build healthy relationships — have very little to do with action or achievement.
Children absorb crucial messages in ordinary moments based on how we respond when they struggle, fail, disagree with us, disappoint us or simply become someone different from who we imagined they would be.
In my experience, there are six things parents of the most successful, confident, resilient and well-adjusted kids teach them early on that have nothing to do with accomplishments.
1. Failure doesn't change who they are to you
Children notice what happens between you when something goes wrong. They see your face when the grade comes back. They notice whether you seem prouder after the win and more distant after the loss.
A child should be able to fail without feeling they have fallen in your eyes. For example, instead of immediately asking "Why didn't you study more?" try "I know you wanted a different result. How are you feeling about it?"
When children know a bad result won't change how we see them, they don't have to be so afraid of getting things wrong. Failure can become something they learn from instead of something they feel they need to hide.
2. Disappointing someone doesn't always mean they did something wrong
If being "good" means pleasing other people, someone else's disappointment can start to feel like proof a child did something wrong. They may learn to read the room before they learn to read themselves.
We can show them a different way. You might say: "Someone else can be disappointed in your choice, and it can still be the right choice for you."
Your child needs to know that you can disagree with them and they can still trust themselves. That matters later, too, with friends, partners and bosses.
3. What they're good at isn't who they are
Even positive labels can feel like pressure. If adults keep saying:
- "You're so smart."
- "You're our athlete."
- "You're the responsible one."
A child can quietly start to hear: This is who I have to keep being. Then a B isn't just a B. Getting cut from the team isn't just disappointing. Struggling can start to feel like losing a piece of who they are.
Instead of making the achievement their identity, notice what went into it. You might say: "You kept going even when that got difficult."
When we separate what children accomplish from who they are, we give them room to become more than whatever they happen to be good at today.
4. They can disagree or be upset with someone and still be loved
Children need to disagree with us sometimes and discover that the relationship is still okay.
That doesn't mean they make every decision. We are still the parents. We can hold a boundary with our kids and stay connected to them at the same time. You might say: "You're allowed to be angry with my decision. The answer is still no, and we're still okay."
A child shouldn't have to choose between having a voice and feeling close to us. If they feel like they have to give up their voice to stay connected at home, saying no can become much harder everywhere else too.
5. Uncomfortable feelings don't need to be fixed right away
Our instinct as parents is often to make our children feel better. We fix, reassure, distract or tell them everything will be fine.
Sometimes they need something simpler: "This is hard. I'm here."
Children need to learn that feeling bad doesn't mean something has gone wrong. They can be embarrassed and get through it. They can be nervous and still walk into the room.
We don't have to rescue children from every uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes staying beside them as they experience those feelings is how they discover: I can handle this.
6. Home is the one place they don't have to impress anyone
Children already live in a world that measures them: grades, teams, rankings, likes and eventually college admissions, job offers and performance reviews.
The outside world will keep asking: "What can you do?" Home should answer a different question with an emphatic yes: Do I still matter when there's nothing to celebrate?
Sometimes it helps to say it directly: "I love watching you succeed. But you never have to impress me to belong here."
Achievement should add to a child's life. It should never become the only reason they feel worthy.
Reem Raouda is a certified conscious parenting coach, speaker and author dedicated to one core idea: that loving your child and making them feel safe are not the same thing. She is the founder of The Safe Mom and creator of The Safe Mom Masterclass, helping parents raise emotionally healthy children through emotional safety, connection and self-awareness. Find her on Instagram.

articles.title: Roth conversions: When the ‘juice isn't really worth the squeeze,’ according to a top-ranked advisor
articles.text:
Roth individual retirement account conversions can potentially reduce lifetime taxes. But the strategy isn't right for everyone, and the choice is now more complex amid updates from President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" and other changes.
Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which kick-starts tax-free growth. The trade-off is that they can trigger more income in the year of the conversion.
The move can be attractive if you have large pretax retirement balances and you expect higher tax rates when it's time to withdraw the funds, experts say.
At year-end 2025, IRA-owning households in the U.S. had $15.9 trillion in assets in traditional IRAs, compared with $2.4 trillion in after-tax Roth IRAs, according to a 2026 report from the Investment Company Institute, an investing trade organization.
Weighing Roth conversions, or partial Roth conversions, is "a strategy that continues to be very popular year-over-year," said Charissa Anderson, a certified financial planner who is an executive vice president at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management in Portland, Oregon. Her firm ranked No. 52 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.
As of March 31, Roth conversions were up 41% this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the latest Fidelity data, based on an analysis of 19.6 million IRA accounts.
But experts say the strategy isn't right for everyone.
"There are just so many variables" when analyzing a possible Roth conversion, said Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo in Orlando, Florida. His firm is ranked No. 44 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.
These could include when you claim Social Security, your life expectancy and legacy goals, among other factors, he said.
Depending on your tax bracket, "sometimes the juice isn't really worth the squeeze," said Lucas. "And we're going to have to squeeze every single year" because multiple factors can change the analysis.
If you're eyeing a Roth conversion before year-end, here are some key things to consider.
Roth conversions impact tax benefits
When deciding on a Roth conversion, projections should include the current year's taxes, along with an analysis of future years, financial advisors say.
"The [tax] bracket you see isn't always the rate you pay," because more income could phase out, or reduce, other tax benefits, according to CFP Tommy Blackburn, senior financial planner and partner at Mason and Associates in Newport News, Virginia. He is also a certified public accountant.
As an example, Blackburn pointed to a client in the 22% tax bracket with a child in college. Income from a conversion could trigger taxes above 30% because the client would lose an education tax credit, which is subtracted from their taxes owed, he said.
By comparison, a client in the 10% tax bracket could convert a limited amount under their standard deduction without owing additional taxes for the current year, he said.
More income could also impact temporary tax deductions enacted via Trump's "big beautiful bill," which have varying income phaseouts.
These could include the bigger federal deduction limit for state and local taxes, known as SALT, worth up to $40,400 for 2026, or the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction, among others.
Retirees should also consider income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level. The surcharge is based on modified adjusted gross income from two years prior.
ACA enrollees should 'proceed with caution'
Boosting your AGI with Roth conversions can also reduce the premium tax credit, which makes Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance less expensive.
Earning even $1 more than a certain income limit can threaten eligibility for the credit — known as the "ACA cliff" — and enrollees could owe full premiums for health coverage.
The cliff affects ACA enrollees when household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty line, which varies by family size. For 2026, those limits are about $63,000 for a single person or $129,000 for a family of four.
That's why marketplace health insurance enrollees should "proceed with caution" before completing a Roth conversion, said CFP Bill Shafransky, a senior wealth advisor with Moneco Advisors in New Canaan, Connecticut.
"This is one of those financial strategies where you really want to dot your i's and cross your t's before acting," he said.
CNBC receives no compensation from placing financial advisory firms on our Financial Advisor 100 list. Additionally, a firm's or advisor's appearance in our ranking does not constitute an individual endorsement by CNBC of any firm or advisor.

articles.title: Boomers are buying into the promise of monthly income from options ETFs, but there's a tax catch
articles.text:
Covered call ETFs have gained a following for their ability to generate monthly cash flow. But a tax surprise could be lurking for many investors.
These actively managed funds have different underlying assets and strategies. But the premise is generally the same. Covered call funds hold equities and sell call options or use related derivatives to generate income. Investors receive attractive income yields in exchange for limited capital upside. The tax piece is more complicated, however.
A fund that realizes option premiums, short-term gains or other income still has taxable amounts to distribute. The tax hit can be easy — and costly — for investors to miss, especially since ETFs are typically understood to be tax-efficient investment vehicles, and especially since most investors aren't looking at the tax implications until they receive a 1099-DIV at tax time, the IRS tax document issued by financial services companies to report dividends and related distributions paid to investors during a tax year.
Even if a fund has good returns and a favorable 30-day SEC yield — which measures the net investment income of bond funds or equity funds and is annualized to reflect the yield an investor would expect to earn over the course of a full year — investors need to look under the hood and understand the tax implications of covered call ETFs. "The after-tax net total return might fall below your expectations," said Matthew Smart, chief investment officer at WWM Investments in Chicago.
Here's what investors need to know about covered call ETFs and taxes:
Not all income distributions are created equal
Distributions from covered call funds come in several forms: dividends, capital gain distributions, or non-dividend distributions. The distribution mix can vary by fund and change year to year. Non-dividend distributions are commonly known as return of capital — payment or distribution from a portion of an investor's original principal rather than an economic profit, capital gain, or dividend earnings. And this is where it can get confusing for investors because ROC distributions aren't treated as current income. Instead, they reduce the investment's cost basis by the distribution amount, so they are tax-deferred until shares are sold.
Covered call ETFs take different approaches to distributions. "Some covered call strategies make distributions characterized only as ordinary dividends. Other strategies make distributions that may include all three types. And since investors' individual tax rates vary significantly, there can be a large difference between what investors receive in fund distributions on a pre-tax basis, and what they keep after paying taxes," ProShares wrote in a blog on covered call strategy and tax efficiency.
Investors surprised by cost-basis and delayed taxes
Some covered call ETF investors are surprised at tax time by the magnitude of the qualified dividends and ordinary income, said Edwin Retter, senior wealth advisor in the Melbourne, Florida, office of Mission Wealth.
They are also confused by the ROC concept. While it seems favorable from a distribution standpoint in the short term, it's investors' own money coming back to them, which reduces the cost basis. Having a lower cost basis generally increases the investor's capital gains tax liability at the time of sale.
"You're not avoiding the taxes; you're just delaying it until you sell," said Aaron Brachman, wealth manager at the Washington Wealth Group of Steward Partners in Washington, D.C.
Use of tax-deferred accounts is recommended
Investors who decide to purchase a covered call ETF should ideally do so within a tax-deferred account such as a traditional IRA, Retter said. "I don't know how many investors give so much thought to that. They just find out at tax time that they've put it in a less tax-desirable account."
By investing in a covered call ETF through a traditional IRA, investors don't have to worry about taxes until they pull money out of the account. "You can really save a lot of time and taxes by putting it in the right account structure," Retter said.
Tax-cost ratio is a key measure to evaluate
Investors who want to better understand how taxes come into play in a covered call ETF can use a measurement known as the tax-cost ratio. The Morningstar Tax Cost Ratio measures how much a fund's annualized return is reduced by the taxes investors pay on distributions. Investors can type in the ticker of the fund they are researching on Morningstar.com, click on the price tab, and scroll down to see the tax-cost ratio.
"It is a flexible tool that can help investors easily compare different time periods, different funds, and different categories. Investors pay taxes when they receive a taxable distribution and these costs are just as relevant as the expense ratio in reducing an investor's take-home return," Morningstar wrote in a paper explaining the methodology for the calculation.
For instance, the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPI) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 3.11, according to Morningstar. That means after-tax returns are reduced by about 3.11 percentage points annually for investors in the highest tax brackets.
Another example is the JPMorgan Nasdaq Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPQ). The fund's three-year tax cost ratio is 4.30. By contrast, the Neos S&P 500(R) High Income ETF (SPYI) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 0.48.
The tax picture can be very ETF-specific because it depends on how the fund is structured, said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst at Tax Alpha Insider. SPYI has a higher return of capital than some of its peers, lowering the more immediate tax consequences, but there's still a cost-basis and fund growth issue for investors to consider, he added.
Pay attention to NAV
It's not just taxes investors have to consider with these funds. "It's good to look at the portfolio returns, and it's good to look at tax consequences, but NAV has to grow faster than the distribution rate," Sullivan said. "The fund's NAV must keep going up to sustain those distributions. It's not magic. The money has to come from somewhere, and it can't just come from new investors," he said.
Investors should also look at a fund's 30-day SEC yield to get a sense of what the company is generating in terms of income. JEPI has a 30-day SEC yield of 7.45%, compared with JEPQ's 11.56%, and SPYI's 0.45%.
Consider other income-generation alternatives
Several financial advisors said they aren't fans of covered call ETFs for tax, complexity and other reasons.
With the 10-year U.S. Treasury continuing to hover around 5%, there are more opportunities for investors to find attractive income in bonds, from ultra-short bond funds to corporate bonds.
"I'd rather have a person in a portfolio that's predominantly fixed income and hedge the interest rate risk with 20% to 40% of the portfolio in high-quality growth stocks," said Andrew Urbanski, founder and chief investment officer at N10 Assets in Greenwich, Connecticut. "If the income isn't enough, draw on the principal from the bond or stock portion of the portfolio in a way that's more risk and cost-efficient," he said.
Covered call ETFs do cap an investor's upside. In a taxable account, an investor might instead buy an S&P 500 ETF — or a total market ETF to get more small and mid-cap exposure — collect the dividends, and make systematic withdrawals through small periodic share sales after a year for tax-efficiency reasons, Retter said.
Index-based ETFs generally have lower expense ratios than their actively managed counterparts. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) has an expense ratio of 0.03%. The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) also has an expense ratio of 0.03%.
By contrast, JEPI and JEPQ each have an annual expense ratio of 0.35%. SPYI has an expense ratio of 0.68%.
Meanwhile, many of the covered call ETF funds include the large tech stocks such as Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta that have been driving the market's growth, so it is important for investors to know whether these stocks are already well represented in their portfolio.

articles.title: Meta Platforms and Tesla are among the companies set to report next week. What to expect
articles.text: The earnings season picks up even more steam this week, with investors looking for clues on how companies are doing at a critical time for the stock market. There are 70 S & P 500 companies reporting this week, including Meta's first quarterly results since the launch of viral AI agent Muse and "Magnificent Seven" counterpart Tesla . Netflix also reports after making multiple big organizational changes last week, as does automaker General Motors . Both the S & P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite fell last week as traders rotated out of tech stocks over concerns of mounting debt from the artificial intelligence build-out. Markets are also contending with high inflation and continued geopolitical tensions . Earnings results are still expected to be strong this week for many of the major companies reporting, however. The quarterly earnings season began in earnest last week, with major U.S. banks reporting . Goldman Sachs , Morgan Stanley and Citigroup beat earnings and revenue estimates. Wells Fargo reported mixed results, while JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America fell short on both the top and bottom lines. Overall, the reporting period is off to a strong start. About 45 S & P 500 companies have reported thus far, with 85% of those exceeding earnings estimates, FactSet data shows. All times ET. Tuesday General Motors is set to report earnings before the bell. Management will then hold a conference call at 8:30 a.m. Last quarter: GM raised its 2026 guidance as its North American business drove strong results . This quarter: According to LSEG, analysts expect nearly a 30% jump in earnings per share but flat revenue compared to this time last year. What to watch: Last week, JPMorgan analysts maintained their overweight rating on the stock but lowered their price target amid expectations of a 2027 outlook "likely to present a cautious tone" in part due to affordability concerns. Vehicle sales for the automaker declined by 5.5% this past quarter. What history shows: Data from Bespoke Investment Group shows General Motors beats analyst earnings estimates 89% of the time. Shares have risen after each of the last four earnings releases. Netflix is set to report earnings after the bell, with a call slated for 4:45 p.m. Last quarter: NFLX shares sank more than 7% after in line results as Wall Street closely watched its engagement numbers. This quarter: The streaming giant is expected to post 40% in earnings growth compared to the year-earlier period, according to LSEG data. What to watch: Barclays analyst Kannan Venkateshwar noted last week that, with engagement choices on streaming services becoming more deliberate, many viewers still view Netflix "as a service for library content," despite Originals making up more than 60% of Netflix's titles. "The issue may not be Netflix itself but rather that the world around Netflix has changed and Netflix hasn't really changed enough with it," Venkateshwar wrote. On top of that, Netflix last week announced plans to lay off around 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and replaced its chief content officer. What history shows: Netflix's stock has struggled after reports in five straight quarters. United Airlines is set to report earnings after the bell, with a conference call on Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. Last quarter: UAL's high fuel costs due to the U.S.-Iran war pressured earnings, with increased jet fuel prices potentially adding $6 billion more to expenses in 2026 than expected. This quarter: Analysts polled by LSEG expect revenue growth of more than 15% — but declining EPS compared to a year earlier. What to watch: Will earnings be able to defy the pressure of still-increasing energy costs? Competitor Delta Air Lines was forced to slash its full-year forecast when it reported earlier this month due to the high fuel prices, despite strong consumer demand. What history shows: United beats analyst expectations 75% of the time, and has done so in every quarter since July 2022. Wednesday AT & T will report earnings before the bell, with a conference call at 8:30 a.m. Last quarter: T rose 3% on better-than-expected earnings despite missing slightly on revenue. This quarter: LSEG data shows analysts expect nearly 11% in earnings growth from the year-earlier period but slower topline growth for the same period at 3.2%. What to watch: Bernstein downgraded T to market perform from outperform after news that SpaceX will acquire a nationwide spectrum portfolio sparked a sell-off of telecom stocks. Investors will look for clues on how the company can contend with the growing competition. What history shows: AT & T only beats bottom line estimates 59% of the time, according to Bespoke. But on average, AT & T's stock is little changed following earnings reports. Meta Platforms will report earnings after the bell and host a conference call at 4:30 p.m. Last quarter: META's cash flow took a big hit , sending shares down 8%. This quarter: Meta's earnings per share are expected to have grown a whopping 460% compared to a year earlier, LSEG data shows. What to watch: Analysts across the board are bullish on Meta after the company released its AI agent Muse Sept. 8. The Magnificent Seven titan's stock has shot up more than 15% since Muse's release. Investors now wonder how that will translate to the company's bottom line. What history shows: Meta beats expectations 88% of the time, Bespoke data shows, but its stock took nearly an 8% hit after its topline miss last quarter. Shares also fell sharply after the company's Q1 2026 and Q3 2025 releases. Tesla is set to report earnings after the bell, with a conference call to follow at 5:30 p.m. Last quarter: TSLA posted weaker-than-expected earnings , with margins coming under pressure and cash flow turning negative. This quarter: According to LSEG, Tesla's revenue and earnings per share are expected to have declined, with a 14.5% drop in earnings and close to a 1% decline in revenue from the year prior. What to watch: Wolfe Research is eyeing a potential merger with SpaceX and Tesla's robotaxi business as potential positive developments for the Elon Musk-led automaker, but says they are estimating earnings below consensus in a "tough quarter for Auto stocks." Tesla's third-quarter delivery numbers declined 2% from the year prior but nevertheless topped estimates, sending the stock surging. What history shows: Tesla has fallen short of analyst earnings estimates in two of the last four quarters and only posts a beat on the topline 58% of the time, per Bespoke. Thursday Procter & Gamble is set to report earnings before the bell, with a call slated for 8:30 a.m. Last quarter: PG's beauty division was its top performer, but the company only reported volume growth in one quarter for the 2026 fiscal year. This quarter: Procter & Gamble is expected to post revenue growth just shy of 2% and a 5.4% decline in earnings, LSEG data shows. What to watch: Citi last week maintained its buy on the personal goods stock and said it has an optimistic outlook on PG heading into earnings. "We expect a closing of the gap vs. consumption in the US in F1Q27 and potential upside in China given the competitive dynamics in diapers, resulting in OSG re-accelerating to ~3%," analyst Filippo Falorni wrote. What history shows: Procter & Gamble beats expectations on earnings 86% of the time and has done so for every quarter since April 2023, Bespoke data shows. American Airlines is slated to report earnings in premarket, with a conference call to follow at 8:30 a.m. Last quarter: AAL cut its full-year earnings outlook once again due to high fuel costs. This quarter: LSEG data shows the airline is expected to post top line growth of 18%. What to watch: American has made a push toward premium over the past quarter as it tries to close its profit gap to rivals United and Delta, adding more first class seats and rolling out redesigned Boeing planes . CEO Robert Isom said at a conference last month that 30% of seats generate half of the airline's revenue . What history shows: The airline exceeds earnings estimates 88% of the time. However, the stock averages a 0.4% decline on earnings days, according to Bespoke.

articles.title: Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks
articles.text:
Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.
Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.
Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.
UnitedHealth
Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.
Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.
The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.
Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.
Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.
Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.
Meta Platforms
Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.
Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.
Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.
"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.
While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.
Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.
Marvell Technology
Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.
After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.
The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.
While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.
Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.
Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

articles.title: Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
articles.text:
Chris Thomas is all-in on AI gadgets.
Thomas, 43, wears a pair of Meta's camera-equipped glasses, a Fieldy note-taking pendant around his neck and a wristband from Amazon's Bee, all of which record his daily life. A Pittsburgh-based business owner and a livestreamer, Thomas relies on the devices to help him stay organized, pay bills on time and set reminders.
"I'm forgetful AF," Thomas said in an interview. "My life is so crazy that not having to remember to remember is fantastic."
Not everyone is on board with his lifestyle. Earlier this week, a bystander at a local bar noticed his Meta Glasses.
"He was like, 'I don't feel comfortable,'" Thomas said. "I don't turn it off, I take it off completely because people don't really believe it's off."
It's the type of interaction users are increasingly navigating as more tech companies introduce AI-powered, always-listening devices and features, which have been marketed as useful tools to transcribe meetings, keep track of conversations, set reminders and offer personalized recommendations.
The latest example of these gadgets arrived Thursday with Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable and Bee Eclipse, a card-shaped device that attaches to a smartphone. Both devices are designed to record, transcribe and analyze a user's day.
Apple's latest Apple Watch Series 12, unveiled in September, will have Siri Recap, which "ambiently" takes notes throughout the day and generates summaries of conversations. Another feature called Live Rewind can recap 15 seconds of a conversation via a text transcription.
Meta's popular smart glasses can take photos, capture video and record voice notes or reminders. Startups including Plaud and Pocket also developed card-sized note-taking devices, while Friend offers an AI necklace.
The devices have fueled concerns that they could erode privacy, by enabling covert recording without obtaining bystanders' consent and collecting sensitive data that's potentially accessible to others.
Amazon, Google and other makers of voice-activated smart speakers faced similar privacy concerns when their devices first hit the market, in some cases leading to lawsuits and regulatory fines.
But this new generation of AI devices is also testing the limits of privacy law.
Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated via a so-called "wake word" and sometimes stored recordings or sent audio to the cloud, some of these products can continuously listen, interpret speech, and extract its meaning without retaining the underlying audio. This capability has raised a largely untested question about whether that processing itself can amount to an unlawful interception.
"With new technology like this, my statement is always to embrace with caution," Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts' School of Engineering and a fellow at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said.
She added, "If I'm giving permission for myself to be recorded, or for everything I look at to be recorded, that doesn't mean everybody else around you has given that consent."
The gray area
Apple and Amazon appear to have sidestepped some of the privacy concerns that dogged earlier voice assistants.
Apple says the feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers, or involve human review. Amazon has said it doesn't store audio from Bee devices, and conversations are processed in a secure environment "where no one, including Amazon, can access your data."
But that may not resolve the legal question.
Many state wiretap and eavesdropping laws are written around whether a private communication was intercepted or its contents were acquired — not simply whether a conventional audio recording was created.
Colin Zick, a privacy and data security attorney at Foley Hoag, said Apple appears to have learned from the first wave of litigation over voice assistants. But the new technology raises questions those earlier cases never had to answer: Can a system that is continuously listening, interpreting speech and turning it into a summary still amount to an interception if it never saves the underlying audio?
Some state laws define interception broadly. Massachusetts, for example, defines an intercepting device to include equipment capable of "transmitting, receiving, amplifying, or recording" a communication, while the "contents" of a communication can include its substance and meaning.
In Zick's view, a device that continuously receives speech and produces a written summary could potentially fall within that language even without retaining an audio file.
And in some states, the bigger legal risk may fall not on Apple, Amazon or other AI gadget makers but on the person wearing the device.
"A non-wearer did not buy the watch, agree to Apple's terms, or choose to have their conversation summarized in the app," Zick said.
Daniel Pi, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law, said New Hampshire's statute is broad enough that he believes the Watch's new audio-intelligence features would qualify as an interception. The law covers not only recordings, but the "aural or other acquisition" of the contents of a communication.
That could create an unusual situation in which an ordinary consumer turns on a feature built into a mainstream device and, at least technically, runs afoul of state law by using it during a private conversation without everyone's consent.
Pi said a user in New Hampshire could potentially face civil or criminal liability for doing so, though he stressed that the practical risk of prosecution is far lower. It could be difficult to know whether someone had the feature enabled in the first place, and he said he would be surprised to see prosecutors pursue cases involving a bare statutory violation where no one was harmed.
The legal questions are also different from those raised by earlier smart speakers and voice assistants. Those cases often centered on devices mistakenly activating or capturing speech that was not intended as a command. Here, the feature is designed to acquire and interpret the substance of a conversation — and the user has deliberately opted in.
That changes the analysis, Pi said, and could also shift responsibility toward the wearer rather than the technology company itself.
The bystanders
The broader privacy concern extends beyond who is legally responsible.
Michael Stokes, a former CIA officer and senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, said the bigger shift is that people can be swept into AI-powered surveillance without owning or knowingly interacting with the device doing the collecting.
"I think the bystander problem is really the concern I have — that you can be surveilled without owning the technology," Stokes said.
He pointed to the growing number of cameras, microphones, and sensors embedded in consumer devices, from smart glasses to watches and AI recorders. The difference now, he said, is that AI can rapidly interpret what those devices collect and draw meaning from far larger volumes of information than earlier generations of consumer technology.
For Stokes, that makes the Apple Watch part of a much larger change in the privacy landscape. During his time at the CIA, he helped develop the concept of ubiquitous technical surveillance, describing a world in which everyday devices continuously generate information that can reveal identities, locations, and associations.
The concern is not simply that more data can be collected, he said, but that the cost of making sense of it has fallen dramatically.
In the past, Stokes said, intelligence collection could require thousands of hours of work to gather, sort and analyze information about a person. AI increasingly automates that process, making it cheaper and easier to extract useful information from data that may have been gathered incidentally.
That creates a new kind of exposure for people who never opted into the technology in the first place — whether it is a private conversation picked up by a nearby wearable or information collected by a device they do not own.
"We no longer have these pockets of small privacy that we thought we did in the past," Stokes said.
Aida Baradari, founder of the startup Deveillance, is trying to give some control back to people worried about being recorded without their consent.
The company created a hockey puck-shaped gadget, called the Spectre I, that uses AI to scan for nearby devices and sends out "adversarial signals" that scramble a person's speech before microphones can process it.
Baradari said she watched as more AI wearables hit the market and felt users should have a greater say in how they interact with them.
"We need to be able to use technology while not giving up our core values or rights," she said.

articles.title: Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely
articles.text:
Hedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.
Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.
"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday.
"It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."
Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
Hedge fund assets swell
With gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.
In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.
But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil.
That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF.
"The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.
Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt.
Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19.
Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.
Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.
Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

By contrast, exports of preparations of milk, cereals, flour, and starch fell (-16.3%); aircraft and parts (-72.5%); crude oil (-100.0%); and mechanical machinery and equipment (-9.0%). articles.title: Nhân viên tang lễ dùng kìm nhổ răng vàng của 250 thi thể, trộm 8 kg vàng cùng trang sức quý giá
articles.text:
Nhân viên tang lễ dùng kìm nhổ răng vàng của 250 thi thể, trộm 8 kg vàng cùng trang sức quý giá
Trong 11 năm làm việc tại một nghĩa trang ở Đức, người đàn ông 63 tuổi bị cáo buộc lấy trộm vàng từ răng của ít nhất 250 thi thể, chiếm đoạt trang sức và đồng hồ đắt tiền. Ông ta cùng người vợ ly thân dùng số tiền này để mua những tài sản giá trị.
- 16-10-2026Phát hiện láng giềng Việt Nam đang gom vàng với tốc độ chưa từng có: Nhập hơn 1.000 tấn vàng trong 8 tháng, dự trữ lên gần 2.400 tấn
- 14-10-2026Nóng: Phi công phát tín hiệu khẩn "Squawk 7500", chiếc Boeing 787 khổng lồ vội vàng bẻ lái, lực lượng rà phá bom mìn xuất hiện ngay lập tức trên sân bay
- 12-10-2026Tịch thu "3 quả trứng vàng" nặng 1,29 kg, trị giá hơn 4,5 tỷ đồng ngay tại sân bay
- 10-10-2026Cuốc đất trúng 5 thỏi vàng trị giá 20 tỷ đồng, người đàn ông nhận cái kết bất ngờ
Một nhân viên tang lễ ở Đức đã lợi dụng công việc để trộm vàng từ răng người chết, đồng thời lấy cắp trang sức và đồng hồ trong quan tài. Trong khoảng 11 năm, người này đã nhắm vào ít nhất 250 thi thể, lấy đi tổng cộng khoảng 8 kg kim loại quý, trị giá 250.000 euro (khoảng 7,2 tỷ đồng).
Người đàn ông 63 tuổi, được xác định danh tính là Karl-Heinz K., làm việc tại một nghĩa trang ở bang Baden-Württemberg, Đức. Từ năm 2013 đến năm 2024, ông ta lợi dụng vị trí công việc để lấy trộm tài sản của những người đã khuất trước khi họ được an táng hoặc hỏa táng.
Theo hồ sơ điều tra, Karl-Heinz K. sử dụng những dụng cụ như kìm để nhổ răng vàng khỏi miệng các thi thể. Sau đó, ông ta dùng búa đập vỡ những chiếc răng này nhằm lấy phần vàng bên trong.
Không dừng lại ở đó, người đàn ông còn lấy trộm trang sức cùng nhiều món đồ có giá trị được đặt trong quan tài.
Trong suốt 11 năm, hành vi của Karl-Heinz K. được cho là đã ảnh hưởng đến ít nhất 250 thi thể. Tổng khối lượng kim loại quý bị chiếm đoạt lên tới khoảng 8 kg, với giá trị ước tính 250.000 euro.
Người vợ đã ly thân của ông ta, Simone, cũng tham gia vào vụ việc. Người phụ nữ có nhiệm vụ mang số vàng và trang sức trộm được đi bán để thu tiền.
Tại tòa, Simone thừa nhận cuộc sống của hai người ngày càng xa hoa nhờ số tài sản này. Những chiếc xe họ sở hữu ngày càng đắt tiền, nhà ở cũng được đổi sang những căn lớn hơn. Cặp đôi thậm chí còn mua vé năm hạng VIP của công viên giải trí nổi tiếng Europa-Park.
Ngày 14, Tòa án khu vực Freiburg tuyên phạt Karl-Heinz K. 2 năm 6 tháng tù giam về các tội trộm cắp và xúc phạm thi thể. Người vợ Simone bị tuyên phạt 18 tháng tù nhưng cho hưởng án treo.
Ngoài hành vi trộm cắp, Karl-Heinz K. còn bị phát hiện từng tự ý chụp ảnh thi thể Dana Walleser, một phụ nữ 46 tuổi bị sát hại dã man, rồi gửi những bức ảnh này cho bạn bè qua ứng dụng WhatsApp.
Hành động này khiến gia đình nạn nhân vô cùng phẫn nộ khi biết rằng ngay cả sau khi qua đời, người thân của họ vẫn bị xâm phạm quyền riêng tư và phẩm giá. Corina Apachite, 48 tuổi, chị gái của Dana, đau đớn cho biết em gái mình ngay cả khi đã chết vẫn không thoát khỏi bạo lực do đàn ông gây ra.
Tòa án yêu cầu Karl-Heinz K. bồi thường 2.000 euro (khoảng 53 triệu đồng) cho gia đình nạn nhân vì tổn thất tinh thần. Tuy nhiên, người thân của Dana cho rằng mức bồi thường và hình phạt vẫn quá nhẹ, đồng thời bày tỏ sự thất vọng trước phán quyết.
Nguồn: ETtoday

articles.title: Nam nghệ sĩ đình đám bỏ showbiz đi bán quán nhậu ở đường Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh, giúp vợ NSND thăng tiến
articles.text:
Nam nghệ sĩ đình đám bỏ showbiz đi bán quán nhậu ở đường Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh, giúp vợ NSND thăng tiến
Tài tử lừng lẫy màn ảnh Việt này nay đã hoàn toàn rời xa showbiz.
- 16-10-2026Nam nghệ sĩ đình đám có nguy cơ mất trắng 271 tỷ đồng
- 15-10-2026Nam nghệ sĩ U60 sang Mỹ được "thuê" làm shipper liền than: Khổ ghê!
- 14-10-2026Nam nghệ sĩ đình đám bán loa đài ở đường Kim Giang, Hà Nội
Từ tài tử màn bạc đến ông chủ quán nhậu, chọn rời ánh hào quang khi đang nổi tiếng
Lê Tuấn Anh sinh năm 1968. Anh được xếp vào một trong 3 tài tử nổi tiếng nhất của dòng phim "mỳ ăn liền" thập niên 1990 cùng với Lý Hùng và Lê Công Tuấn Anh.
Nam diễn viên gây thương nhớ cho khán giả qua những vai diễn mang màu sắc phong trần, lãng tử, đôi khi phản diện. Trong số các tác phẩm gắn với tên tuổi của anh có Lệnh truy nã, Hải đường trắng, Công tử Bạc Liêu và Gió qua miền tối sáng.
Thời kỳ đỉnh cao, Lê Tuấn Anh từng nhận mức cát-xê 30 triệu đồng cho một bộ phim điện ảnh. Đây là khoản thù lao đáng mơ ước trong bối cảnh lúc bấy giờ, thậm chí đủ để mua một căn nhà.
Tuy nhiên, khi đang nổi đình nổi đám, Lê Tuấn Anh lại bất ngờ quyết định từ giã nghiệp diễn khi chưa đầy 30 tuổi. Vai Quang trong phim Gió qua miền tối sáng được nhắc đến như một trong những vai diễn cuối cùng của anh trước khi rời xa màn ảnh.
Sau đó, dù nhận được nhiều lời mời tham gia các dự án nghệ thuật, nam tài tử vẫn không mặn mà trở lại. Thay vì tiếp tục tận dụng sức hút của một ngôi sao nổi tiếng, anh chuyển hướng sang kinh doanh.
Sau khi kết hôn với Hồng Vân, Lê Tuấn Anh mở nhà hàng Ngã Ba Sông trên đường Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh, TP.HCM, còn Hồng Vân mở Sân khấu kịch Phú Nhuận. Quán nằm ở vị trí ven sông Sài Gòn, nổi tiếng từ nhiều năm trước là điểm hội ngộ quen thuộc của bạn bè nghệ sĩ và thực khách yêu thích ẩm thực dân dã, đặc biệt là các món nhậu như da heo chiên giòn.
Lê Tuấn Anh vừa kinh doanh, vừa lo chu toàn gia đình để vợ toàn tâm toàn ý theo đuổi nghệ thuật. Anh nhiều lần dùng nguồn thu từ nhà hàng để bù đắp các khoản chi phí cho sân khấu của Hồng Vân. Chính sự đồng hành âm thầm của chồng đã giúp NSND Hồng Vân ngày càng thăng hoa trong nghệ thuật.
Tuy vậy, sau nhiều năm kinh doanh, quán của Lê Tuấn Anh đã đóng cửa để anh chuyển hướng sang các công việc khác và tập trung cho gia đình.
Chuyện tình đẹp thành giai thoại của showbiz, lùi về phía sau để vợ tỏa sáng
Bên cạnh sự nghiệp điện ảnh nhiều thành công, cuộc hôn nhân của Lê Tuấn Anh với NSND Hồng Vân cũng là một trong những chuyện tình đẹp bậc nhất của showbiz Việt.
Hai người quen nhau khi còn là sinh viên Trường Cao đẳng Nghệ thuật - Sân khấu TP.HCM. Tình cảm nảy nở từ những ngày cùng theo đuổi nghệ thuật, nhưng một hiểu lầm thời trẻ khiến họ chia tay. Hồng Vân từng kể rằng cô nhìn thấy Lê Tuấn Anh chở một cô gái khác và quyết định chấm dứt mối quan hệ khi chưa nghe anh giải thích.
Sau cuộc chia tay ấy, mỗi người bước vào một mối quan hệ riêng. Hồng Vân kết hôn với một kiến trúc sư, còn Lê Tuấn Anh từng gắn bó với một nữ ca sĩ nổi tiếng. Nhưng cuộc hôn nhân đầu tiên của cả hai đều không đi đến cuối cùng. Sau khoảng 10 năm xa cách, họ gặp lại, nhận ra tình cảm vẫn còn và quyết định nối lại duyên xưa.
Năm 2003, Hồng Vân và Lê Tuấn Anh tổ chức đám cưới. Họ từng trải qua nhiều ngã rẽ trước khi trở về bên nhau. Lê Tuấn Anh chấp nhận hoàn cảnh riêng của vợ, yêu thương hai con riêng của chị là Xí Ngầu và Trê Phi như con ruột. Sau đó, gia đình đón thêm con gái chung Ngọc Châu, thường được gọi thân mật là Bí Ngô.
Sau khi kết hôn, trong khi Hồng Vân tiếp tục hoạt động nghệ thuật, phát triển sân khấu kịch và tham gia các dự án phim ảnh, Lê Tuấn Anh chủ động lùi về phía sau. Anh tập trung kinh doanh, chăm lo gia đình và hỗ trợ vợ trong những giai đoạn công việc gặp khó khăn.
NSND Hồng Vân từng chia sẻ rằng sự nghiệp của cô có đóng góp đáng kể từ chồng. Lê Tuấn Anh không chỉ là chỗ dựa tinh thần mà còn tư vấn công việc, hỗ trợ tài chính để vợ theo đuổi những dự án nghệ thuật. Sự hy sinh ấy giúp Hồng Vân có thể dành nhiều tâm sức cho hoạt động biểu diễn, đào tạo diễn viên và phát triển sân khấu riêng.
Hiện tại, vợ chồng Lê Tuấn Anh - Hồng Vân có cuộc sống kín tiếng. Họ sở hữu một biệt thự sang trọng tại trung tâm TP.HCM. Cơ ngơi này mang phong cách hiện đại, song vẫn tạo cảm giác ấm áp nhờ không gian sân vườn rộng mở ở cả phía trước lẫn phía sau. Khoảng sân trước được chăm sóc tỉ mỉ với nhiều loại cây ăn trái như khế, roi xen lẫn cây cảnh, non bộ và các tiểu cảnh hài hòa, mang đến bầu không khí xanh mát, dễ chịu.
Ngoài ra, gia đình Lê Tuấn Anh còn có một biệt thự rộng lớn tại Vũng Tàu cũ (nay là TP.HCM). Nơi đây có không gian sân vườn, ao cá và nhiều cây trái do chính anh thiết kế và xây dựng. Biệt thự này từng khiến các đồng nghiệp như MC Quyền Linh phải thốt lên rằng giống như "một khu du lịch thu nhỏ".
Ở tuổi U60, Lê Tuấn Anh lựa chọn cuộc sống ít phô trương, không chạy theo sự chú ý của công chúng. Anh dành thời gian tận hưởng cuộc sống, chăm sóc gia đình. Nam nghệ sĩ thường sang Mỹ thăm con cháu, thỉnh thoảng lại lên đường trải nghiệm những chuyến đi.

articles.title: Nàng Mona Lisa là ai?
articles.text:
Nàng Mona Lisa là ai?
Danh tính thực sự của người phụ nữ đã trở thành một đề tài bàn tán suốt nhiều thế kỷ.
- 15-10-2026Thứ đáng sợ trong những viên thuốc mua theo quảng cáo: Người bệnh không biết mình đang đưa gì vào cơ thể dù nhớ rất rõ người quảng cáo là ai
- 11-10-2026Người giữ kỷ lục nín thở lâu nhất thế giới là ai?
- 11-10-2026Người đầu tiên chơi Ai Là Triệu Phú Việt Nam không mang quốc tịch Việt Nam, vẫn ẵm 40 triệu, là ai?
Trong suốt hơn 500 năm qua, bức họa Mona Lisa của thiên tài Leonardo da Vinci vẫn luôn là kiệt tác nghệ thuật nổi tiếng và thu hút nhiều sự chú ý nhất trên thế giới. Ngồi trước tác phẩm đặt tại bảo tàng Louvre (Pháp), hàng triệu du khách mỗi năm không khỏi tự hỏi về người phụ nữ có nụ cười bí ẩn trong tranh.
Giả thuyết phổ biến nhất: Lisa Gherardini
Theo nhận định của hầu hết các nhà nghiên cứu nghệ thuật và lịch sử, người mẫu trong bức tranh chính là Lisa Gherardini (sinh năm 1479), một người phụ nữ quý tộc thuộc dòng họ Gherardini ở Florence và Chianti (Ý).
Năm 15 tuổi, bà kết hôn với Francesco del Giocondo, một thương gia buôn tơ lụa giàu có. Chính vì vậy, bức tranh còn có tên gọi khác trong tiếng Ý là La Gioconda (hoặc La Joconde trong tiếng Pháp), mang ý nghĩa vừa là "vợ của Giocondo", vừa biểu thị sự vui vẻ, hạnh phúc. Nhiều tài liệu lịch sử chỉ ra rằng Francesco del Giocondo đã đặt hàng Leonardo da Vinci vẽ chân dung vợ mình vào khoảng năm 1503 để kỷ niệm việc mua nhà mới hoặc nhân dịp ra đời của người con thứ hai.
Năm 2005, một phát hiện quan trọng tại Thư viện Đại học Heidelberg (Đức) đã củng cố mạnh mẽ cho giả thuyết này. Tiến sĩ Armin Schlatter đã tìm thấy một ghi chú bằng tay bên lề cuốn sách cổ của Agostino Vespucci, một quan chức người Florence và là bạn của Leonardo da Vinci.
Trong ghi chú từ tháng 10 năm 1503, Vespucci đã so sánh Leonardo với họa sĩ cổ đại Apelles và đề cập rằng Leonardo đang thực hiện bức chân dung về "Lisa del Giocondo". Bằng chứng này gần như đã khép lại những nghi vấn kéo dài nhiều thế kỷ về danh tính nguyên mẫu.
Những giả thuyết kỳ lạ và hấp dẫn khác
Trước khi ghi chú của Vespucci được xác minh, có rất nhiều giả thuyết mang tính suy đoán được đưa ra. Một số nhà nghiên cứu dùng phân tích kỹ thuật số để so sánh đường nét khuôn mặt của Mona Lisa với bức chân dung tự họa của Leonardo và cho rằng hai khuôn mặt có sự trùng khớp đáng kinh ngạc, từ đó đưa ra giả thuyết danh họa đã vẽ chính mình dưới dạng nữ giới.
Bên cạnh đó, cũng có ý kiến cho rằng nhân vật trong tranh là Caterina Sforza (một nữ chúa xứ Forlì), Pacifica Brandani (mình tình của Giuliano de' Medici), người mẹ quá cố Caterina của họa sĩ, hoặc thậm chí là Salai - học trò kiêm người tình lâu năm của Leonardo.
Tại sao danh tính nàng lại trở thành ẩn số?
Sở dĩ có nhiều tranh cãi là do Leonardo da Vinci chưa bao giờ giao lại bức tranh cho Francesco del Giocondo. Ông mang theo bức họa bên mình suốt những năm tháng còn lại của cuộc đời, liên tục chỉnh sửa cho đến khi qua đời tại Pháp vào năm 1519.
Bức tranh sau đó được Vua François I của Pháp mua lại và trở thành tài sản của Hoàng gia Pháp. Vì tác phẩm không gắn kèm nhãn tên và chưa từng bàn giao cho gia đình Giocondo, danh tính thực sự của người phụ nữ đã trở thành một đề tài bàn tán suốt nhiều thế kỷ.
Dù khoa học và lịch sử ngày nay đã nghiêng mạnh về phương án Lisa Gherardini, nét quyến rũ của Mona Lisa vẫn không giảm bớt. Chính nụ cười mờ ảo cùng đôi mắt như biết theo dõi người xem của bà - sản phẩm từ kỹ thuật tô màu sfumato bậc thầy của Leonardo - mới là điều biến người phụ nữ quý tộc Florence này trở thành biểu tượng vĩnh cửu của nghệ thuật nhân loại.

articles.title: Nhan sắc thời thiếu nữ của Hoa hậu Hà Kiều Anh
articles.text:
Nhan sắc thời thiếu nữ của Hoa hậu Hà Kiều Anh
Những bức ảnh hiếm hé lộ nhan sắc thời trẻ của Hoa hậu Hà Kiều Anh với gương mặt thanh tú, mái tóc đen dày và vẻ đẹp dịu dàng, nền nã.
- 17-10-2026Người đàn ông Phương Oanh gọi là “hoa hậu thân thiện”: Đồng nghiệp tung hô “giàu nhất miền Bắc”, chủ loạt bất động sản khủng
- 17-10-2026Top 3 Hoa hậu Việt Nam 2004: Người trở thành tiến sĩ, người sống bí ẩn
- 17-10-2026Chân dung con gái diệu 19 tuổi của Hoa hậu đã ly thân chồng đại gia
Mới đây, nhà báo Lê Quang Thanh Tâm chia sẻ những bức ảnh thời trẻ của Hoa hậu Hà Kiều Anh . Đây là những tấm ảnh trong kho tư liệu của báo Màn ảnh Sân khấu.
Trong loạt ảnh được chia sẻ, Hà Kiều Anh mang vẻ đẹp nền nã, giản dị, phù hợp với thị hiếu thẩm mỹ đương thời. Cô sở hữu mái tóc đen dày, gương mặt thanh tú, đôi mắt sáng và phong thái nữ tính. Không cần tạo hình cầu kỳ, người đẹp vẫn gây chú ý nhờ nét trẻ trung và thần thái tự nhiên trước ống kính.
“Hà Kiều Anh của ngày ấy, cô gái trẻ với nét đẹp trong sáng và ánh mắt đầy sức sống, vẫn hiện diện qua những bức ảnh lưu trữ”, nhà báo Lê Quang Thanh Tâm nhận xét.
Theo anh, việc lưu giữ và giới thiệu lại những tư liệu hình ảnh này cũng là cách gìn giữ ký ức văn hóa nghệ thuật bởi đằng sau mỗi khuôn hình không chỉ là một nhan sắc, mà còn là câu chuyện về tuổi trẻ, những bước khởi đầu và một thời đã qua.
Hà Kiều Anh sinh năm 1976 tại Hà Nội, theo mẹ vào TP.HCM sinh sống từ nhỏ. Năm 1992, khi mới 16 tuổi, cô đăng quang Hoa hậu Việt Nam, khi đó cuộc thi mang tên Hoa hậu báo Tiền Phong.
Thời điểm dự thi, Hà Kiều Anh là sinh viên năm thứ nhất khoa Thanh nhạc của Nhạc viện TP.HCM. Danh hiệu hoa hậu đưa cô trở thành một trong những gương mặt được chú ý của làng giải trí Việt Nam những năm 1990.
Trước khi đăng quang, Hà Kiều Anh đã có cơ hội tham gia điện ảnh. Cuối năm 1991 và đầu năm 1992, cô góp mặt trong bộ phim Người tình trong mơ của đạo diễn Trần Phương, diễn cùng các ngôi sao như Lê Tuấn Anh và Thu Hà.
Trong phim, Hà Kiều Anh đảm nhận vai một nữ sinh viên. Tác phẩm có những cảnh quay nghệ thuật với hình ảnh nhân vật làm mẫu cho họa sĩ trên đảo ở Nha Trang. Đây là trải nghiệm đáng nhớ của người đẹp khi bước vào môi trường điện ảnh.
Sau này, cô tiếp tục tham gia một số bộ phim như Ván cờ tình yêu, Đẻ mướn, Áo lụa Hà Đông, Lối sống sai lầm... Dù không hoạt động điện ảnh liên tục, Hà Kiều Anh vẫn duy trì sự hiện diện trong lĩnh vực giải trí, đồng thời tham gia các sự kiện văn hóa và chương trình liên quan đến sắc đẹp.
Sau nhiều năm hoạt động nghệ thuật, Hà Kiều Anh chuyển hướng sang kinh doanh, trong đó có lĩnh vực làm đẹp. Cô thỉnh thoảng xuất hiện tại các sự kiện giải trí, tham gia ban giám khảo những cuộc thi nhan sắc và duy trì sự quan tâm của công chúng.
Năm 2007, Hà Kiều Anh kết hôn với doanh nhân Huỳnh Trung Nam sau một lần đổ vỡ. Vợ chồng Hà Kiều Anh có 3 người con: Vương Khang, Vương Khôi và Huỳnh Vian. Trong nhà hoa hậu không tồn tại khái niệm “con chung, con riêng”. Bố mẹ chăm lo, yêu thương các con đồng đều.
Hiện người đẹp sinh năm 1976 sống trong biệt thự sân vườn rộng khoảng 450m² tại TP.HCM, nằm ven sông Sài Gòn. Khác với nhiều nghệ sĩ kín tiếng, Hà Kiều Anh khá thoải mái chia sẻ cuộc sống gia đình trên mạng xã hội. Những chuyến du lịch, khoảnh khắc đời thường bên chồng con thường xuyên được cô cập nhật, cho thấy một cuộc sống viên mãn, hạnh phúc.
